request: Why doesn't a crate slide down a ramp?

commands.speak: A crate sits on a ramp and doesn't slide. Gravity pulls on it all the time, so what holds it still? Every force on it, one at a time.
Gravity pulls straight down, however the ramp tilts.
Split it in two: one part presses the crate into the ramp, the other pulls it down along the slope.
The ramp pushes back against the first part — the normal force, at a right angle to the surface.
Friction pulls up the slope, matching the second part exactly. Every force has a partner, so nothing moves.
Tilt the ramp steeper, and more of the weight points downhill — until friction cannot keep up, and the crate slides.
Friction can only grow so far: Guillaume Amontons found in 1699 that its limit is a fixed fraction of the normal force.

quiz.question: The ramp is made steeper. What happens to the normal force?
quiz.right: It shrinks: on a steeper ramp less of the weight presses into the surface, so the ramp pushes back less.

details.force_along: The downhill part of the weight is $mg\sin\theta$: at $\theta = 30°$, half the weight.
details.force_into: The part pressing into the ramp is $mg\cos\theta$ — it shrinks as the ramp gets steeper.
details.force_friction: Static friction grows to match the downhill pull, up to a limit $f \le \mu N$, where $\mu$ depends on the two surfaces. The crate slides when $\tan\theta > \mu$.

request: Why is benzene so stable?

commands.speak: Benzene is one of chemistry's most stable rings, and its usual drawing hides why. Six carbons, one at each corner, each with a hydrogen.
The usual sketch alternates single and double bonds. Double bonds are shorter, so this ring should have long sides and short sides.
But measured, all six bonds are exactly the same length — in between a single and a double.
The six shared electrons aren't parked in three bonds. They spread around the whole ring, which is why many chemists draw a circle inside instead.
Spreading out lowers their energy. Adding hydrogen to benzene releases far less heat than three ordinary double bonds would — that missing energy is the extra stability.
August Kekulé said the ring shape came to him in 1865, in a daydream of a snake biting its own tail.

quiz.question: Why are all six bonds in benzene the same length?
choices: The electrons are shared around the whole ring
The double bonds swap places too fast to see
Carbon can only form single bonds
quiz.right: The electrons are shared around the whole ring, so every bond is the same: part single, part double.

request: Why do proteins fold into helices and sheets?

commands.speak: Why does almost every protein fold into the same two shapes, helices and sheets? This chain, read from its N end, starts with a helix.
Then it stretches out flat into beta strands, drawn as arrows: two here, with a tight turn between them.
A protein works by its shape, and these two are the bricks most shapes are built from.
The puzzle: chains are strung from twenty kinds of amino acid in endless orders, yet these same two shapes turn up nearly everywhere.
Unroll a helix into its amino acids. Each has the same backbone: an oxygen on one side, an N–H hydrogen on the other.
In a helix, the oxygen of amino acid one grabs the hydrogen of amino acid five: a hydrogen bond, four places along.
Two grabs six, three grabs seven, and so on. Each bond tugs the chain round, one turn for every three point six amino acids.
Those bonds belong to the backbone, which every amino acid has. So almost any sequence can wind into a helix.
A strand is the opposite: stretched nearly straight, so its oxygens and hydrogens point out sideways instead of along the chain.
Lay a second strand beside it, running the other way, and the same bonds join them like ladder rungs: a flat sheet.
That is what this tight turn is for: the chain folds back, and its two strands lie side by side and pair up.
Linus Pauling worked out the alpha helix in 1951 from the geometry of the backbone alone.
You can feel the difference: the keratin in hair is mostly helices, which can stretch, and silk is mostly sheets, already stretched out.

quiz.question: What holds an alpha helix together?
choices: Hydrogen bonds along the backbone, four amino acids apart
Bonds to a second protein chain
quiz.right: Hydrogen bonds along the backbone: each oxygen grabs the hydrogen four amino acids ahead, and every amino acid has that backbone.

request: Why isn't methane flat?

commands.speak: What shape is a methane molecule, and why? Textbooks often draw it as a flat cross with right angles, but the real molecule isn't flat. Carbon sits in the middle.
Its four bonds push each other as far apart as they can — and in three dimensions, as far apart as possible is the corners of a tetrahedron.
Every angle between two bonds is a hundred and nine and a half degrees — wider than a flat cross allows.
Van 't Hoff predicted this shape in 1874, long before anyone could see a molecule.
Walk around it: a different hydrogen comes to the front, and the shape is the same from every side.
And this shape is where water's bend and ammonia's pyramid come from: take hydrogens away, and the electron pairs left behind still point to the same four corners.

quiz.question: Why do methane's bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron?
choices: They repel, and that spreads them furthest apart
quiz.right: They repel: four bonds get furthest apart at a tetrahedron's corners, 109.5° from each other.

request: What does the acetyl group on aspirin actually do?

commands.speak: Aspirin eases pain and thins the blood for days, and it does both with one small piece of its molecule. Every bare corner here is a carbon.
The red letters are oxygens: an acid group along the bottom, and at the upper right, the piece that does the work.
That piece is an acetyl group: two carbons and an oxygen, hooked onto the ring through one more oxygen.
Without it, the rest is salicylic acid, the old willow-bark remedy for pain, and hard on the stomach.
Aspirin's target is an enzyme called COX. Inside it runs a narrow channel.
A fat from our cell walls, arachidonic acid, is what normally slides in.
COX turns it into prostaglandins: signals for pain, for fever, and in platelets, for clotting.
Now aspirin arrives, and slips into the same channel.
It hands its acetyl group to the enzyme, which binds it for good, right inside the channel. The plug is now part of COX.
The fat can no longer get in. No prostaglandins: less pain, less fever, and platelets that stop clumping.
Aspirin itself is broken down within an hour or so. The plug stays.
Ibuprofen blocks the same channel, but only by sitting in it. It lets go, so its effect fades within hours.
Most cells just build new COX. Platelets can't: they have no nucleus. So one aspirin disables a platelet for its whole life, eight to ten days.
That is why a daily 75-milligram tablet guards the heart, and why surgeons ask you to stop aspirin a week before an operation.
Aspirin was sold from 1899, yet nobody knew how it worked until John Vane showed it in 1971. It won him a Nobel Prize.

quiz.question: Why does one aspirin affect platelets for about a week?
choices: Aspirin stays in the blood all week
The acetyl group wears off slowly
quiz.right: Platelets have no nucleus, so they cannot replace the COX that aspirin disabled; clotting recovers only as new platelets are made.

request: What happens to price and quantity when demand shifts right?

commands.speak: What happens to a market when demand shifts right? Take roses in one city: how many the florists sell a day, and the price of one rose.
Demand slopes down: the cheaper a rose, the more of them people buy.
Supply slopes up: at a higher price, it pays growers and florists to bring more roses in.
In an ordinary week they meet here: two dollars a rose, and a thousand roses a day.
Then Valentine's week arrives. Here is a copy of demand, for now lying exactly on the old one.
At every price, buyers now want four hundred more roses a day, so the whole demand curve slides right.
The tempting guess: four hundred more roses sold, out to here, still at two dollars each.
But at two dollars, florists still offer only a thousand. Four hundred buyers find nothing, and the price gets bid up.
The market settles here instead: about two dollars thirty-five a rose, and twelve hundred sold.
Only half the extra demand gets served. The higher price does two jobs: it talks some buyers out of it, and brings more roses in.
How it splits depends on supply. Most roses sold in America are grown in Colombia and Ecuador, planted months ahead, so a week's notice adds few.
With supply this steep, the same jump in demand turns almost entirely into price: barely more roses, each one much dearer.
So the Valentine's price rise is not greed stepping in. It is how a market shares out the roses it has, and calls for more.

quiz.question: Suppose not one extra rose could reach the city in Valentine's week. What does the jump in demand do?
quiz.right: Only the price rises: with the roses fixed at a thousand, the price must climb until buyers want exactly the roses there are.

request: How does a decision tree choose between surgery and medication?

commands.speak: A decision tree picks a treatment when every option is a gamble. Here, the same disease can be operated on or treated with tablets.
The square is the choice we make. Choose surgery, and we reach a circle: from here on, chance decides.
Eighty-five times in a hundred the operation works, and the patient can expect nine quality-adjusted life years.
Fifteen times in a hundred there is a serious complication, and only three.
Medication is a gamble too, only a milder one.
Seven in ten are well controlled, at eight QALYs; the other three in ten get six.
Compare the best cases and surgery wins, nine to eight.
Compare the worst cases and medication wins, six to three. Neither comparison is the answer.
Instead, fold the tree back: weight each ending by its chance. Nine times 0.85 plus three times 0.15 gives surgery 8.1 expected QALYs.
Eight times 0.7 plus six times 0.3 gives medication 7.4.
Surgery, by 0.7 QALYs a patient, even though about one patient in seven ends up worse off than on tablets.
How safe is that verdict? Let the complication risk be p. Surgery keeps winning until p passes about 0.27.
So the question for the evidence is not the average risk, but whether it could plausibly be above one in four.
Costs fold back the same way. The difference in expected cost, over these 0.7 QALYs, is the price of each QALY gained.

quiz.question: The complication risk turns out to be 0.2, not 0.15. Which option does the tree now pick?
choices: It depends on the best case
quiz.right: Still surgery: nine times 0.8 plus three times 0.2 is 7.8, above medication's 7.4. The switch comes only past about 0.27.

request: What does 'QALYs gained' by a treatment actually measure?

commands.speak: Health technology assessment counts what a treatment does in QALYs gained. Here is what that number is. Time runs across; quality runs up, from zero, dead, to one, full health.
A patient has just been diagnosed. Without treatment, quality of life starts at 0.6, declines, and the patient dies after eight years.
Each year counts by its quality: a year at 0.6 is 0.6 of a healthy year. The area under the curve, 3.8 here, is the QALYs left.
With treatment, the first months are worse: side effects push quality down to 0.4. Then it rises to 0.7, and the patient lives twelve years.
That dip is a real loss, shaded red. For a few months the treated patient is worse off than the untreated one.
The green is the gain, and it comes in two kinds.
For the first eight years, better years: net of the red dip, almost one QALY.
After that, extra years. But they are lived at quality 0.5, so four extra years count as two QALYs, not four.
Together, about three QALYs gained: 6.75 with treatment against 3.8 without. Divide the extra cost by that area, and you have the price per QALY.
So a QALY gained is never just years added: easing pain for years can gain as much as extending life.
The name was coined in 1976 by the economists Richard Zeckhauser and Donald Shepard.

quiz.question: A drug adds four years of life, all lived at quality 0.25. How many QALYs does it add?
quiz.right: One: four years times 0.25. A QALY weighs every year by how good it is.

request: What do mitochondria actually do?

commands.speak: What do mitochondria actually do? They turn food into the one fuel a cell can spend, a molecule called ATP. Here is an animal cell.
The nucleus holds the instructions, but everything the cell does, building, moving, pumping, is paid for in ATP.
Follow one molecule of sugar, glucose, arriving from your last meal.
Out here in the cytoplasm, the cell can split it without any oxygen, and earn just two ATP.
The pieces then go into this bean-shaped compartment: a mitochondrion.
Inside, burned with oxygen all the way to carbon dioxide and water, the same glucose yields about thirty ATP.
Fifteen times as much. That gap is why you breathe: without oxygen, a cell is stuck with the two.
The trick is in its inner membrane, folded back and forth into ridges called cristae.
On those folds, electrons from food pass down a chain of proteins, pumping protons across the membrane like water behind a dam.
The protons flow back through a tiny turbine, ATP synthase, that really spins; each turn makes ATP. More folds hold more turbines.
A mitochondrion even has its own DNA: it descends from a bacterium that moved into another cell over a billion years ago.
So a cell that works hard carries many. In heart muscle, which never rests, mitochondria fill about a third of each cell.

quiz.question: The oxygen you breathe in: where does it end up?
choices: In the carbon dioxide you breathe out
In water, made in the mitochondria
quiz.right: In water: at the end of the chain, oxygen takes up the spent electrons with hydrogen. The carbon dioxide comes from the food.

request: How does a magnifying glass make things look bigger?

commands.speak: How does a magnifying glass make a letter look bigger, and where is the bigger letter? Here is the lens, edge-on.
Its focal length is ten centimetres: parallel light meets at F, ten centimetres out on either side.
Hold a small letter 7.5 centimetres away, just inside the focal length.
A ray leaving the top of the letter parallel to the axis is bent through the far F.
A ray through the centre of the lens goes straight on.
Past the lens these two rays spread apart. They never meet, so there is no picture on this side for a screen to catch.
But your eye can't know the rays were bent. It traces them straight back, to where they seem to come from.
They seem to come from here: an upright letter thirty centimetres behind the glass, four times as tall. A virtual image.
Four times as tall, but four times as far away: it fills the same angle as the letter itself, seen from 7.5 centimetres.
That is the trick. Your bare eye can't focus closer than about twenty-five centimetres, where the letter looks small.
The lens moves the image out past that limit, so you see the letter sharp as if from 7.5 centimetres: over three times bigger.
Slide the letter out to 8.5 centimetres: the image is now nearly seven times the letter's height, but 57 centimetres away.
Height over distance hardly changes. What magnifies is getting close; the lens only makes close focusable.
The near point creeps outward with age, which is why people past about forty start holding menus at arm's length.

quiz.question: A stronger magnifier has a shorter focal length. Why does it magnify more?
choices: It lets you hold the object closer and still see it sharp
It makes the image taller at the same distance
It lets more light into your eye
quiz.right: It lets you hold the object closer: a shorter focal length puts the letter nearer your eye while its image stays far enough away to focus.

request: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction without being used up?

commands.speak: How can a catalyst speed a reaction up a million-fold and come out unchanged? Energy runs up, the reaction's progress across.
Start with hydrogen peroxide, which breaks down into water and oxygen.
The products sit lower: breaking down releases energy. So why does a bottle of peroxide keep for months?
Because bonds must stretch and break before new ones form: first the molecules climb over this hump.
That climb is the activation energy. At room temperature only the rare molecule, jostled hard enough, gets over.
Heating would push more molecules over the same hump. A catalyst does something else.
It opens another route with a lower pass. Catalase in your blood is one, which is why peroxide fizzes on a cut.
The rate depends on the barrier exponentially: at room temperature, every 5.7 kilojoules per mole taken off makes it ten times faster.
So halving a barrier of eighty kilojoules to forty is seven of those steps: about ten million times faster.
What does not change is the drop from reactants to products. Same start, same finish, same energy released.
And the pass is just as much lower from the far side: the catalyst speeds the reverse reaction by the same factor.
So it can't change how much product you end up with, only how quickly you get there.
Catalase is among the fastest enzymes known: one molecule can break down millions of peroxide molecules every second.

quiz.question: A catalyst is added to a reaction already at equilibrium. What happens to the amount of product?
choices: Some product turns back into reactant
quiz.right: It stays the same: the lower pass speeds the forward and the reverse reaction alike, so the balance between them does not move.

request: Why does DNA pair A with T and C with G?

commands.speak: Why does DNA always pair A with T, and C with G? Because that rule lets a cell copy its DNA. Start with one strand.
A second strand winds around it. Each is a backbone of sugar and phosphate: the two rails of a twisted ladder.
The rungs are bases, one from each strand, meeting in the middle. There are four kinds: A, T, C and G.
Unroll a short stretch of the ladder. Along the top strand it reads A, T, G, C, C, A.
Across from every A sits a T, across from every G a C, and never anything else.
Size, first. A and G are big, with two rings; T and C are small, with one. Big with small always spans the same width.
Two big ones would bulge the ladder, two small ones pinch it. And A holds T by two hydrogen bonds, G holds C by three.
Now unzip the ladder. Those bonds are weak, so the strands part, and the bottom strand's letters are gone.
But nothing is lost: the top strand dictates every partner, so the cell rebuilds the missing strand letter for letter.
Watson and Crick saw this at once, and ended their 1953 paper coyly:
'It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism.'
So the pairing rule is a copying rule: each strand carries the other. That is how your three billion letters are copied at every cell division.

quiz.question: A sample of DNA is 30% A. What share is G?
quiz.right: Twenty per cent: every A has a T, so T is thirty too, and the remaining forty is split evenly between G and C.

request: What do a wave's wavelength and amplitude actually measure?

commands.speak: Two lengths describe a wave: its wavelength and its amplitude. Here they are for a sound, the note A, 440 hertz, from a speaker.
Sound is air squeezed and stretched in turn. Frozen for an instant: above the line, the air is squeezed; below it, stretched.
Wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next. For this note, seventy-eight centimetres.
Amplitude is how far a crest rises above still air: how hard the air is squeezed. That is what you hear as loudness.
Turn the volume up and only the amplitude grows. The crests stay seventy-eight centimetres apart: still the same note.
Why 78? Sound crosses air at 343 metres a second, and 440 crests leave the speaker each second.
Spread over 343 metres, that puts the crests 78 centimetres apart.
Play the A an octave up, 880 hertz: twice as many crests a second at the same speed, so they crowd in half as far apart.
Thirty-nine centimetres. The wave doesn't choose its wavelength: the air sets the speed, the source sets the frequency.
Across what you can hear, from 20 hertz to 20,000, the wavelength runs from seventeen metres down to under two centimetres.

quiz.question: You sing the same note, but louder. What happens to its wavelength?
quiz.right: It stays the same: loudness is amplitude, and the wavelength is fixed by the note's frequency and the speed of sound.

request: How much oxygen does burning methane use, and what comes out?

commands.speak: When natural gas burns, how much oxygen does it use, and what comes out? A first guess: methane plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water.
Count the hydrogens: four go in, inside methane, but only two come out, in one water.
Atoms are never made or destroyed, so add a second water: four hydrogens in, four out.
Now count oxygen. Two go in, but four come out: two in the carbon dioxide, and one in each water.
So each methane needs two oxygen molecules. That is the whole of balancing: counting until both sides agree.
Written out as chemists do, with a delta over the arrow for the heat that sets it going.
One carbon, four hydrogens and four oxygens on each side: the same atoms, only partnered differently.
Now weigh it, per mole: sixteen grams of methane burns with sixty-four grams of oxygen.
Out come forty-four grams of carbon dioxide and thirty-six of water: eighty grams in, eighty out.
The surprise is how small the fuel is. Four-fifths of what burns is oxygen, taken from the air.
So a kilogram of gas makes two and three-quarter kilograms of carbon dioxide: most of its weight is borrowed oxygen.
Antoine Lavoisier showed this in the 1770s by weighing reactions in sealed vessels: burning moves mass around, but never destroys it.

quiz.question: A stove burns 1 kg of methane. How much carbon dioxide comes out?
choices: Less than 1 kg: the gas burns away
quiz.right: About 2.75 kilograms: each carbon leaves with two oxygen atoms from the air, and those outweigh the methane.

request: Why does moving some things across a cell membrane cost energy and others not?

commands.speak: Why do some things cross a cell membrane for free, while others cost energy? First the membrane: a double sheet of fat molecules, oily in the middle.
Above it is the fluid outside a nerve cell, below it the cell's inside. Charged ions like potassium and sodium cannot slip through the oily core.
Potassium is crowded inside: about 140 millimolar, against only 5 outside.
A channel protein opens a watery pore through the fat.
So potassium leaks out through it, from crowded to sparse. That is diffusion: downhill, and random jostling pays for it.
Sodium is the other way round: about 145 outside, only 12 inside.
Yet this protein, a pump, pushes sodium out, toward the side that already has more.
That is uphill, like pumping water into a full tank, and every turn is paid for with ATP, the cell's energy currency.
Each ATP throws out three sodium ions and carries two potassium ions back in, against both gradients at once.
Stop the pump, and sodium seeps back in through small leaks. The difference shrinks, and the cell runs down.
Restart it, and the gradient is rebuilt. So the pump never rests: it keeps a battery charged.
And a nerve impulse spends that battery: sodium channels open and sodium rushes in, downhill, for free.
Jens Skou found this pump in crab nerves in 1957. Forty years later it won him a Nobel Prize.
So the cost depends on the direction, not the molecule: with the gradient is free, against it takes energy.

quiz.question: A cell moves a molecule from where there is less of it to where there is more. What must be doing it?
choices: Diffusion, if it is fast enough
quiz.right: A pump spending energy: diffusion only ever runs from more to less, so going the other way is uphill and needs ATP.

request: How are humans, chimps, mice, rats and chickens related?

commands.speak: How are these five animals related, and is a mouse closer kin to you or to a chicken? A tree of descent answers it.
The tempting picture is a ladder: chickens at the bottom, climbing through mice and chimps up to humans.
But evolution isn't a ladder. All five are alive today, and none of them descends from another.
Instead, every fork is a common ancestor whose descendants split into two lines. To compare two tips, trace both back to where they meet.
Human and chimp meet at the youngest fork.
Their lines split only six or seven million years ago.
Mouse and rat, likewise, share a recent rodent ancestor.
Now trace a mouse and a human back. They meet in an early mammal, around ninety million years ago.
The chicken's line joins theirs only at the root, over three hundred million years back.
So a mouse is far closer kin to you than to any chicken, however alike a mouse and a chicken may look beside you.
Forks spin freely, like a mobile. Swap human and chimp…
…and the tree says exactly the same thing. Read the forks, never the order of the names.
And no tip is more primitive: all five lines have been evolving for the same three hundred million years since the root.

quiz.question: Which pair shares the more recent common ancestor?
quiz.right: Mouse and human: their lines meet about ninety million years ago, while the chicken's joins only at the root, over three hundred million years ago.

request: What do sensitivity and specificity actually measure?

commands.speak: Sensitivity and specificity say how good a diagnostic test is, and they are easy to misread. Test a thousand people, and sort them two ways.
Two hundred of them really have the disease. The test catches 180: true positives.
It misses twenty: false negatives, sick people sent home reassured.
Of the 800 healthy people, 760 correctly test negative.
Forty test positive anyway: false positives, healthy people told they may be ill.
Sensitivity reads down the sick column: of those who have the disease, how many does the test catch? 180 of 200, 90 percent.
Specificity reads down the healthy column: of those without it, how many does it clear? 760 of 800, 95 percent.
Both are counted among people whose true state we already know. So they describe the test, whoever it is used on.
A patient holding a positive result asks the other question, reading across the row: of 220 positives, 180 are ill, 82 percent.
Use the same test where only 2 in 100 are ill, and that row turns: 18 true positives against 49 false, 27 percent.
Sensitivity and specificity have not moved. The row depends on how common the disease is; the columns do not.
The two terms come from Jacob Yerushalmy, who in 1947 used them to compare how well doctors read chest X-rays for tuberculosis.

quiz.question: The same test is used in a clinic where half the patients have the disease. What is its sensitivity?
quiz.right: Still 90 percent: sensitivity is counted only among the sick, so it does not depend on how many are sick. What changes is how often a positive is right.

request: Why do research projects almost always take longer than planned?

commands.speak: Why do research projects nearly always run late, even when planned with care? Here is a typical plan: twelve months, in four steps.
Two months for ethics approval, five to collect data, three to analyse, two to write up.
The team expects the real project to look exactly like the plan. Each step was estimated honestly, by people who know the work.
Then the ethics committee asks for changes, and recruiting patients runs slow. The first two steps take fourteen months instead of seven.
Nobody planned those delays, because a plan lists the steps as they go when they go right. The things that go wrong are not in the list.
Analysis turns up a coding error; the journal asks for revisions. Twenty-four months in all, double the plan.
Why don't the early steps make up for it? A step can finish a little early, but it can run very late. Delays add; they seldom cancel.
Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky named this the planning fallacy in 1979: we forecast from the plan, not from how such projects usually go.
In one study, students guessed they'd finish their thesis in about 34 days, and 49 at worst. They took about 55: later than their own worst case.
So the useful question isn't how long each of your steps will take. It's how long projects like yours have actually taken.

quiz.question: Your team wants a realistic time estimate. What helps most?
choices: Planning each step in more detail
Checking how long similar projects took
Asking each member for a careful guess
quiz.right: Similar projects: their real durations already include the delays nobody plans for, while more detail only makes the best case look surer.

request: Why does each extra worker add less than the one before?

commands.speak: Why does each extra worker add less than the one before? Economists call it diminishing returns. Take a bakery with one oven.
Hire bakers one by one, and the loaves per day climb — but the curve bends over.
If every baker added the same, output would climb on this straight line instead.
The first baker, alone, makes twenty-six loaves a day.
The next ones add nineteen, then fourteen, then eleven.
The fifth adds only eight.
Nobody got lazier. Each new baker shares the same oven and the same counter, so each has less to work with, and adds less.
Economists first saw this on farms: in 1815, David Ricardo and Thomas Malthus argued that more labour on the same land yields less and less.

quiz.question: The bakery swaps its oven for one twice the size. What happens to the fifth baker's extra loaves?
quiz.right: They rise: the returns diminish because the oven is fixed, so a bigger oven gives every extra baker more to work with.

request: How does a Markov model follow patients through the years?

commands.speak: A Markov model follows a group of patients over years, as illness comes, goes and returns. First, it sorts everyone into a few health states.
Each cycle, here a year, people may move. Ten percent of the well fall sick.
Thirty percent of the sick recover.
And some die: five percent of the sick each year, one percent of the well.
Everyone else stays put. The loops hold what's left, so each state's arrows add up to one.
Dead has no way out. It is absorbing, and in the end the whole cohort arrives there.
Now run it. Start a thousand people, all well.
In the first cycle, a hundred fall sick and ten die.
That leaves 890 well, 100 sick, 10 dead.
In the second cycle the sick feed back: thirty of them recover.
Now 822 well, 154 sick, 24 dead.
Weight each state by its quality, say 0.9 well and 0.5 sick, and every cycle yields QALYs: 851 in the first year.
Run it for a lifetime, discounting later years, at 3.5 percent in England. Rerun with a drug that lowers these ten percent, and the difference is the QALYs gained.
The catch is the model's lack of memory. Sick for ten years or since yesterday, everyone here faces the same five percent.
And someone who recovered falls sick again as easily as someone never ill. When history matters, modellers add extra states to remember it.
Andrey Markov invented these chains in 1906, and in 1913 tested them on the vowels and consonants of Pushkin's Eugene Onegin.

quiz.question: Two sick patients: one ill for ten years, one since last month. In this model, who is likelier to die next year?
choices: The one ill for ten years
quiz.right: Equally likely: a Markov model knows only the current state, so both face the same five percent.

request: How do you read a cost-effectiveness plane?

commands.speak: A cost-effectiveness plane shows whether a new treatment is worth its price. Standard care sits at the centre; extra QALYs run right, extra cost runs up.
Two corners are easy. Cheaper and better, down and right, simply wins. Dearer and worse, up and left, simply loses.
The hard cases are up and right: better, but at a price.
Like this new drug: 0.4 QALYs more per patient, for eight thousand pounds more.
Its incremental cost-effectiveness ratio, the ICER, is extra cost over extra effect: twenty thousand pounds per QALY gained.
On the plane, that ratio is the slope of a line from the centre to the dot.
The dashed line is what the payer will pay: thirty thousand pounds per QALY. A dot below it is cost-effective.
Say the health service will pay up to thirty thousand pounds per QALY: England's NICE uses a threshold of this kind.
Surgery gains more, 0.7 QALYs, but costs thirty-two thousand more: about forty-six thousand per QALY, above the line.
Suppose the payer would pay fifty thousand. The line swings up, and surgery falls under it.
Yet surgery should still lose. The real choice is between the two: going from the drug to surgery adds 0.3 QALYs for twenty-four thousand pounds.
That is eighty thousand pounds for each extra QALY, far above even fifty thousand.
So each option is judged against the next best one, not against doing nothing: the drug is the choice.

quiz.question: At £50,000 per QALY, surgery lies below the line. Should the payer choose it over the new drug?
choices: Yes, it is below the line
No, its extra QALYs over the drug cost too much
Yes, it gains the most QALYs
quiz.right: No: against the drug, surgery's extra 0.3 QALYs cost £80,000 each, well above £50,000.

request: Why do both prisoners confess in the prisoner's dilemma, and how can they escape it?

commands.speak: Why do two people end up worse off when each does what's best for them? The classic case: two suspects, questioned in separate rooms.
If both stay silent, the police can prove only a small crime: one year each. The numbers are years lost.
If one confesses and the other stays silent, the confessor walks free and the other gets ten years.
If both confess, five years each.
Take A's view. If B stays silent, confessing means walking free instead of one year.
If B confesses, confessing means five years instead of ten. Whatever B does, A does better by confessing.
B reasons the same way. The underlines mark each one's best reply: confessing, every time.
So both confess and get five years — the Nash equilibrium — though silence would have cost them one year each.
Why not promise each other silence? Alone in the room, breaking the promise still pays. Nothing in the table has changed.
One way out: meet again and again, as firms, neighbours and countries do. Round one: both stay silent.
Say B is tempted in round two and confesses. A plays tit for tat: start silent, then copy what the other did last round.
Confess once, and you are punished the very next round.
Go back to silence, and so does the other. Today's betrayal costs tomorrow's cooperation.
In Robert Axelrod's 1980 tournaments of computer strategies, this simplest one, sent in by Anatol Rapoport, won.

quiz.question: The suspects meet once, but talk first and promise to stay silent. What happens?
choices: Each still does better by confessing
Only the one who promised first stays silent
quiz.right: Each still does better by confessing: a promise changes no number in the table, and in one meeting there is no next round to punish a betrayal.

request: How do you get the most out of a fixed budget?

spec.title: The best mix on a budget

card.title: The best mix on a budget

commands.speak: How do you get the most out of a fixed budget? Take a student with sixty dollars a week for coffee, at three dollars, and sandwiches, at six.
All on coffee buys twenty cups; all on sandwiches, ten. The budget line joins every mix that costs exactly sixty dollars.
This curve joins mixes the student likes equally well: fewer coffees, made up for by more sandwiches.
Twenty coffees and no lunch is affordable, but it sits low: the twentieth coffee adds little, while a first sandwich would add a lot.
Wherever the budget line cuts through a curve like this one, sliding along the line toward the middle reaches mixes the student likes more.
This higher curve would be better still, but every mix on it costs more than sixty dollars.
The best reachable curve is the one that does not cut the line at all, but just touches it.
It touches at ten coffees and five sandwiches: thirty dollars on each.
At the touch, the curve runs parallel to the line: the student would swap one sandwich for two coffees, exactly the swap the prices offer.
Put another way, the last dollar on coffee pleases as much as the last dollar on sandwiches. If it didn't, moving a dollar across would help.
Now coffee goes up to five dollars. The line swings in, and the best mix slides to six cups.
Francis Edgeworth drew the first indifference curves in 1881, in a book with the unlikely title Mathematical Psychics.

quiz.question: At the student's best mix, which is true?
choices: The last dollar on each pleases equally
As much of the favourite as possible
quiz.right: The last dollar on each pleases equally: if coffee did better, moving a dollar to coffee would reach a higher curve.

request: What does it mean for an economy to be efficient, and what can it not reach?

commands.speak: What does it mean for an economy to be efficient, and what can it never reach? Guns along the bottom, butter up the side.
Every worker and machine goes to one or the other. This curve is every mix that uses all of them: the edge of the possible.
Anything under it can be made. Scarcity is simply that the shading stops.
On the curve nothing is idle, so more guns means less butter. This is where trade-offs live.
Inside, workers stand idle. Here there is no trade-off at all: put them to work and you get more of both.
In 1940 about one American worker in seven had no job. When war production soared, civilian spending did not fall: the idle built the guns.
Outside lies what today's workers and machines cannot make, however they are arranged.
Only growth moves the edge: more workers, more machines, better ways of working push the whole frontier out.
And the mix that was out of reach becomes an ordinary choice inside it.
So an economy can fall short in two ways: waste inside the curve, which can be fixed now, and the curve itself, which only grows slowly.

quiz.question: An economy sits inside its frontier. What does one more gun cost?
quiz.right: No butter: idle workers can make the gun, so nothing has to be given up until the economy reaches the curve.

request: What does a monopoly cost, beyond high prices?

commands.speak: What does a monopoly cost us, beyond high prices? Take the only ferry to an island: tickets a day along the bottom, dollars up the side.
Demand: at ninety dollars nobody sails, and every dollar off the fare brings more passengers.
Marginal cost is what one more passenger costs to carry: cheap at first, then dearer as extra sailings need overtime crews.
A sole seller must cut the fare for everyone to fill more seats, so each extra ticket earns less than its fare. That is marginal revenue.
The ferry sells up to where marginal revenue meets marginal cost: about 4,300 tickets a day, at fifty-six dollars each.
Why not sell a hundred more tickets, at fifty-five dollars? They bring in $5,500, but the fare falls for all 4,300 passengers.
Eighty cents off 4,300 fares is about $3,400. That leaves about twenty-one dollars a ticket, just what carrying them costs. Not worth it.
Competing ferries would keep sailing out to where the fare meets marginal cost: about 5,400 passengers, at around forty-seven dollars.
The eleven hundred passengers in between would each pay more than their crossing costs. The trips are worth making, and nobody makes them.
The high fare itself mostly moves money from passengers to the owner. The triangle is different: value that nobody gets at all.
Economists call these Harberger triangles, after Arnold Harberger, who measured them across American industry in 1954 and found them surprisingly small.

quiz.question: Suppose the ferry could charge each passenger exactly what they would pay. What happens to the deadweight loss?
quiz.right: It vanishes: a cheaper ticket no longer lowers everyone else's fare, so the ferry carries every passenger worth more than the trip costs, and keeps the gain.

request: When a whole economy spends more, why doesn't it just produce more?

commands.speak: When a whole economy spends more, does it simply produce more? Take one that makes a thousand billion dollars of goods a year, at a price level of 100.
Aggregate demand is all the spending there is. The lower the price level, the more that spending buys.
Aggregate supply is what firms produce. They turn out more only if prices rise enough to cover dearer overtime and materials.
The two cross at a thousand billion dollars of output and a price level of 100.
Suppose that is also full capacity: everyone who wants a job has one. Economists call it potential output.
Now the government spends two hundred billion more a year. Here is a copy of demand, for now lying exactly on the old one.
At every price level, spending rises by two hundred billion, and the demand curve slides right.
If prices stayed put, output would rise by the full two hundred billion, out to here.
But firms produce more only at higher prices. The economy lands here: output up a hundred billion, and prices up ten percent.
And that extra hundred billion lies beyond full capacity. Workers are scarce, overtime is everywhere, and it cannot last.
As wages catch up, supply pulls back until output returns to potential. In the long run the extra spending buys higher prices, not more goods.
After the spending surge of 2021, US inflation reached 9.1 percent in June 2022, a forty-year high. Economists still argue how much of it demand caused.

quiz.question: In the long run, what does the extra two hundred billion of spending buy?
quiz.right: Higher prices: output cannot stay beyond potential, so once wages catch up, the extra spending ends up raising prices rather than production.

request: How do you read a survival curve and a hazard ratio?

commands.speak: A Kaplan–Meier curve shows how a trial's patients fare over time, and a hazard ratio sums up the gap between two of them.
On control, a quarter of those alive die each year: 75 percent are left after one year, 56 after two.
On the drug, 87 percent are alive after one year, 75 after two.
Each step multiplies. To be alive at year two you survive year one, 0.866, then year two given year one, 0.866 again.
This tick is a patient who moved away at year three, still alive.
Patients join a trial at different times, so many can't be followed to the end. Counting deaths per arm would get them wrong.
Kaplan–Meier counts this patient as alive while followed, then drops them from the later steps, as neither a death nor a survivor.
Median survival is where a curve first falls to half: year three on control, year five on the drug.
The hazard ratio compares death rates among those still alive. Here, at every moment, patients on the drug die at half the rate.
Yet by year five, 51 percent have died on the drug, against 76 percent on control. Fewer, but not half as many.
A rate applies only to the living, and the drug keeps more people alive to be at risk. So the totals differ by less than the rates.
Edward Kaplan and Paul Meier published the method in 1958. It became one of the most cited papers in all of statistics.

quiz.question: A drug has a hazard ratio of 0.5 for death. What does that mean?
choices: Among those still alive, the death rate is halved
The survival curve is twice as high
quiz.right: Among those still alive, the death rate is halved. Over five years here that means 51 versus 76 percent dead, not half as many.

request: How can four inconclusive trials add up to a clear answer?

commands.speak: A meta-analysis pools several trials into one estimate, and it can see what none of them could alone. Here, four trials of a drug against relapse.
Each reports a risk ratio: the risk of relapse on the drug over the risk on placebo. Left of this line at 1, the drug helps.
Arnesen found 0.78, 22 percent fewer relapses. But the interval, 0.55 to 1.10, crosses 1: no effect can't be ruled out.
The other three look alike: every estimate below 1, every interval crossing it.
Count votes, and the drug fails four times.
But the squares differ in size. Each trial is weighted by its precision, one over the square of its standard error.
Chen's interval is more than twice as wide as Dahl's, so it gets about a fifth of the weight: 9 percent against 48.
The four disagree no more than chance would make them, so it is fair to treat them as estimates of one effect.
The weighted average of their log risk ratios gives the diamond: 0.82, with an interval from 0.72 to 0.94.
The whole diamond sits left of 1. Pooling adds up the trials' information, and the interval shrinks until it clears the line.
So the vote count was wrong. Not significant meant too small to tell, not no effect.
The Cochrane Collaboration's logo is a forest plot like this: trials of steroids before premature birth, which together showed they save babies' lives.

quiz.question: Three small trials of another drug all find risk ratios near 0.8, none significant. What should you conclude?
choices: Pool them: together they may show an effect
Nothing, until one large trial is run
quiz.right: Pool them: not significant means each was too small to tell, and their pooled information may be enough to settle it.

request: What is a confounder, and what does adjusting for it do?

params.edges: Coffee -> Heart disease; Smoking -> Coffee; Smoking -> Heart disease

commands.speak: A confounder makes two things look linked when one doesn't cause the other. Here is how, and what adjusting for it does, with coffee and heart disease.
In a study, 14 percent of coffee drinkers get heart disease within ten years, against 8 percent of non-drinkers: a risk ratio of 1.75.
The tempting reading is this arrow: coffee raises the risk by three quarters.
But coffee drinkers smoke more. Here, 60 percent of them smoke, against 20 percent of non-drinkers.
Smoking goes with the coffee, and it causes heart disease. A common cause of both is what makes it a confounder.
Smokers bring their higher risk into the coffee group. That path, round the back through smoking, carries a link without any effect of coffee.
Adjusting means comparing like with like. Among smokers, 20 percent get heart disease, coffee or not. Among non-smokers, 5 percent.
Within each group the risk ratio is 1. The whole 1.75 came from mixing groups with different shares of smokers.
Holding smoking fixed closes the back door: within a group, smoking can no longer differ between drinkers and non-drinkers.
What remains is the arrow we set out to test, and in this example it was never there.
Coffee really was suspected this way in the 1970s. Heavy coffee drinkers smoked more, and studies that ignored smoking overstated the link.
Adjusting closes every path through the factor held fixed, so it helps only when that path is a back door.

quiz.question: Suppose coffee raised blood pressure, and high blood pressure caused heart disease. Should the study adjust for blood pressure?
choices: Yes, adjust for every risk factor
No, it lies on coffee's own path
Only if it is measured well
quiz.right: No: blood pressure would be a step on coffee's own path, so holding it fixed would block the very effect the study wants to measure.

request: What happens to an epidemic when immunity wears off?

commands.speak: What happens to an epidemic when immunity doesn't last? An SEIR model tracks it. Everyone starts here, susceptible: able to catch it.
Catching it moves you to E, exposed: infected, but not yet able to pass it on. The rate needs a susceptible to meet an infectious person.
After about five days of incubation you become infectious.
About a week later you recover, and for now you are immune.
Take a disease where each case infects three others in a fresh population. If immunity lasts, infections surge, peak, and vanish.
It burns out because the S box empties: once more than two in three are immune, each case passes it to fewer than one other.
Now let immunity fade after a year, on average. Recovered people leak back into S.
The first wave looks the same. But S refills, and when the immune share slips below two in three, cases climb again.
Each wave is smaller, until infections settle at a level that never reaches zero. The disease has become endemic.
At that level, new infections replace fading immunity exactly, which holds the immune share right at the threshold: two in three.
The four common-cold coronaviruses behave like this: people followed for years were reinfected with the same virus, often about a year apart.

quiz.question: In this model, what keeps the disease from ever dying out?
quiz.right: Fading immunity: every recovered person who loses protection refills S, so the disease always finds someone new. The model has no mutation at all.

request: What does p < 0.05 actually tell you?

commands.speak: p below 0.05 is research's most common verdict, and its most misread. This curve shows what it does and doesn't say.
A blood-pressure drug is tested against placebo. If the drug did nothing, the gap between the groups would still wobble around zero, by chance.
With this trial's size, the wobble has a standard error of 2 millimetres. Most results land within two of these steps.
Before the trial, mark the five percent most extreme results a useless drug could produce: beyond 1.96 steps, 2.5 percent in each tail.
The trial finds blood pressure 5 millimetres lower on the drug: 2.5 standard errors from zero, inside the shaded region.
The p-value is the area beyond the result itself: if the drug did nothing, results this extreme would come up 1.2 percent of the time.
Both tails count, because a drug raising pressure by 5 would have been just as surprising. That is what two-sided means.
So the p-value is the chance of data this extreme, given no effect.
The common misreading flips it: a 1.2 percent chance that the drug does nothing, given the data.
That is a different number. It depends on how likely the drug was to work before the trial, which the p-value never uses.
Nor does it measure size: a trial of many thousands could make a trivial half-millimetre drop just as significant.
The 0.05 line itself is a convention.
Ronald Fisher suggested it in 1925 as a convenient limit for judging a result, not a law.

quiz.question: A trial reports p = 0.012. Which statement is right?
choices: There is a 1.2% chance the drug does nothing
If the drug did nothing, results this extreme would occur 1.2% of the time
The drug lowers blood pressure a lot
quiz.right: If the drug did nothing, results this extreme would occur 1.2 percent of the time. The p-value assumes no effect; it cannot give the chance of no effect, or its size.

request: What do 'and' and 'or' mean in a Venn diagram?

commands.speak: A Venn diagram sorts things into groups, and it settles what 'and' and 'or' really mean. The box is everyone in one office.
This circle holds the thirty who drink coffee.
This one, the twenty who drink tea. The circles overlap, because some people drink both.
Eight drink both. Coffee AND tea means only this middle region.
Coffee OR tea means any of the three regions: twenty-two only coffee, twelve only tea, and the eight in the middle.
So how many drink coffee or tea? Not thirty plus twenty: the eight sit in both circles, so adding the circles counts them twice.
Take them off once: fifty minus eight, forty-two.
John Venn drew these diagrams in 1880 to make exactly this kind of logic visible.

quiz.question: 15 people play football, 10 play chess, and 4 do both. How many play at least one?
quiz.right: Twenty-one: fifteen plus ten counts the four who do both twice, so take them off once.

request: How can an angle bigger than 90 degrees have a sine?

spec.title: Sine and cosine on the unit circle

commands.speak: How can 150 degrees have a sine, when no right triangle has such an angle? The unit circle answers it: a circle of radius one.
Turn a radius thirty degrees up from the positive x-axis. Its tip is a point on the circle.
It makes a right triangle whose long side is one. So cosine, adjacent over one, is simply how far across the point sits.
And sine, opposite over one, is how far up it sits. Sine and cosine are the point's two coordinates.
For thirty degrees: 0.87 across, and exactly 0.5 up.
Exactly one half, while the sine of thirty-one degrees is a messy 0.515. Why is thirty so tidy?
Mirror the radius below the axis, to minus thirty. Two radii of length one, with sixty degrees between them.
Their triangle has two equal sides around sixty degrees, so its other two angles are sixty too: it is equilateral, and this chord is also one.
The sine is the upper half of that chord: exactly one half.
The name remembers this. Indian astronomers called the sine a half-chord, and a mistranslation through Arabic turned it into the Latin sinus, a fold.
Now keep turning, past ninety degrees, where the triangle definitions give up.
At 150 degrees the point has swung to the left. Its cosine is now negative, minus 0.87.
But its height is still one half: the sine of 150 equals the sine of 30, mirrored across the vertical axis.
Sweep on to 330 degrees, where the mirror radius stood: now the point hangs half a unit below the axis, a sine of minus one half.
So sine and cosine are not really triangle ratios. They are where a turning point sits, and that works for any angle at all.

quiz.question: What is the sine of 210 degrees?
quiz.right: Minus one half: 210 is thirty degrees past the negative x-axis, so the point sits half a unit below the axis.

request: Why is x > 1 drawn with an open circle?

commands.speak: An inequality like x greater than one has infinitely many solutions. A number line shows them all at once — with one odd detail.
Start at one. Is one itself a solution? No: one is not greater than one. So the circle is left open, a hole.
Everything to the right is shaded: two, three, one and a half, one point zero zero one — and on past five, forever.
Why a hole, not a dot on the first solution? There is no first solution: name any number just above one, and there is a smaller one still above one.
Write x greater than or equal to one instead, and the circle is filled: now one itself belongs.
The symbols are Thomas Harriot's, printed in 1631.

quiz.question: How do you draw x ≤ 3?
choices: A filled dot at 3, shaded to the left
An open circle at 3, shaded to the left
A filled dot at 3, shaded to the right
quiz.right: A filled dot at 3, shaded to the left: 3 itself belongs, and so does everything smaller.

request: Why is an angle in a semicircle always a right angle?

commands.speak: Why is an angle drawn in a semicircle always exactly ninety degrees? Start with a circle and a diameter from A to B.
Pick a point C on the circle and join it to both ends. Wherever C sits, this angle measures ninety degrees. But why?
The key is the centre, O. Draw one more line, from O to C: it is a radius.
O A and O B are radii too. Three equal lengths, and they split the big triangle into two smaller ones.
Take the left one, A O C. Two of its sides are radii, so it is isosceles.
An isosceles triangle has equal base angles: here sixty-five degrees at A, and the same sixty-five at C. Call it alpha.
The right one, B O C, is isosceles too: twenty-five degrees at B and twenty-five at C. Call it beta.
Now the whole triangle A B C. Its angles are alpha at A, beta at B, and alpha plus beta at C, and they add to 180.
Halve both sides: alpha plus beta is ninety. And alpha plus beta is exactly the angle at C.
So the angle at C is a right angle, forced by nothing more than three equal radii.
Move C anywhere else on the circle and the base angles change, but they always pair up the same way: ninety again.
Off the circle, it fails. From a point inside, the diameter looks wider: 133 degrees here, and a point outside sees less than ninety.
The story goes that Thales, around 600 BC, sacrificed an ox when he found this: it is among the first theorems anyone is said to have proved.

quiz.question: C moves so that its angle at A becomes 40°. What is the angle at B?
quiz.right: Fifty degrees: the base angles still pair up at C, so the angles at A and B add to ninety wherever C sits.

request: What does (A AND B) OR NOT A really say?

commands.speak: What does 'A and B, or not A' actually say? A truth table checks every case, and it turns out to say something much shorter.
Two variables give four cases: A true or false, B true or false, one row each.
Make it concrete. A: it is a weekday. B: the alarm rings.
When A is false, not A is true, so the whole thing is true whatever B does. On a Sunday, anything goes.
When A is true, not A drops out and only A and B is left. A weekday with no alarm: false.
A weekday with the alarm: A and B holds, true.
Three trues and one false. The only way to break it is A true and B false.
And that is exactly how you break the rule 'if it is a weekday, the alarm rings'.
So the formula is 'if A then B', written A arrow B. Its column matches, row for row.
Why the 'A and' adds nothing: not A already covers every row where A is false.
And where A is true, A and B is just B. So the formula shrinks to B or not A.
The surprise is these two rows: 'if A then B' counts as kept whenever A is false. Logicians call that vacuously true.
Tables like this were popularised in 1921, by Wittgenstein's Tractatus and, independently, by Emil Post.

quiz.question: The rule: 'if it is a weekday, the alarm rings.' On Sunday it stays silent. Is the rule broken?
quiz.right: Kept: with A false, not A is true, so the formula is true. Only a silent weekday breaks the rule.

request: Why does modus ponens work, when a similar-looking argument fails?

spec.title: Modus ponens, and its evil twin

premises.text: If it rains, the ground gets wet.

commands.speak: When does a conclusion follow for certain, and when does it only look as if it does? Start with a rule: if it rains, the ground gets wet.
Second premise: it is raining.
Then the ground is wet. There is no way out: the rain is here, and the rule turns rain into wet ground.
Neither premise does it alone; together they force it. That is what valid means: true premises cannot give a false conclusion.
Only the shape matters: if P then Q, and P, so Q. Its Latin name, modus ponens, means the mode that affirms.
Now the tempting twin. Keep the same rule, but start from what you see instead.
You step outside, and the ground is wet.
So it rained? It feels just as solid, and it is the same rule and the same two sentences, only turned round.
Its shape is if P then Q, and Q, so P. The premise now affirms the consequent, the Q, instead of the P.
One counterexample breaks it: the sprinkler was on. Both premises are true, and yet it never rained.
So it is invalid. The rule says rain is enough for wet ground, not that rain is the only way to get it.
The difference is direction: the rule runs from P to Q, and only an argument that travels the same way is safe.
People fall for it all the time: in Peter Wason's 1966 card puzzle, most people check for confirming cases instead of the one that could break the rule.

quiz.question: If you have flu, you have a fever. Ana has a fever. Does it follow that she has flu?
choices: Only if she has no cold
quiz.right: No: a fever has other causes, as wet ground has the sprinkler. Going from Q back to P is affirming the consequent.

request: Where does the quadratic formula come from?

spec.title: Where the quadratic formula comes from

card.title: Where the quadratic formula comes from

commands.speak: The quadratic formula solves any equation with x squared in it, and it comes from a picture. Take this one: x squared plus six x makes sixteen.
With x in two places, you can't simply undo the steps one by one.
So draw it. x squared is a square with side x.
Six x is two strips, each three by x, laid along two of its sides. Together they cover sixteen.
Now the shape is almost a square — one corner is missing, three by three. Fill it in: that is nine more.
Add nine to both sides, and sixteen becomes twenty-five.
And the left side is now a whole square, with side x plus three.
A square of area twenty-five has a side of five — x appears only once now.
Five — or minus five, since minus five squared is twenty-five as well.
So x is two, or minus eight. Both work.
That move is completing the square, and it is literally a square. Al-Khwarizmi drew this picture in Baghdad around 820, in the book whose title gave us the word algebra.
Now do the same with letters instead of numbers — any a, b and c.
Out comes the quadratic formula. It is this picture, done once for every quadratic there is.
The plus-or-minus is the five and the minus five.
And the number under the root plays the twenty-five: if it is negative, no square has that area, and there is no real solution.

quiz.question: For x² + 2x + 5 = 0, b² − 4ac is 4 − 20 = −16. How many real solutions?
quiz.right: None: the square would need an area of minus sixteen, and no real number squares to a negative.

request: Why does a tiny bit of mass hold so much energy?

steps.note: Mass and energy, one exchange rate.

commands.speak: E equals m c squared says a little mass holds an enormous amount of energy. Here is why, and how much.
Every second the Sun turns four million tonnes of its mass into light. Mass and energy are one thing in different units, and c squared is the exchange rate.
c is the speed of light: three hundred million metres per second.
Does mass really disappear? Yes, measurably: when a uranium nucleus splits, the pieces weigh slightly less than the nucleus did. The missing mass has left as energy.
Square it, and the rate becomes ninety thousand trillion.
So one gram — about a paperclip — holds ninety trillion joules.
That is the same order as the Hiroshima bomb, which turned less than a gram of its matter into energy.
So mass is energy packed so densely that we never notice it — until a sliver of it gets out, in a reactor or a star.

quiz.question: If two grams were turned into energy instead of one, how much energy?
quiz.right: Twice as much: energy grows in step with mass — it is c that is squared, not m.

request: Why does e to the i pi equal minus one?

spec.title: Euler's identity, as half a turn

commands.speak: Why does e to the i pi equal minus one? It sounds like nonsense, but it is a picture: half a turn around a circle.
It is often called the most beautiful equation in mathematics. Start with the number one.
Multiplying by i turns a number a quarter turn: one becomes i, straight up.
Turn again and you reach minus one — which is all that i squared equals minus one says.
Between those quarter turns lie all the other angles, on a circle of radius one.
e to the i theta is the turn by an angle theta. Where it lands is cosine theta across and sine theta up: that is Euler's formula.
Now turn by pi radians — a hundred and eighty degrees, half a turn.
Half a turn from one lands exactly on minus one.
So e to the i pi is minus one: not a coincidence of numbers, but a half turn written as a power.
Move the one across, and e, i, pi, one and zero share a single line.
At fourteen, Richard Feynman wrote in his notebook that this was the most remarkable formula in mathematics.

quiz.question: Where does e to the 2iπ land?
quiz.right: At 1: two pi is a full turn, which brings you back to where you started.

request: What does Bayes' theorem actually do?

spec.title: Bayes' theorem, on a spam filter

steps.note: Turns one conditional into its reverse.
Half of spam says 'free'; a fifth of mail is spam.
Every way an email can say 'free'.

commands.speak: Bayes' theorem is the rule for changing your mind when evidence arrives. A test comes back positive, an email says free: how much should that move you?
We usually know how often the evidence shows up when something is true. Bayes' theorem flips that into what we want: how likely it is true, given the evidence.
And it needs one more number, easy to forget: how common the thing was before you saw anything — the prior.
Take a spam filter. Half of all spam contains the word free, and one email in five is spam.
But normal mail says free too — one in twenty. Add both routes, and fourteen percent of all mail says free.
So an email that says free is spam about seventy percent of the time — not fifty, and not certain.
Look at the flip. Half of spam says free, yet an email that says free is spam seventy-one percent of the time.
The two conditionals are different numbers, and mixing them up is the most common mistake in weighing evidence.
The denominator is the whole trick: it weighs the evidence against every other way it could have turned up.
Paul Graham's 2002 essay A Plan for Spam built a filter on exactly this rule.

quiz.question: If spam fell to 2% of all mail, would an email saying 'free' be more or less likely to be spam?
quiz.right: Less likely: a smaller prior shrinks the numerator, so the same word is weaker evidence.

request: What is a saddle point?

commands.speak: A saddle point is a spot where a surface is perfectly flat, yet neither a peak nor a pit. Here is the classic one.
z equals x squared minus y squared. Along x it curves up; along y it curves down — the shape of a horse's saddle.
Right in the middle, the surface is level in every direction.
Walk around it. Along one direction, the middle is the lowest point of the curve…
…and along the other, it is the highest. A ball placed there would balance, then roll off at the slightest nudge.
That matters when a computer searches for the lowest point of a surface, as when a machine-learning model is trained.
In many dimensions, saddles like this far outnumber true bottoms, and a search can stall on one.

quiz.question: At a saddle point the surface is flat in every direction. Is it a minimum?
choices: No: it is a minimum one way and a maximum the other
quiz.right: No: along one direction it is the bottom of a valley, along the other the top of a ridge.

request: What is a helix?

spec.title: A helix: a circle that climbs

commands.speak: A helix is the shape of a spring, a screw thread and DNA. What exactly is it?
Go round a circle, and climb steadily while you do: x is cosine t, y is sine t, and z rises as t over ten.
Look straight down the axis, and the climb disappears: all you see is the circle.
Look from the side, and the circle disappears instead: what is left is a wave.
So a helix is a circle and a climb at once. It turns up wherever something turns while moving forward: a drill bit, a climbing vine.
In 1953, DNA's helix was read from Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photograph, whose X-shaped pattern is the mark of a helix seen side-on.

quiz.question: Looking straight down a helix's axis, what do you see?
quiz.right: A circle: from above, the steady climb is invisible, and only the turning is left.

request: Does the current get used up as it goes round a series circuit?

commands.speak: Does current get used up as it goes round a circuit? Take a series circuit: one loop, no branches, driven by a nine-volt battery.
The current passes through bulb A, thirty ohms…
…then bulb B, another thirty ohms, and back to the battery. There is no other way round.
Current flows clockwise, out of the battery's plus terminal and round to its minus.
A common guess: bulb A, first in line, uses some of the current up, and B gets what is left.
It can't. Charge has nowhere else to go: every bit that passes A must pass B. The current is the same all the way round.
How big is it? One bulb alone would take nine volts over thirty ohms: 0.3 amps.
Two bulbs in a row resist twice as much: nine over sixty, 0.15 amps, through A and B alike.
What the bulbs share is the energy, not the current: each takes 4.5 of the battery's nine volts.
Half the current and half the voltage: each bulb gets a quarter of the power one bulb alone would, and glows dimmer.
Old Christmas lights were wired like this: one burnt-out bulb broke the only loop, and the whole string went dark.

quiz.question: In this loop, a meter beside bulb A reads 0.15 amps. What would it read beside bulb B?
quiz.right: 0.15 amps: in a single loop every charge passes both bulbs, so the current is the same everywhere; only the energy is shared.

request: Why does a launch at 45 degrees go the farthest?

commands.speak: At a fixed speed, the launch angle alone decides how far a ball goes. Why is 45 degrees best? Here, 20 metres a second, at 45.
Split the launch velocity in two: about fourteen metres a second across, and fourteen up.
Gravity takes 10 metres a second off the upward part every second. At the top, 1.4 seconds in, only the 14 across is left.
It lands 2.8 seconds after launch, as fast as it left, the upward part now pointing down.
The range is the speed across times the time in the air: fourteen times 2.8, about forty metres.
The angle trades one against the other. Keep the speed, and tilt the launch.
At seventy degrees it climbs high and stays up longer, but crawls across: it lands at about twenty-six metres.
Now lower it. At 45 the range peaks, then shrinks again: at 20 degrees it races across but drops within 1.4 seconds.
Twenty-six metres again, the same spot. Any two angles that add up to ninety land together.
In a formula, the range goes with sine of twice the angle, which peaks at ninety, when the angle is forty-five.
Galileo proved both results in 1638: forty-five goes farthest, and angles equally above and below it land together.
Real air drags hardest on long, high flights, so outside the textbook the best angle is somewhat lower.

quiz.question: At this speed, a ball launched at 30° lands 35 metres away. Which other angle lands at the same spot?
quiz.right: Sixty degrees: thirty and sixty add up to ninety, so what one angle gains in time aloft the other gains in speed across.

request: How does a growth signal tell a cell to divide, and how does cancer jam it on?

params.edges: NF1 -| RAS; EGFR -> RAS; RAS -> RAF; RAF -> MEK; MEK -> ERK

commands.speak: How does a signal outside a cell tell it to divide, and how does cancer fake that signal? It starts with a growth factor, EGF.
EGF docks on its receptor, EGFR, which spans the cell membrane and switches on at its inner end.
The receptor flips on RAS, a molecular switch: on while it holds a molecule called GTP, off once it has cut that to GDP.
Active RAS starts a relay of kinases: RAF switches on MEK, each by tagging the next with phosphate.
MEK switches on ERK, the last runner.
ERK enters the nucleus and turns on the genes for cell division. Signal in, division out.
Just as vital is the off switch. Proteins like NF1 make RAS cut its GTP quickly, so division stops when the signal stops.
The flat bar means 'turns off', where an arrow means 'turns on'.
Now the cancer. Change one amino acid in RAS, famously number twelve, and NF1 can no longer switch it off.
Take the growth signal away entirely…
…and the relay keeps firing anyway. The cell hears 'divide' with nobody asking.
Mutant RAS is among the commonest drivers of cancer: over ninety percent of pancreatic cancers carry a mutant KRAS gene.
So this cancer adds no new signal. It breaks an off switch, like an accelerator jammed to the floor.

quiz.question: A tumour's RAS is stuck on. Which drug target could still stop the relay?
quiz.right: MEK: it lies after RAS, so blocking it cuts the relay. Blocking the receptor does nothing, which is why EGFR drugs fail in colon cancers with mutant KRAS.

request: If both parents carry cystic fibrosis, what are the chances for their child?

commands.speak: When both parents carry a hidden recessive gene, what are the odds for their child? A Punnett square works it out. Take cystic fibrosis.
Everyone has two copies of the CF gene. This parent has one working copy, big F, and one broken copy, small f.
One working copy is enough, so the parent is healthy: a carrier. The other parent is a carrier too.
Each egg or sperm gets just one of the two copies, a coin toss between F and f.
Every pairing is equally likely, so the four boxes are four equal chances for one child.
Only small f with small f, no working copy at all, gives cystic fibrosis. One box in four.
So each child has a three in four chance of no CF, and a one in four chance of CF.
The surprise hides in the three unaffected boxes: two of them are F small f.
So two out of three healthy children are carriers themselves, just like their parents.
And the odds belong to each child, not to the family. A coin has no memory: four children could all have CF, or none.
About one in 25 people of European descent carries a CF gene, almost always without knowing it.
That is how a recessive disease hides for generations, passed on silently by carriers, until two of them have a child together.

quiz.question: Two carriers' first child has cystic fibrosis. What are the odds for their second child?
choices: Lower: the unlucky box is used up
quiz.right: One in four: each child is a fresh draw of one copy from each parent, so the square starts over every time.

request: What does a food web show, and what happens when one species disappears?

params.links: Kelp -> Sea urchin; Kelp -> Abalone; Plankton -> Mussel; Sea urchin -> Sea otter; Abalone -> Sea otter; Mussel -> Sea otter; Sea urchin -> Sea star; Mussel -> Sea star; Sea otter -> Orca

commands.speak: What does a food web show, and what happens when one species disappears? Take a kelp forest off the coast of Alaska.
At the bottom are the producers: giant kelp and drifting plankton algae, making food from sunlight.
Grazers eat them: urchins and abalone chew kelp, mussels filter plankton. Each arrow runs from the eaten to the eater.
Sea otters and sea stars eat the grazers. An otter has no blubber and eats about a quarter of its weight every day.
At the top, orcas, which mostly hunt seals and fish, and now and then an otter.
Read upward, the arrows carry energy: kelp to urchin, urchin to otter, otter to orca.
Now take the otters away. You might expect only their prey to notice.
And at first they do: freed from otters, the urchins multiply.
But urchins eat kelp. Whole forests are grazed down to bare rock, called urchin barrens.
So the otter protects kelp it never eats. The effect runs down the arrows, two levels: a trophic cascade.
This happened in the Aleutian Islands in the 1990s: orcas apparently turned to eating otters, otters crashed, urchins boomed, and the kelp went.
So a food web is more than a menu. Each level holds the one below in check: more orcas, fewer otters, more urchins, less kelp.

quiz.question: If orcas stopped hunting otters, what would happen to the kelp?
choices: No change: orcas never eat kelp
quiz.right: More kelp: the otters recover, eat the urchins, and fewer urchins graze the kelp. Each level flips the one below it.

request: Why is a water molecule bent?

commands.speak: Why is a water molecule bent, not straight? Its Lewis structure, a bookkeeping of electrons, holds the answer. Oxygen brings six outer electrons.
Each hydrogen shares one pair with it: two bonds.
That leaves two pairs on oxygen that belong to no bond — lone pairs. Now oxygen has eight around it, a full shell.
The drawing is flat, but those four pairs repel each other in three dimensions, and spread to the corners of a tetrahedron, like methane's bonds.
Two corners hold hydrogens and two hold lone pairs, so the molecule is bent, at about a hundred and four degrees.
Carbon dioxide has no lone pairs on its carbon, and it is dead straight.
The bend is why water is polar: its oxygen end slightly negative, its hydrogen end slightly positive. That is why water dissolves salt and clings together as a liquid.

quiz.question: Carbon dioxide has no lone pairs on its central carbon. What shape is it?
quiz.right: Straight: with only its two bonds to place, carbon puts them on opposite sides.

request: How does a titration measure how much acid is in a solution?

commands.speak: A titration finds how strong an acid is by counting how much base it takes to cancel it. In the flask: 25.0 millilitres of hydrochloric acid, strength unknown.
Above it, a burette of sodium hydroxide, a base of known strength: 0.100 moles per litre, with every millilitre read off its scale.
Each hydroxide ion from the base cancels one hydrogen ion from the acid, making water. One for one.
Drop by drop, the acid is used up, and the flask looks exactly the same throughout. So how do you know when to stop?
A few drops of phenolphthalein went in first: colourless in acid, pink once base is left over. At 20.0 millilitres, a single drop turns the flask pink.
Why one drop? At that point almost no acid is left to soak up base, so one drop swings the pH by several units at once.
The burette tells how much base went in: 0.100 moles per litre times 0.0200 litres is 0.00200 moles.
One for one, so the flask held exactly 0.00200 moles of acid.
Spread over 25.0 millilitres, that is 0.0800 moles per litre: the unknown, found.
The pink measures nothing by itself. It only marks the moment; the burette does the counting.
Phenolphthalein had a second career, too: for decades it was the active ingredient in common laxatives.

quiz.question: You fill the flask with 50.0 mL of the same acid instead. When does it turn pink?
quiz.right: At 40.0 millilitres: twice the acid takes twice the base, and the strength you calculate, 0.0800 moles per litre, comes out the same.

request: Why is Scholar's Mate so hard to see coming?
title: Scholar's Mate

commands.speak: Scholar's Mate wins a game of chess in four moves. Why do so many players walk straight into it? It starts from the opening position.
e4: White's king pawn steps forward, and opens a door for the queen and the king's bishop at once.
e5: Black mirrors it.
Bishop to c4 looks like ordinary development, a piece stepping toward the centre.
But it aims at f7, the one square in Black's camp that only the king defends.
Knight to c6: Black develops and guards the pawn on e5, watching the centre rather than the corner.
Then the queen swings out to h5, aimed at that same square.
Count them: two attackers on f7, one defender. On a square, the side with more pieces bearing on it wins it.
One pawn move would do it: g6 cuts the queen's line to f7 and chases her away.
But the pawn stays where it is.
Knight to f6 instead, attacking the queen. It feels active, and it answers the wrong threat.
Queen takes f7: checkmate.
The king cannot take her back, because the bishop has guarded that square since move three.
So the trap is arithmetic on one square. Black watched the queen, when what mattered was how many pieces bore on f7.
There is a faster mate still: Fool's Mate takes two moves, and there it is Black's queen that delivers it.

quiz.question: After Qh5, Black plays Qe7 instead of Nf6. Is f7 still lost?
choices: No: two attackers now meet two defenders
Only if White brings a knight first
quiz.right: No: the queen on e7 also guards f7, so Qxf7 is answered by Qxf7, and White ends a bishop down for a pawn.

request: Three chess openings all begin 1.e4 e5 — where do they part company?

openings.name: Vienna Game
openings.idea: Guard your own centre pawn first, and keep the other knight's options open.

openings.name: Italian Game
openings.idea: The bishop aims at f7, the square only the king defends.

openings.name: Ruy Lopez
openings.idea: Lean on the knight that defends e5, rather than on e5 itself.

commands.speak: The Vienna, the Italian and the Ruy Lopez all open with the same two moves. Where do they split, and what does each one want?
e4, e5: each side puts a pawn in the centre, and each pawn is now a target.
The Vienna splits off at once: knight to c3.
