It guards White's own pawn on e4. Defend first, attack later.
The other two bring out the other knight instead.
Knight to f3 attacks the pawn on e5. Where the Vienna guarded, this knight asks a question.
Knight to c6 answers it. Now the bishop picks its diagonal, and with it the name.
Bishop to c4 is the Italian.
It aims at f7, the one square near Black's king that only the king defends.
One square further along, the same bishop makes a different opening.
Bishop to b5: the Ruy Lopez.
It attacks the knight on c6, the piece defending e5. It goes after the defender, not the target.
So all three are about the same pawns. The Vienna guards its own; the Italian looks past them to f7; the Ruy Lopez undermines Black's.
The Ruy Lopez is named after a Spanish priest, Ruy López de Segura, who wrote about it in 1561.

quiz.question: Why does the Ruy Lopez bishop attack the knight on c6?
quiz.right: The knight defends e5: press on the defender, and e5 is under pressure without being touched.

commands.speak: Now drill the three yourself. Play a wrong move, and you will hear which of the others you wandered into.

request: What is the difference between the Nordic countries and Scandinavia?
title: Nordic or Scandinavian?

commands.speak: Are the Nordic countries the same as Scandinavia? Not quite, and the difference shows what each word is about. These five are the Nordic countries.
Scandinavia, in the strict sense, is only these three: Norway, Sweden and Denmark.
It can't be geography: Denmark isn't on the Scandinavian Peninsula at all, while a corner of northern Finland is.
Listen instead. 'Thank you' in Oslo, Stockholm and Copenhagen: [norwegian:takk], [swedish:tack], [danish:tak].
Three close cousins from one North Germanic root: a Norwegian, a Swede and a Dane can mostly follow each other, each speaking their own language.
In Helsinki it's [finnish:kiitos]. Finnish isn't Germanic at all: it's a Uralic language, kin to Estonian and, distantly, Hungarian.
Yet Finland is Nordic: six centuries inside the Swedish realm, until 1809, and Swedish is still an official language there.
In Reykjavik it's [is-IS:takk] again. Iceland was settled from Norway in the late 800s, and Icelanders can still read their medieval sagas.
So by language Iceland is Scandinavian, and many count it; the strict sense keeps the word for the three old kingdoms.
Scandinavian names a family of languages; Nordic names a shared history. All five flags carry the same off-centre cross, borrowed from Denmark's.

quiz.question: Is Finland Scandinavian, Nordic, or both?
quiz.right: Nordic but not Scandinavian: Finnish is a Uralic language, not a Scandinavian one, but six centuries under Sweden make Finland part of the Nordic family.

request: Why does so much growth follow an S-curve?

spec.title: Why growth bends into an S

card.title: Why growth bends into an S

commands.speak: Why does so much growth trace an S: slow, fast, then flat? Bacteria in a dish, a rumour, a new phone: each first grows faster the bigger it is.
Left alone, that is exponential growth — doubling and doubling, straight off the chart.
But the dish is only so big. There is a ceiling.
So real growth bends: slow, then fast, then flattening against the limit.
The reason fits in one line. Growth is proportional to how many there already are…
…times the share of room still left. Early on that share is almost one, so growth compounds; near the ceiling it is almost zero, and growth stalls.
The two pull hardest against each other exactly halfway: the curve is steepest when the dish is half full.
Pierre-François Verhulst wrote this down in 1838 to describe human populations; the same S now describes epidemics and the spread of new technology.

quiz.question: Where on the S-curve is growth fastest?
quiz.right: Half way: there are enough to grow from, and still half the room left to grow into.

request: What does a half-life actually mean?

spec.title: Half-life: the same fraction, every time

commands.speak: A half-life says how fast something disappears, but not in the way most people think. Take a drug with a half-life of thirty hours: how long until it's gone?
If the body removed the same amount every hour, half in thirty hours means all of it in sixty.
But it removes the same FRACTION every hour — so the less there is, the less goes.
After thirty hours, half is left.
After thirty more, half of that: a quarter — not zero.
Then an eighth. Every half-life halves whatever is there, so the curve never quite reaches zero.
The formula says exactly that: start with N nought, and multiply by one half once for every half-life that has passed.
This exponent counts the half-lives. Carbon-14's is about five thousand seven hundred years — which is how a bone's age can be read from how much is left.

quiz.question: A drug's half-life is 6 hours. How much of a dose is left after 24 hours?
quiz.right: A sixteenth: 24 hours is four half-lives, and one half times itself four times is one sixteenth.

request: Why does light fade so fast as you move away from it?

commands.speak: Light fades faster than you would guess as you step away, and the reason is geometry. Call a lamp's brightness a hundred up close. At twice the distance, how bright?
Half as bright is the natural guess.
The real answer falls much faster.
Twice as far: twenty-five — a quarter as bright.
Four times as far: a sixteenth.
The reason is geometry. The lamp's light spreads over a sphere around it…
…and a sphere's area grows with the square of its radius. Double the distance and the same light covers four times the area, so each patch gets a quarter.
Sound, gravity and electric force thin out by the same law, for the same reason: whatever spreads evenly from a point is shared over a sphere.

quiz.question: Move three times as far from a lamp. How bright does it look?
quiz.right: A ninth: three times the distance spreads the light over three squared, nine times, the area.

request: What does a fish really cost an islander? Explain opportunity cost with a dialogue #qa

commands.speak: Opportunity cost is what you give up to get something. Picture one islander, with each day split between fishing and picking coconuts.
A whole day in the trees brings fifty coconuts. A whole day fishing brings ten fish.
This curve joins every best mix of the two: more of one always means less of the other.
Fifty coconuts or ten fish. So a fish costs five coconuts — easy?
That would be this straight line, the same swap every time. The real curve bows out above it.
Start fishing, and the first six fish cost only ten coconuts. Forty are still picked.
Ten coconuts for six fish? That's under two each — cheaper than my five.
The next two fish cost another ten coconuts: five each.
And the last two cost all thirty coconuts left — fifteen apiece.
Oh — so a fish has no single price. Each one costs more than the last?
Yes. The first fish come from the easy shallows; the last mean hours out at sea, each hour taken from the trees.
That rising cost is why the curve bows. Its slope at any point is the price of one more fish, paid in coconuts.
So the cost of my next fish is the coconuts I stop picking — and it depends on where I stand.
Frédéric Bastiat, in 1850, called it what is not seen: the real cost of a choice is the thing you did not do.

quiz.question: The islander catches 8 fish and picks 30 coconuts. What do two more fish cost?
choices: Nothing: fish are free to catch
quiz.right: Thirty coconuts: the last two fish take every hour left in the trees, and the further along the curve, the dearer each fish.

request: Does raising the minimum wage help low-paid workers, or cost them jobs? #debate

spec.title: Does a minimum wage cost jobs?

card.title: Does a minimum wage cost jobs?

commands.speak: Does a higher minimum wage help low-paid workers, or cost them their jobs? One side says a higher floor always destroys jobs.
The other says it never does. Both point to evidence.
Start with the textbook. Employers buy fewer hours of work as it gets dearer: demand for labour slopes down.
And more people want work, and longer hours, at a better wage.
Left alone, the market settles on a wage and a number of hours.
Now a law sets the lowest wage a little above that market wage.
At that wage more hours are offered than employers want to buy. In this picture, the gap is lost work.
Some evidence fits. When Seattle raised its minimum to thirteen dollars in 2016, a University of Washington team found low-wage hours fell about nine percent.
Some doesn't. Across 138 state minimum-wage rises, low-wage jobs barely changed in number: jobs below the new floor vanished, and as many appeared just above it.
The picture can fail where few employers compete for workers: they can pay below the market wage, and then a floor can raise pay without costing jobs.
Where the studies agree is size. Push the floor far above the local wage, and the gap becomes hard to argue away.
In 2019 the Congressional Budget Office judged that a fifteen-dollar federal minimum would raise pay for 17 million workers, and cost about 1.3 million jobs.
So neither claim survives as stated. The real question is not whether a floor costs jobs, but how high it can go before it does.

quiz.question: Where is a $15 minimum most likely to cost jobs?
choices: A city where most jobs pay $20
A town where most jobs pay $10
quiz.right: The town: there fifteen dollars is far above the market wage, so the gap between work offered and work wanted is widest.

request: How does an epidemic spread? #fun

commands.speak: How does an epidemic spread, and why does it stop? Take a town of ten thousand, and a zombie outbreak. Everyone starts un-bitten.
A bite moves you across: now you are infectious, a zombie looking for others. Beta is how often a zombie meets someone and bites.
After about five days each zombie is removed — cured, or chased out of town. Gamma is that rate. The removed can't be bitten again.
Each zombie bites two people before it is removed: R nought is two. So one becomes two, then four, eight, sixteen.
Over time, the zombie count shoots up, then turns and falls, though nobody fought back any harder.
It turns when half the town has been bitten.
Zombies still bite two people each, but now half those people are already bitten or removed. Each zombie makes only one new zombie.
That's herd immunity: once one minus one over R nought are out of reach — here a half — each case replaces only itself, or less.
Yet it doesn't stop at half. The zombies still roaming keep biting on the way down, and about eighty percent are bitten by the end.
Mathematicians in Ottawa really did publish a zombie epidemic model, in 2009: their advice was to strike hard and early.

quiz.question: A faster zombie strain bites four people each. What share must be out of reach before it starts to fade?
quiz.right: Three quarters: with four bites each, a zombie must find only one un-bitten target in four — one minus one over four.

request: How did the Phillips curve rise, and why did it break? #story #human #male

commands.speak: This is the story of a curve that seemed to offer governments a choice between jobs and prices, and of how it broke. It begins with an engineer.
Bill Phillips, a New Zealander at the London School of Economics, had built a machine that ran a model economy as water through pipes.
In 1958 he turned to a century of British records: how fast money wages rose, and how many people were out of work.
From 1861 to 1913 the pattern was plain. When jobs were scarce, wages barely moved; when workers were scarce, wages raced.
At two and a half percent unemployment his curve gave wages rising about two percent a year, roughly what productivity grew, so prices could hold steady.
In 1960 Paul Samuelson and Robert Solow redrew it with American prices and called it a menu: order less unemployment, pay with more inflation.
In the late 1960s Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps doubted the menu. Once people expect inflation, they write it into every wage deal and every price.
Then the curve does not hold still. It rides up by the inflation everyone expects, and the same unemployment comes with far more inflation.
The 1970s bore them out. In 1975 American unemployment averaged eight and a half percent, and prices still rose about nine percent: far off the old menu.
So the trade-off was real, but only until people learned to expect it. That is why central banks today work so hard to keep expected inflation low and steady.

quiz.question: Why did the menu stop working in the 1970s?
quiz.right: Expected inflation was built into wages and prices, so the whole curve rose: the same unemployment came with far more inflation.

request: What does a statin change for 100 people like me?

commands.speak: What does a statin actually change for you? Take a hundred people like you, each with a ten-in-a-hundred risk of a heart attack within ten years.
Without the pill, ten of them will have one. In England, that ten percent risk is where doctors start offering a statin.
Now all hundred take it for ten years. Eight still have a heart attack.
Two are spared. Those two are the entire benefit.
The other ninety never had a heart attack coming, pill or no pill.
The leaflet says twenty percent fewer heart attacks, and that is true: two out of the ten who would have had one.
But many people hear twenty percent as twenty people in a hundred saved. That would look like this.
The real picture is two.
Two in a hundred is the absolute risk reduction. Turned around, fifty people take the pill for ten years so that one is spared.
That number, fifty, is the number needed to treat — a measure proposed in 1988 by David Sackett and colleagues, to make exactly this visible.
The same twenty percent means more when your risk is higher. At thirty in a hundred, it spares six.
Six of the thirty: still twenty percent.
But six in a hundred, not two. The drug's relative effect travels with it; what it does for you depends on where you start.

quiz.question: Your ten-year risk is 5 in 100. A statin cuts it by 20 percent. How many in 100 like you are spared?
quiz.right: One: twenty percent of five in a hundred is one in a hundred, so a hundred people take it for one to be spared.

request: How do you read a normal ECG?

commands.speak: How do you read an ECG? It draws the heart's electrical signal over time, and each bump is one step of a heartbeat.
Time runs to the right. Each square is a fifth of a second, so five squares make one second.
Here are three seconds of a healthy heart. The same shape repeats with every beat.
First the small P wave: the electrical signal spreading across the two atria, the upper chambers, which makes them squeeze.
Then the tall spike, the QRS complex: the signal racing through the two ventricles, the main pumps.
It is tall because the ventricles hold far more muscle than the atria, and more muscle firing makes a bigger signal.
Last, the T wave: the ventricles recharging for the next beat. Their squeeze happens between the spike and the T.
Now the part that looks like nothing: the flat line between P and the spike.
It is a deliberate pause, less than one square long.
The signal is held at the AV node, the only gate from atria to ventricles, so the atria can finish topping up the ventricles first.
To get the rate, count the squares between two spikes: four, which is 0.8 seconds per beat.
Three hundred divided by four squares gives seventy-five beats a minute: a normal resting rate.
So a normal beat is a sequence: atria, pause, ventricles, recovery. Every rhythm disorder is one of those steps going wrong.
Willem Einthoven recorded the first clear ECGs in the early 1900s, named the waves P to T, and won the 1924 Nobel Prize.

quiz.question: On another ECG the flat line between P and QRS is 0.3 seconds long. Where is the signal delayed?
quiz.right: At the AV node: that flat stretch is the signal waiting at the gate, so a longer one means a slow gate — first-degree heart block.

request: How does blood flow through the heart and lungs?

commands.speak: How does blood travel through the heart and lungs? It runs two loops: one to the lungs to pick up oxygen, one to the body to deliver it.
The heart sits between them: four chambers, with a solid wall down the middle that makes it two pumps.
The heart's right side is drawn on your left, as if it faces you. It handles oxygen-poor blood, shown blue.
The left side handles oxygen-rich blood, shown red. The wall keeps the two apart.
Used blood comes back from the body through the vena cava into the right atrium, a holding chamber.
It passes through a valve into the right ventricle, the pump.
That sends it up the pulmonary artery to the lungs. It is an artery because it leaves the heart, even though its blood is oxygen-poor.
In the lungs the blood drops carbon dioxide, picks up oxygen, and returns red through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium.
From there it fills the left ventricle.
That drives it out through the aorta to every organ, and back round to the right side again.
A figure of eight. At rest each side moves about five litres a minute — roughly all the blood you have.
Same volume, very different push. The left ventricle drives blood round the whole body at about 120 millimetres of mercury.
The right needs only about 25 for the lungs. Their vessels are short and delicate, and high pressure would flood them with fluid.
So the left ventricle's wall grows about three times thicker than the right's.
Why two pumps at all? A fish has one: it pumps blood through its gills and on to the body, and most of the push is lost in the gills.
Our second pump gives blood a fresh, strong push after the lungs. Two pumps side by side: equal in volume, unequal in force.

quiz.question: The right ventricle pumps five litres a minute. How much does the left pump?
quiz.right: About five litres: every drop passes through both loops in turn, so both sides move the same volume — the left just pushes harder.

request: How does a signal travel along a nerve cell?

commands.speak: How does a signal travel along a nerve cell? It starts at the dendrites, the branches that collect messages from other cells.
The cell body adds them up. At rest its inside sits at minus seventy millivolts, charged like a tiny battery.
That is the resting level.
If the inputs lift it to about minus fifty-five, the threshold, the neuron fires. Below that, nothing is sent at all.
Firing means sodium channels open, sodium ions rush in, and the inside flips to about plus thirty, for roughly a millisecond.
That spike happens first where the axon begins: the long output cable.
The inrush of charge lifts the next patch of membrane past threshold, so it fires too, then the next — like a fuse burning along.
A current in a wire fades with distance. This signal doesn't: every patch rebuilds it to full size, so it arrives as strong as it left.
And it runs one way only. A patch that has just fired needs a moment to reset, so the wave cannot turn back.
Myelin wraps the axon in insulation. The spike is rebuilt only at the gaps, the nodes, and leaps between them, which is far faster.
At the terminals it releases chemical messengers that pass it to the next cell.
Every spike is the same size. So how does a neuron say 'stronger'? It fires more often: a light touch, a few spikes a second; a firm press, many more.
Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley worked this out in 1952, in a squid's giant axon, nearly a millimetre thick. It won them a Nobel Prize.

quiz.question: You press harder on your fingertip. What changes in the signal its nerve sends?
choices: There are more spikes per second
quiz.right: More spikes per second: each spike is all or nothing, always the same size and speed, so strength is sent as how often it fires.

request: Why can screening look better than it is?

commands.speak: Why can screening look better than it is? Survival is counted from the day of diagnosis, and screening moves that day. One patient's timeline shows how.
First, life without screening. A cancer starts at year one, silently.
By year two and a half a test could find it, but nobody is testing.
Symptoms appear at year five and a half, and that is when it is diagnosed.
The patient dies at year eight and a half. Survival, counted from diagnosis: three years.
Now the same patient and the same cancer, but screened.
A test at year three finds it, two and a half years before any symptom.
Suppose treating it early changes nothing. Death still comes at eight and a half, and the dashed line shows the very same moment.
Now survival is five and a half years. This patient counts as a five-year survivor, and died on the same day.
The gain is only lead time: the stopwatch started earlier, and the finish line never moved.
So the honest test is deaths, not survival. In a trial, do fewer screened people die of the cancer than unscreened people?
The Mayo Lung Project, begun in the 1970s, screened smokers with chest X-rays. Lung-cancer survival rose, yet lung-cancer deaths did not fall.
Screening can save lives, but only when finding it early moves this cross. Only a count of deaths can show that it did.

quiz.question: A new screening test raises five-year survival from 40% to 70%. What does that prove?
choices: Nothing yet: diagnosis may simply come earlier
quiz.right: Nothing yet: an earlier diagnosis lengthens survival even when death doesn't move. Only fewer deaths in a trial shows that screening saves lives.

request: Bacon raises cancer risk by 18 percent — should I panic?

commands.speak: Should 'bacon raises cancer risk by eighteen percent' scare you? That depends on a number the headline leaves out. Here are a hundred people.
Among people who eat little processed meat, about six in a hundred get bowel cancer in their lifetime.
That six is the number the headline left out: the starting risk.
Now give all hundred fifty grams of processed meat every day — a couple of rashers of bacon. The count rises to about seven.
Ninety-three never get bowel cancer, bacon or no bacon.
Seven against six is eighteen percent more. That's the relative risk, and it's the headline.
Seven minus six is one person in a hundred. That's the absolute risk, and it's the one to weigh.
Eighteen percent of a small risk is a small risk: for a daily bacon eater, about one more case in a hundred, over a lifetime.
In 2015 the World Health Organization's cancer agency put processed meat in its top group, beside tobacco.
That group ranks how sure the evidence is, not how big the risk. Smoking multiplies lung-cancer risk about twenty times; daily bacon, 1.18.
So no panic. A real but small effect, and whether it's worth giving up your breakfast is yours to weigh.

quiz.question: A rare cancer strikes 1 in 1,000 people. A food raises its risk by 50 percent. How many extra cases is that?
quiz.right: About one in two thousand: fifty percent of one in a thousand is half a case per thousand people.

request: What does atrial fibrillation actually look like?

elements.text: blood thinners: about 2 in 3 of those strokes prevented

commands.speak: What does atrial fibrillation look like, and why does it matter? It is the commonest lasting heart-rhythm disorder, and an ECG shows it at a glance.
Six seconds of it. Each spike is the ventricles beating, but the gaps between spikes keep changing: no two are alike.
In a normal heart a small P wave sits before every spike: the atria firing in step. Here there is none.
Instead the baseline shivers. The atria fire in chaos, some 300 to 600 times a minute, too disorganised to squeeze.
All that chaos hits the AV node, the gate to the ventricles. It lets through only some impulses, at uneven moments, so the spikes land unevenly.
Count the spikes in these six seconds: eleven. Times ten gives about 110 beats a minute.
Doctors call the pulse irregularly irregular: even the irregularity never repeats. Two fingers on the wrist can often feel it.
A common treatment slows the gate with drugs. The spikes spread out to about seventy a minute.
But they are still uneven, and there are still no P waves. The atria keep quivering.
Quivering atria don't squeeze, so blood lingers in a small pouch of the left atrium and can clot. A clot that escapes can lodge in the brain.
That is why atrial fibrillation makes a stroke about five times more likely — even in the many people who feel nothing at all.
So a key treatment isn't about the rhythm: blood thinners prevent about two in three of those strokes.

quiz.question: The drug slows the heart to seventy a minute. Is the stroke risk gone?
choices: Yes, the rate is normal now
Yes, if the pulse feels regular
quiz.right: No: slowing the gate doesn't restore the atria's beat, so blood can still pool and clot — that risk needs its own treatment.

request: Why doesn't third-degree heart block stop the heart?

commands.speak: In third-degree heart block, the wire from the heart's upper chambers to its lower ones is cut. So why doesn't the heart simply stop?
Normally each beat starts up in the atria, drawing a small bump, the P wave, then crosses one narrow bridge to the ventricles: the tall spike.
Mark every P wave: nine in six seconds, evenly spaced. The atria are beating at ninety a minute.
Now every tall spike: only four, just as evenly spaced. The ventricles beat at forty.
Two steady clocks in one heart, and neither listens to the other.
In a healthy heart each spike answers a P wave, always about a sixth of a second behind it. Here the gap keeps changing.
One P wave even lands inside a spike and vanishes: the atria fired, and nothing below heard it.
So who drives the ventricles? A backup pacemaker below the break. Many heart cells can fire on their own; they are just slower.
The lower the backup sits, the slower it fires: forty to sixty a minute near the junction, twenty to forty deep in the ventricles.
Normally they never get the chance: the faster signal from above sets them off before their own clocks run out. Cut the wire, and the next in line takes over.
Forty beats a minute keeps you alive, but only just. People tire, get dizzy and faint, and the backup itself can falter.
In 1958 in Stockholm, Arne Larsson, fainting again and again from this block, received the first implanted pacemaker. He outlived both its inventors.

quiz.question: A strip shows a heart rate of forty. What proves it is complete heart block?
choices: P waves with no fixed gap to the spikes
quiz.right: P waves with no fixed gap to the spikes: a slow heart can be healthy, but atria and ventricles on separate clocks means no signal is crossing.

request: Is a hole in the heart always a disaster?

commands.speak: A hole in the wall between the heart's two sides is one of the commonest defects babies are born with. Is it always a disaster? It depends on its size.
The right side collects used blood from the body and pumps it the short way, up to the lungs.
The left side takes the fresh blood back and pumps it hard, out to the whole body.
So the left ventricle squeezes to about 120 millimetres of mercury, the right to only about 25.
Now open a hole in the wall between the ventricles. Blood takes the easy way: from 120 down to 25, left to right.
The blood that leaks is the fresh red blood, so the child is not blue. It simply goes round the lungs a second time.
Through a large hole, the lungs can get two or three times as much blood as the body, and the left ventricle pumps it all.
Flooded lungs make a baby breathe fast, sweat while feeding and grow slowly — often from a few weeks old, as the newborn's lung vessels relax.
Left open for years, a large leak thickens the lung vessels until the right side's pressure rises and the flow can reverse. That is when a child turns blue.
A small hole lets only a trickle through, often with a loud murmur, and does no harm. Many close by themselves; large ones are closed by surgery.
And before birth every one of us had a hole, between the atria, the foramen ovale. Blood crossed right to left, skipping lungs that were not yet breathing.
With the first breaths the pressure on the left rises above the right, and pushes the hole's flap shut.
In about one adult in four it never fully seals. The higher left pressure holds the flap closed, and most never know.

quiz.question: A newborn has a large hole between the ventricles. Why is the baby not blue?
choices: The leak is fresh blood going left to right
The hole is too small to matter
quiz.right: The higher pressure on the left sends fresh, oxygen-rich blood to the right, so the cost is extra work for heart and lungs, not less oxygen.

request: How fast does a nerve signal travel?

elements.text: body position: up to 120 m/s → 1 metre in 0.01 s
dull ache: about 1 m/s → a whole second

commands.speak: How fast does a nerve signal travel? Anywhere from walking pace to four hundred kilometres an hour, depending on how the fibre is built. It starts in one nerve cell.
Its axon is a single thin cable. The ones reaching from your lower spine to your toes are about a metre long.
The signal, an action potential, is a brief flip of voltage across the cable's membrane, rebuilt at every point it reaches.
Along a bare axon it creeps, like a burning fuse: in a thin fibre, about a metre a second.
The fast fibres are wrapped in myelin, many layers of fatty membrane that insulate the cable.
The signal is now rebuilt only at the bare gaps, the nodes of Ranvier, about a millimetre apart.
Between them, current races through the insulated stretch, so the signal leaps node to node: up to a hundred and twenty metres a second.
At the end it must cross to the next cell as a chemical, which costs about half a millisecond at each crossing.
Your sense of where your foot is rides the thickest wrapped fibres: a metre in a hundredth of a second.
Stub your toe, and the sharp jolt comes on thinly wrapped fibres, at about twenty metres a second.
The throbbing ache follows on bare fibres, at about a metre a second: it arrives a full second later.
Same toe, same metre: the fibre's wrapping and thickness make the difference between a hundredth of a second and a whole one.
In multiple sclerosis the immune system strips myelin in the brain and spinal cord; signals slow or fail, blurring sight or weakening a leg.
In 1850 Hermann von Helmholtz first timed a nerve, in a frog's leg: about thirty metres a second. His teacher had thought it could never be measured.
So thought is not slowed by its wires: a simple reaction takes about a fifth of a second, most of it spent inside the brain.

quiz.question: You stub your toe. Why does the throbbing ache arrive about a second after the sharp jolt?
choices: It travels on bare, slower fibres
quiz.right: It rides bare fibres at about a metre a second, while the sharp jolt takes wrapped ones at about twenty: same distance, different cable.

request: When does a twice-a-day pill actually reach its working level?

commands.speak: A pill taken twice a day doesn't reach its full level on day one. How long it takes is set by one number: the drug's half-life.
The target is this band: enough drug to work, not so much that it harms. Doctors call it the therapeutic window.
Take one pill every twelve hours, of a drug whose half-life is also twelve hours.
Each dose lands on what is left of the ones before, so the level climbs in a sawtooth.
Twelve hours after the first pill, half of it is still in the blood when the second arrives. The first dip sits below the window.
So each dip climbs: half the final level, then three quarters, seven eighths, fifteen sixteenths.
Each step closes half the remaining gap. After five half-lives, sixty hours or two and a half days, it is within three percent of the plateau.
There each pill replaces exactly what the body cleared since the last one: in equals out. That is steady state.
A double pill each time doesn't get there sooner: every step still halves the gap. It only makes the plateau twice as high, above the window.
Only the half-life sets the clock. A drug with a one-day half-life takes five days to settle, however it is dosed.
The shortcut is a bigger first dose. Two pills at the start, once, and the level jumps almost straight to the plateau.
Amiodarone, a heart-rhythm drug, has a half-life of weeks. Started without loading doses, it would take months to reach its full effect.

quiz.question: You double every dose of this twice-a-day pill. When is steady state reached?
choices: After the same two and a half days, twice as high
quiz.right: After the same two and a half days: the half-life alone sets the pace, and a bigger dose only raises the plateau.

request: What does heart failure do to the heart's pressure-volume loop?

elements.text: stroke volume {sv:0} ml   ejection fraction {ef:0}%   filling {edp:0} mmHg

commands.speak: Heart failure changes one picture doctors draw of the heart's main pump, the left ventricle: its volume across, its pressure up, one lap per heartbeat.
One: the ventricle fills, from 65 to 140 millilitres, at almost no pressure.
Two: both valves are shut and the muscle squeezes. Pressure soars, but the volume can't change.
Three: at 80 millimetres of mercury the aortic valve opens, and blood is thrown out.
Four: the valve shuts, the muscle relaxes, the pressure falls, and the next lap begins.
The loop's width is what one beat delivers, the stroke volume: 140 minus 65, seventy-five millilitres.
Seventy-five out of 140 is 54 percent, the ejection fraction. A healthy heart ejects more than half of what it holds.
The area is the work of one beat, about a joule. A hundred thousand beats a day would lift a car ten metres.
This dashed line is the muscle's strength: the highest pressure it can reach at each volume. Every lap ends on it.
In heart failure the muscle weakens. The line tilts down, the ventricle can't empty as far, and each beat delivers under forty millilitres.
The body fights back: the kidneys hold on to salt and water, the ventricle stretches to 160, and the stroke volume climbs back near sixty.
Yet the ejection fraction has fallen from 54 to 37 percent. A bigger, weaker chamber can pump a fair amount and still be failing.
The price is on the bottom edge, where the ventricle fills.
Its pressure has risen from about 11 to 19 millimetres, and that pressure backs up into the lungs.
That is why heart failure leaves people breathless, worst lying flat, and why water pills that shed the extra fluid bring quick relief.

quiz.question: A patient's stroke volume is near normal. Can the ventricle still be failing?
choices: Yes, if it is stretched and weak
Only if the pressure is low
quiz.right: Yes: a stretched, weakened ventricle can keep its stroke volume by filling to a larger volume, at a high filling pressure and a low ejection fraction.

request: How much urine do your kidneys actually make?

commands.speak: How much urine do your kidneys make? About one and a half litres a day, but they start from far more. It starts in a glomerulus.
Blood pressure pushes plasma through this knot of capillaries. Cells and proteins stay in the blood; water, salt, sugar and waste fall into the capsule.
Your two million or so nephrons filter about a hundred and eighty litres a day: all your plasma, some sixty times over.
So the rest of the tubule is about taking it back. The proximal tubule reclaims about two thirds of the water and salt at once.
And normally all the glucose. When blood sugar runs too high, this step is swamped and sugar spills into the urine: diabetes mellitus means honey-sweet.
Then the loop of Henle dives into the medulla, where the tissue grows saltier the deeper it goes.
Going down, water seeps out into that salt. Coming up, salt is pumped out but water can't follow — that is what keeps the deep tissue salty.
The distal tubule trims the sodium, on orders from the hormone aldosterone.
The collecting duct runs back down through the salty zone. Antidiuretic hormone opens water channels here, and the salt pulls water out.
What's left is urine: about one and a half litres of the hundred and eighty. Over ninety-nine percent came back.
Why filter so much only to take it back? Because anything the tubule doesn't choose to reclaim — waste, toxins, drugs — leaves by default.
It also makes control fine. Keep ninety-nine percent of 180 litres and you pass 1.8; keep ninety-eight, and it doubles to 3.6.
So your water balance is set here, by a percent or two of reabsorption, not by filtering less.

quiz.question: You drink two extra litres of water. What mainly changes?
choices: The collecting duct keeps less water
The proximal tubule stops taking back glucose
quiz.right: The collecting duct keeps less water: filtration stays near 180 litres, and with less antidiuretic hormone more of it is let go as urine.

request: How do you read an event-study plot, and why start on the left?

commands.speak: An event-study plot shows what a policy did, year by year, and whether to believe it at all.
Say twelve cities made buses free in 2019, and forty similar cities did not. The dashed line is 2019.
Each dot is the gap in bus trips between the two groups, measured against their gap in 2018. So 2018 sits at zero by construction.
From 2019 the gap jumps, and it holds year after year.
About fifteen percent more bus trips in the free-fare cities.
The whiskers are 95 percent confidence intervals, and none after 2019 comes near zero.
Yet the right side counts only if the left is flat. Before 2019 there was no policy, so these gaps should sit at zero, and they do.
That flatness backs the real assumption, parallel trends: without free buses, the gap would have stayed at zero after 2019 too.
Suppose instead the free-fare cities had been gaining riders anyway, a little more each year.
Then this jump could be that climb carrying on. The plot cannot tell the policy from momentum.
Now widen the whiskers, as a smaller sample would. Every one before 2019 crosses zero, so a pre-trend test passes.
Yet the climb is still there. A pre-trend that is not significant may only be too noisy to see.
What earns belief is what we started with: dots flat on zero, with whiskers tight enough to have caught a trend.
The method began in finance: in 1969 Fama, Fisher, Jensen and Roll traced share prices month by month around stock splits.
So read an event study from the left. The right side says how big the effect is; the left says whether to believe it.

quiz.question: Every dot before the policy has a whisker that crosses zero. What does that establish?
choices: Only that no pre-trend was detected
That the policy caused the jump
quiz.right: Only that no pre-trend was detected. Wide whiskers can hide a real trend, and the years after the policy are assumed to be parallel, never tested.

request: How does difference-in-differences measure a policy's effect against what never happened?

commands.speak: Difference-in-differences measures what a policy did by borrowing the world without it from a group the policy missed.
Say one region starts an apprenticeship scheme in 2020. Young workers' pay there goes from $18 an hour to $22 by 2025.
Before and after, the scheme seems worth $4 an hour.
But pay rose everywhere. In a similar region without the scheme it went from $16 to $17.50, with no scheme at all.
Before 2020 the two lines run parallel. The scheme region was $2 ahead, but the two moved in step.
The key assumption is that they would have kept moving in step: without the scheme, pay there would also have risen $1.50, to $19.50.
That dashed path is never observed. It is borrowed from the other region.
The effect is the gap between what happened and that path: $22 minus $19.50.
Two differences: the change with the scheme, minus the change without it. $2.50 an hour.
Not $4: before-and-after handed the scheme a rise that everyone got.
Subtracting changes, not levels, removes the $2 head start, which never moved, and the $1.50 rise both regions got anyway.
But suppose the scheme region had been pulling ahead anyway, and would have reached $20.50. Then the effect is only $1.50.
Nothing after 2020 can tell those two paths apart. Only the years before can make parallel trends believable.
John Snow used the idea in 1850s London: cholera deaths among customers of a water company that moved its intake upstream, against a company that did not.
So the groups need not be alike. They need to be groups that would have changed alike.

quiz.question: Before the policy, pay in the treated region was $5 higher than in the control. Does that break difference-in-differences?
choices: Yes: the groups must start at the same level
No: only their trends must match
Only if the gap is larger than the effect
quiz.right: No. A steady gap is subtracted away with the first differences; what breaks the method is a gap that would have changed without the policy.

request: How can an arbitrary cutoff reveal a causal effect?

commands.speak: Regression discontinuity turns an arbitrary cutoff into something close to an experiment. Say every student who scores 85 or more on an exam wins a scholarship.
Each dot is the share of students at a score who finish a degree. Without the scholarship, it climbs from 48 percent at 75 to 52 at 84.
Above the line, with the scholarship, it runs from 60 percent at 85 to about 74 at 95.
Comparing all winners with all losers, 66 against 49 percent, mixes the scholarship with ability: a student on 95 would finish more often anyway.
So fit a line to each side and look only at the cutoff. Students on 84 and 85 differ by one point, and by the scholarship.
The jump there, from 52 to 60 percent, is the scholarship's effect: 8 points, not the naive 17.
That holds only if nothing else changes at 85, and if students cannot choose which side of the line they land on.
The check is to count students at each score. If nobody can steer their score, the count runs smoothly through 85.
If teachers nudged 83s and 84s up to 85, there would be a hole below the line and a heap above it.
Then those just above would be different students, pushed over by someone, and the jump would mix them up with the scholarship.
Here the count is smooth: no sign of sorting at the line.
The price of this cleanness: 8 points is the effect for students near 85. It says nothing sure about a student who scored 60.
The design came from psychologists.
Donald Thistlethwaite and Donald Campbell used it in 1960 on students just either side of a National Merit cutoff.

quiz.question: The count of students shows a spike at exactly 85 and a gap at 84. What does that threaten?
choices: Nothing: there are simply more winners
The comparison: students at 85 may differ from those at 84
Only the width of the confidence interval
quiz.right: The comparison. If some students were pushed over the line, those just above are no longer like those just below, so the jump mixes who they are with the scholarship.

request: Does more schooling really mean higher pay, and what does a binned scatter show and hide?

commands.speak: Does more schooling mean higher pay? A survey of a hundred thousand workers can answer it, but plotted person by person it is a shapeless cloud.
A binned scatter groups people by schooling and plots each group's average: one dot per year of schooling, each an average of thousands.
Pay is on a log scale, so equal steps up mean equal percentage raises, not equal dollars.
The dots lie close to a straight line: each extra year goes with about 9 percent higher pay.
The line is fitted to all hundred thousand people, not to the dots. The dots only show whether a straight line is fair.
What the averages hide is the spread. Two in three people with exactly twelve years earn somewhere in this range.
That spread is wider than the whole climb from twelve years to a degree. The dots are tight because averages are precise, not because people are alike.
A binned scatter also cannot say why. If able people both stay longer in school and earn more, part of the slope is ability, and the causal line is flatter.
Studies that compare twins, or use reforms that raised the school-leaving age, still find a sizeable return. So most of the slope seems to survive.
Across well over a hundred countries, one more year of schooling goes with roughly 9 percent higher pay on average.
So a binned scatter shows the shape of an average, sharply. It shows neither how much people vary around it, nor what caused it.

quiz.question: Each dot sits close to the line. What does that tell you about people with twelve years of schooling?
choices: Most earn close to the dot's value
Little: pay varies widely around each dot
Their pay is caused by their schooling
quiz.right: Little. A dot is an average of thousands, and people with the same schooling differ more than neighbouring dots do; a tight dot means a precise average, not similar people.

request: What does the Gini coefficient measure, and what can one number not tell you?

commands.speak: The Gini coefficient squeezes a country's whole income distribution into one number. To see what it keeps and what it drops, start with a curve.
Line everyone up from poorest to richest, and plot the share of all income held by each share of the people. With equal incomes, that is this diagonal.
A real distribution sags below it. In country A, the poorer half of people get 30 percent of the income, not 50.
Here: half the people, 30 percent of the income.
Everything below the diagonal makes up this triangle, half of the square.
The Gini is the share of that triangle lying between the diagonal and the curve.
For A it is 0.27. Zero would be perfect equality; one, a single person holding everything.
Now country B. Its poorest 40 percent get 25 percent of the income, against 20 percent in A.
But its richest tenth take 24 percent of the income, against 17 in A. The two curves cross.
And B's Gini is also 0.27. What B's curve gains at the bottom it loses at the top, and the areas balance exactly.
So which country is more unequal? When curves cross, it depends on whether you care more about the bottom or the top, and one number has chosen for you.
Max Lorenz drew his curve in 1905, as a graduate student.
Corrado Gini turned the idea into a single number in 1912.
So a Gini is a fair summary only when curves do not cross. Otherwise, quote it with a share at each end.

quiz.question: Two countries both have a Gini of 0.35. What follows?
choices: Their poorest 40 percent get the same share
Nothing definite about any group's share
quiz.right: Nothing definite. Equal areas can come from curves that cross, one kinder to the bottom, the other richer at the top.

request: Why doesn't extra government spending raise output by the full amount?

commands.speak: Why doesn't extra government spending raise output by the full amount? The IS-LM diagram tracks output and the interest rate together, and shows where the rest goes.
The IS curve is the goods market. Lower interest rates make borrowing to invest cheaper, so the lower the rate, the more output is bought.
The LM curve is the money market. More output means more payments and more demand for money; with the money supply fixed, the rate must rise.
They cross here: output of fifty-seven billion dollars a year, at an interest rate of four and a half percent.
Now the government spends more on roads and schools, and the contractors it pays spend part of their new income in turn.
At any given interest rate, that spending and the incomes it creates would add twenty billion of output. IS shifts twenty to the right.
If the rate stayed at four and a half percent, output would rise the full twenty billion, out to here.
But more output needs more money for payments, and the central bank hasn't printed any. Borrowers compete for it, and the rate climbs.
The economy settles here instead: output of sixty-seven billion, up only ten, with the rate at five point two percent.
The missing nine or ten billion is crowding out: at the higher rate, firms and households skip investments they would have made.
So the state's spending did not add to private spending; it partly replaced it. About half the stimulus here became output, half became a higher rate.
Keynes never drew this diagram. John Hicks did, in 1937, to summarise Keynes's General Theory, and the summary is what generations of students learned.
The lesson is that a stimulus is only as strong as the interest rate lets it be, which is why fiscal and monetary policy are judged together.

quiz.question: Suppose the central bank holds the rate at 4.5% by supplying whatever money is demanded. How much does output rise?
quiz.right: The full twenty billion: crowding out works through the rising rate, so if the rate cannot rise, no private investment is pushed aside.

request: If a country saves more, will it grow faster forever?

spec.title: Saving and growth in the Solow model

commands.speak: Does a country that saves more grow faster forever? The Solow model says no, and shows why. Along the bottom, machines per worker; up the side, output per worker.
More machines per worker means more output, but each extra machine adds less than the last, so the curve flattens.
This country saves thirty percent of its output and invests it in new machines: the same curve, scaled down to thirty percent.
Meanwhile machines wear out and new workers need equipping. Just standing still costs a fixed share of the capital: a straight line that never flattens.
Where saving just covers that cost, capital per worker stops growing: the steady state. Left of it, saving wins and capital builds; right of it, wear wins.
Whatever isn't saved is consumed: the gap between output and saving, which is what the machines are for.
Now the country saves forty percent instead. The saving curve lifts, and the steady state slides right.
At the old capital level, saving now outruns the wear by this gap, so capital, and output with it, grow again.
But the gap narrows as capital piles up, and closes at the new steady state. Growth speeds up for a while, then falls back to where it was.
What saving buys is a higher level: output per worker ends about fifteen percent higher. A one-time step up, not a faster pace forever.
Not even more to eat: at forty percent, the bigger output minus the bigger saving leaves slightly less consumption per worker than before.
So what keeps growth going? Only better technology, which lifts the whole output curve. Solow found in 1957 that it explained about seven-eighths of American growth per worker-hour.

quiz.question: A country raises its saving rate from 30% to 40%. In the long run, what happens to its growth rate?
choices: Higher for a while, then back
quiz.right: Higher for a while, then back: capital builds until wear catches up with the larger saving. The level of output rises; the long-run growth rate does not.

request: Why do threats so often fail to deter?

commands.speak: When is a threat worth believing? A game tree answers by reading the game backwards. A budget airline is deciding whether to fly a route one carrier has alone.
Stay out, and nothing changes: the newcomer earns zero, the incumbent keeps its monopoly profit of ten million dollars a year.
Enter, and the next move is the incumbent's.
It has threatened a fare war: fares below cost, the newcomer losing two million, and the incumbent's own profit crushed to two.
Or it can share the route: five million to the incumbent, three to the newcomer after its start-up costs.
If the newcomer believes the threat, staying out is right: zero beats losing two, and the incumbent keeps its ten. The threat works, if believed.
So start at the end instead. Suppose the newcomer is already flying the route. The incumbent now picks between two million from a war and five from sharing.
It shares. Knowing that, the newcomer enters and earns three. The fare war never comes.
The threat was empty: carrying it out would hurt the threatener more than giving in. Only a threat you would want to carry out, when the moment comes, is credible.
Reinhard Selten made this precise in 1965 as subgame perfection: a plan must be best at every point it could reach. He shared the 1994 Nobel prize.
So real deterrence is commitment: spare planes bought in advance, fare-matching promises in writing, anything that makes fighting pay once the newcomer is in.

quiz.question: Which change would make the incumbent's threat of a fare war credible?
choices: Making a fare war pay it more than sharing
quiz.right: Only a change to the incumbent's own payoffs: if fighting beats sharing once entry has happened, the newcomer, reading backwards, stays out.

request: What does a cost-effectiveness acceptability curve tell you, and what doesn't it?

commands.speak: What does an acceptability curve tell a committee, and what doesn't it? Along the bottom: what we would pay for one quality-adjusted life year, up to a hundred thousand dollars.
Take a new drug against standard care. Its effect, costs and quality of life are uncertain, so the model runs a thousand times, each with fresh draws of every input.
At each price, a run is a win when the drug's extra QALYs, valued at that price, outweigh its extra cost. The curve is the share of wins.
At zero it is just the chance the drug is cheaper: almost never. Far to the right, it nears the chance it adds any health at all.
With only two options, standard care is the mirror image: in every run, one or the other wins.
At thirty thousand dollars per QALY, the drug wins in only about one run in six.
The curves cross the half-way line at fifty thousand: there, the drug is as likely as not to be good value.
That crossing is not the ICER. Average extra cost over average extra QALYs gives forty thousand here.
A few runs where the drug works very well pull the averages up, so at its own ICER the drug wins in only thirty percent of runs.
Above forty thousand, the drug's expected net benefit is positive, so it is the better choice on average, even where it wins less than half the runs.
So the curve measures how sure we can be, not what to choose: the chance the choice turns out wrong, and whether more research could be worth paying for.
Van Hout and colleagues proposed the curve in 1994, as a way to show uncertainty about a cost-effectiveness ratio without confidence intervals that break down.

quiz.question: At $45,000 per QALY the drug wins in 40% of runs, and its ICER is $40,000. What should a committee aiming for the most health do?
choices: Adopt it: expected net benefit is positive
quiz.right: Adopt it: above the ICER the expected net benefit is positive. The curve says how uncertain that choice is, not which choice is best.

request: What does a tornado diagram show, and what does it miss?

commands.speak: Which uncertain input could overturn a cost-effectiveness result? A tornado diagram ranks them. Here, a new drug's net benefit: eight thousand dollars per patient in the base case.
Move one input alone, the treatment effect, from its lowest plausible value to its highest, holding every other input at its base value.
Net benefit swings from minus twenty thousand to plus thirty-five. Left of about here it drops below zero, and the drug is no longer worth its cost.
Then the drug's price, alone: from two thousand to fourteen. A wide swing, but it never goes below zero.
Then each remaining input in turn. Sorted widest first, the bars narrow like a funnel: the tornado.
So the effect estimate is the one input that can overturn the decision on its own: the first place to look for better evidence.
But every bar froze the other inputs. Take the high price, which costs six thousand…
…together with the low quality of life, which costs five. Eight minus six minus five: roughly minus three.
Neither bar crosses zero, yet together they flip the decision. And if two inputs move together, correlated, the diagram cannot show that either.
Nor does a bar say how likely its ends are: its width is set by the range someone chose. A generous range makes a minor input look important.
That is why agencies such as NICE ask for a probabilistic analysis, drawing all the inputs at once, and not one-way ranges alone.
A tornado ranks what matters one input at a time: a good guide to where to look, blind to how uncertainties combine.

quiz.question: Two inputs' bars both stay above zero. Can they together flip the decision?
choices: Yes: each bar varies one input alone
Only if they are the top two bars
quiz.right: Yes: each bar holds every other input at its base value, so combinations, and correlations, are exactly what a tornado cannot show.

request: What does the C major scale look like — and sound like?

params.notes: C4:q D4:q E4:q F4:q G4:q A4:q B4:q C5:h

commands.speak: What is the C major scale, and why does it sound as it does? Eight notes from C up to C — on a piano, only the white keys.
It starts on middle C, on its own little ledger line below the staff.
Then up, one step at a time — line, space, line, space — until C comes round again.
The names are the seven letters of the musical alphabet, then back to the start.
On the staff every step looks the same size. On the keyboard it isn't: between E and F there is no black key.
B to C is the other gap with no black key. These two are half steps; every other step is a whole one.
Whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half: that pattern, not the letters, is what makes a scale major.

commands.play: D4:q E4:q F4:q G4:q A4:q B4:q C5:q D5:h
commands.speak: Start on D and keep to the white keys, and the half steps land elsewhere. The same keys now sound darker.
The two Cs are the scale's frame. The top one vibrates exactly twice as fast: 523 times a second against 262.
Played together they melt into one sound — the octave — which is why the two share a letter.
Singers call the steps do, re, mi. Around 1025, Guido of Arezzo took them from a hymn whose lines each began one step higher.

quiz.question: Which step of the C major scale is a half step?
quiz.right: E to F: there is no black key between them, so it is the smallest step a piano has.

request: Why does a major chord sound so good?

spec.title: Why a major chord sounds sweet

card.title: Why a major chord sounds sweet

commands.speak: Why do C, E and G sound so sweet together, when two neighbouring keys grate? The answer is in how fast each note vibrates.
Middle C: its string swings back and forth about 262 times a second.
Slow that right down and draw a sliver of it: four swings of C.
E swings faster, about 330 times a second.
So in the time C makes four swings, E makes five.
G is faster still, about 392 a second.
Six swings in the same stretch.
Four, five, six: at the end of the stretch all three begin a swing together, and the pattern repeats exactly, over and over.
The ear hears waves that keep falling back in step as one smooth, settled sound.
Now C with its neighbour, C sharp. Hear how they rub.
In C's four swings, C sharp makes about four and a quarter. The two slip out of step and take a long time to meet again.
Back to E, and back in step.
So the ear likes small whole numbers. C, E and G vibrate almost exactly as four to five to six.
The Pythagoreans found such ratios on strings 2,500 years ago: a string two thirds as long sounds a fifth higher, like C up to G.
Try it on the keys: press C, E and G, then F, A and C — the same four, five, six from a new root.

quiz.question: Which pair sounds smoothest together?
quiz.right: C and G: two swings against three, so their waves fall back in step almost at once.

request: How does ABC notation write a tune like Twinkle, Twinkle as text?

params.abc:
X:1
T:Twinkle
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
C C G G | A A G2 | F F E E | D D C2 |

elements.text: C C G G | A A G2 | F F E E | D D C2 |

commands.speak: How can a tune be written with nothing but typed letters? ABC notation does it, and this line is Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.
A short header comes first: X numbers the tune, T gives its title.
Each capital letter is the note of that name, from middle C up: C, C, G, G, A, A, G.
The names under the staff are the very letters typed above. ABC is simply the note names, written in a row.
A bare letter lasts one unit, and L sets the unit: a quarter note, one beat.
A number after a letter multiplies it. G2 lasts two units: the open half note that ends the bar.
M is the metre, four beats to a bar, and the typed strokes are the bar lines.
Every bar adds up to four: C C G G, then A, A and a two-beat G.
Then F F E E D D C2 walks back down and comes home to C.
K, the key, always closes the header: C major, so no sharps or flats to add.
The tune itself is an old French song, [french:Ah, vous dirai-je, maman]. The alphabet song borrowed it, and Mozart wrote twelve variations on it.

quiz.question: With L:1/4, what does E2 mean in ABC?
quiz.right: E held for two beats: the 2 doubles the unit length, a quarter note, into a half note.

request: I tested positive on a 90 percent accurate test. Do I have the disease?

commands.speak: What does a positive result on a ninety percent accurate test tell you? Percentages hide the answer, so count people instead: a thousand like you.
The disease is rare, one in a hundred. Ten of the thousand have it; nine hundred and ninety do not.
Ninety percent accurate for the sick: the test catches nine of the ten, and misses one.
And for the healthy it is right ninety percent of the time, so it wrongly flags a tenth of them: ninety-nine people.
You tested positive, so you stand in one of these two boxes: nine sick people, and ninety-nine healthy ones.
Your chance of being sick is nine in a hundred and eight. About eight percent, not ninety.
The test did its job. Ten percent of a big healthy crowd simply outnumbers ninety percent of a small sick one.
Now suppose you had tested negative instead. Read the other two boxes: one sick person among eight hundred and ninety-two.
A negative leaves you healthy with 891 chances in 892. The same test barely rules the disease in, but almost rules it out.
In a 1978 study, sixty Harvard doctors and students got a question like this. Only eleven answered right; the commonest answer was ninety-five percent.
So when a disease is rare, trust a good test's negatives, and treat its positives as a reason to look again.

quiz.question: You test negative on this test. Your chance of being sick?
quiz.right: About one in nine hundred: one sick person among 892 negatives. With a rare disease, a negative is very reliable.

request: Why are averages bell-shaped, even when the data isn't?

commands.speak: Why do averages come out bell-shaped when the data isn't? Take hospital stays: most patients leave within two or three days, a few stay a week or more.
The average stay is 2.7 days, pulled to the right of the peak by that long tail.
Now pick four patients at random. Say they stayed one, two, three and six days.
Their average, three days, becomes one dot on the lower line.
Repeat that thousands of times, and the dots pile up into this: averages of four. Already close to a bell, centred on the same 2.7.
The tail can't survive averaging: an average of seven days needs all four patients to be long stays at once, which almost never happens.
An average near 2.7 can come from countless mixes of short and long stays. More ways in, a taller middle.
The bracket is the typical miss of an average of four: just under a day either way.
Average eight patients instead, twice as many, and the bell narrows: the typical miss falls to about two thirds of a day.
Twice the patients, yet the miss shrank by under a third, not by half: precision grows only with the square root of the sample.
The patients themselves stay as lopsided as ever. The bell isn't in the data; it's in the averaging.
That is the central limit theorem, and it holds for almost any data with a finite spread. George Pólya named it in 1920: central to probability.

quiz.question: Averages of four patients miss by about 0.9 days. How many patients halve that miss?
quiz.right: Sixteen: the miss shrinks with the square root of the sample, so halving it takes four times as many patients.

request: What does 95 percent confidence actually mean?

commands.speak: What does '95 percent confidence' actually promise? Less than most people think. Suppose a pill truly lowers blood pressure by 5 points: this dashed line.
Nobody gets to see that line. A trial measures some patients and reports an interval: here, 3.4 to 7.3 points.
A second trial, with other patients, lands somewhere else, and so does the next. The truth stays put; the intervals move.
Run twenty trials, and most of the intervals straddle the dashed line…
…but this one, from 2.1 to 4.6, misses it entirely. No mistake by its authors, just an unlucky sample.
Nineteen of twenty caught the truth. That catch rate, over many repeats, is all that 95 percent means.
From the inside, the red trial looks exactly like the others: its authors are just as confident, and wrong.
So the 95 percent belongs to the method, not to any one interval. Once computed, an interval either holds the 5 or it doesn't.
'A 95 percent chance the truth is in my interval' pictures the truth wandering. The truth is fixed; it's the intervals that wander.
Jerzy Neyman introduced confidence intervals in the 1930s, and defined them exactly this way: by how often the method catches the truth.

quiz.question: A trial reports a 95% interval of 2 to 8 points. What does the 95% describe?
choices: How often the method's intervals catch the truth
The chance the true effect is between 2 and 8
The share of patients who improved by 2 to 8
quiz.right: The method: across many trials, 95 in 100 such intervals catch the true effect. This one either does or doesn't, and nobody can tell which.

request: Where does the bell curve come from? Show me with a Galton board.
playlist:
playlist:
  title: Where the bell curve comes from
  advance: auto
  gap: 1
---
title: The Galton board
template: galton_board
params:
  rows: 8
  show_path: true
  show_curve: true
  box: { x: 40, y: 200, w: 920, h: 440 }
commands:
  - card: { title: "Where the bell curve comes from" }
  - draw: [pegs]
    speak: "Why does the bell curve turn up everywhere, from heights to measurement errors? A board of pegs shows where it comes from. Each ball meets eight rows."
  - draw: [path]
    speak: "At every peg it bounces left or right, a coin toss each time. This ball went right five times and left three."
  - draw: [bin_4, bin_3, bin_5, bin_2, bin_6, bin_1, bin_7, bin_0, bin_8]
    speak: "Let thousands fall, and the bins fill into a shape: tall in the middle, thin at the edges. Every single time."
  - focus: { target: [bin_0] }
    speak: "Only one path ends in the far-left bin: left, eight times in a row. That is one path out of 256."
  - focus: { target: [bin_4] }
    speak: "The middle bin is reached by any four lefts and four rights, in any order: seventy different paths. So it gets seventy times the balls."
  - highlight: { target: [pegs] }
    speak: "The pegs favour neither side, and no ball is steered. There are simply far more ways to land in the middle than at the edge."
  - draw: [curve]
    speak: "Add up many small, independent pushes, and the total follows this smooth bell: the normal distribution."
---
title: The bell curve
template: distribution_curve
