  shade: { from: 2, side: two, label: "2.3% in each tail" }
  box: { x: 40, y: 150, w: 920, h: 520 }
elements:
  - { id: portrait_1, type: portrait, of: Francis Galton, x: 838, y: 545, width: 130 }
commands:
  - draw: [axis, curve]
    speak: "Up close, the shape of those bins is the normal curve: the smooth limit of many coin tosses added together."
  - draw: [mean_line]
    speak: "It is symmetric about its mean, which on the board is the spot straight under the drop."
  - draw: [sd_tick_0, sd_tick_1, sd_tick_2, sd_tick_3]
    speak: "Its width is measured in standard deviations. About two thirds of the balls land within one of the mean…"
  - draw: [shade, shade2, shade_label]
    parallel: true
    speak: "…and about 95 percent within two. Beyond two, each tail holds just over two percent."
  - highlight: { target: [curve] }
    speak: "The recipe is adding. When small effects multiply instead, as interest does on wealth, the result is lopsided, which is why incomes are not bell-shaped."
  - draw: [portrait_1]
    speak: "Francis Galton built the board in the 1870s. He wrote that the Greeks would have made this law a god, had they known of it."
  - quiz:
      question: "Why do so few balls land in the far-left bin?"
      choices: ["Only one of the 256 paths leads there", "The pegs push balls toward the middle", "The edge bins are harder to reach through the gaps"]
      correct: 1
      right: "Only one path, eight lefts in a row, leads there, while seventy lead to the middle. Every peg is a fair coin toss."

request: Why did Darwin wait twenty years to publish his theory?

commands.speak: Charles Darwin had natural selection worked out by 1838, and published it in 1859. Why did biology's most famous idea wait twenty years?
Here are those years to scale. First the Beagle's voyage round the world, 1831 to 1836: finches, fossils, and growing doubts that species are fixed.
Home in 1837, he sketched a branching tree in a notebook under the words 'I think'. A year later, reading Malthus, he had the mechanism.
The book, On the Origin of Species, came out in November 1859.
Twenty-one years apart: most of the line. The usual story is that he feared the scandal, and hid the idea in a drawer.
But the drawer was full. By 1844 he had written the theory out as a long essay, with a letter asking his wife Emma to publish it if he died.
Then eight years on barnacles, 1846 to 1854: the expert standing, and the habit of patient evidence, that a heretical claim would need.
In June 1858, deep in a huge book on species, he opened a letter from Alfred Russel Wallace in the Malay Archipelago. It described the same idea.
Within two weeks both men's papers were read together in London, and the Origin, which Darwin called a mere abstract, followed the next year.
So the idea was finished early. What filled the gap was evidence, and what ended it was a rival.
Historians still argue over his motives, and some doubt it was a delay at all: for a naturalist then, twenty years of evidence was simply thoroughness.

quiz.question: How much of his theory had Darwin written down by 1844?
choices: Nothing: it was all in his head
A long essay setting it out
quiz.right: A long essay, with instructions to publish it if he died: the gap was not an empty drawer but twenty years of gathering evidence.

request: Why should a country that is better at everything still trade? Explain comparative advantage, with a portrait of David Ricardo.

commands.speak: Why would a country that makes everything more cheaply still buy from abroad? The answer came in 1817, from David Ricardo.
He was a stockbroker who grew rich on the London exchange, then turned to economics after reading Adam Smith on holiday in Bath.
His example: two countries, two goods, and the hours of work each needs for one unit.
Portugal needs eighty hours for a unit of wine, ninety for a unit of cloth.
England needs more for both: a hundred and twenty, and a hundred. Portugal is better at everything.
So why would Portugal buy anything from England? Because the real price of wine is the cloth you don't make.
In Portugal, eighty hours of wine could have made eight ninths of a cloth. Wine is cheap there.
In England, a hundred and twenty hours of wine could have made one point two cloth. Wine is dear there — so cloth is relatively cheap.
Now Portugal moves ninety hours out of cloth: one cloth less, and an eighth more than one wine.
England moves a hundred and twenty hours out of wine: one wine less, and one point two cloth more.
Same hours, same workers — and together they have more of both goods. Trade then shares the extra out.
What counts is not who is faster, but who gives up less. Even a country worse at everything is relatively best at something.
Asked for one idea in social science that is both true and not obvious, Paul Samuelson named this one.

quiz.question: When would trade between the two countries gain nothing?
choices: When one is better at both goods
When both give up the same cloth per wine
When one is worse at both goods
quiz.right: When both give up the same cloth per wine: with equal opportunity costs, no switch of hours makes more of anything.

request: What did Adam Smith see in a pin factory? Tell the story, and link his portrait to the book: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wealth_of_Nations and https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/3300
title: Smith's pin factory

commands.speak: Why are some nations rich? Adam Smith's answer, in 1776, begins with an unlikely object: a pin.
He compared two ways of running the same small workshop of ten men.
A man doing every step himself — drawing the wire, cutting, pointing, fitting the head — could not make twenty pins a day. Perhaps not one.
Split the job into eighteen operations, two or three per man, and the ten made over forty-eight thousand a day.
Same men, same wire, same day: at least two hundred and forty times as many pins.
Why? First, a man who only points pins gets very quick at pointing pins.
Second, nobody loses time walking from one task and tool to the next.
Third, a job cut small enough is easy to hand to a machine. Smith called the whole thing the division of labour.
But forty-eight thousand pins a day only pay if someone buys them. Smith's rule: the division of labour is limited by the extent of the market.
From 2007 the Bank of England's twenty-pound note carried Smith and his pin factory. Click his portrait: its card opens the book itself.

quiz.question: Why would a lone village of 200 people never build Smith's pin factory?
choices: Its workers would be too slow
Nobody could use 48,000 pins a day
Pins need a machine it lacks
quiz.right: Nobody there could use forty-eight thousand pins a day: the division of labour only pays in a market big enough to buy what it makes.

request: How does a rise in demand move the market price? Quiz me at the end.

spec.title: A heat wave and the price of fans

commands.speak: When people want more of something, what happens to its price, and to how much is sold? Take electric fans in one city, week by week.
Demand slopes down: the cheaper a fan, the more people buy.
Supply slopes up: a higher price makes it worth shipping more fans to the city.
In an ordinary week they meet here: forty dollars a fan, and a thousand sold.
Then a heat wave arrives. Here is a copy of demand, lying on the old curve for now.
At every price, people now want four hundred more fans a week, so the whole demand curve slides right.
But at forty dollars, the shops still have only a thousand fans. Buyers compete for them, and the price is bid up.
It settles here: about forty-seven dollars a fan, and some twelve hundred sold.
The dearer fans put some buyers off, but that is a slide along the new curve. Demand itself stays out as long as the heat does.
Alfred Marshall compared supply and demand to the blades of scissors: asking which one sets the price is like asking which blade cuts.

quiz.question: After demand rises, what happens to the equilibrium price?
quiz.right: It rises: more buyers now compete for fans that the shops can only add at a higher price.
quiz.wrong: Compare the new crossing with the old one.

quiz.question: The price has risen to $47. Does that push demand back to where it started?
choices: Yes, the curve shifts back left
No, buyers only move along the new curve
quiz.right: No: a higher price moves buyers along the new demand curve. Only the heat ending would shift the curve back.

commands.speak: You got {score} of {score_total}. A shift of the curve moves the price; a change in price only moves buyers along it.

request: Why is gold's chemical symbol Au? Make it a personalized warm-up: ask my name, greet me, and let me type the answer.

commands.speak: A warm-up on chemical symbols, and why some share no letters with their English names — gold's above all. First, who am I talking to?

ask.question: What should I call you?

commands.speak: Nice to meet you, {name}. Gold's symbol belongs where the question mark is. Do you know it?

ask.question: Type gold's chemical symbol.
ask.right: Au — and there is no U in gold.
ask.wrong: Think Latin, not English.

commands.speak: Au is short for aurum, the Romans' word for gold.
Iron is Fe, from ferrum.
Silver is Ag, from argentum.
Lead is Pb, from plumbum — and a plumber is named after the lead pipes Roman plumbers laid.
Why Latin?
The Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius set up letter symbols around 1813, and took them from Latin, then science's shared language.
So the symbols belong to no one's language: a chemist in Oslo, Tokyo or Lima writes gold the same way.

quiz.question: Na is the symbol for which element?
quiz.right: Sodium: Na is from natrium, its Latin name. Nitrogen is N, and neon is Ne.

commands.speak: That's the warm-up, {name}. Next time a symbol looks odd, try its Latin name.

request: How much does a bigger sample tighten an average? Let me pick the sample size myself.

commands.speak: How much does a bigger sample tighten an average? You'll choose the size yourself. The data: scores on a ten-point test, in a class split in two.
One group scored around three, the other around seven: two humps, nothing like a bell.
The class average is 4.8, a score almost nobody actually got.
Now average four random students, over and over. The averages make one hump, not two, centred on the same 4.8.
A three and a seven average to five, and four random students rarely all come from the same group.
The bracket is the typical miss of an average of four students: about one point either way.

ask.question: How many students behind each average? Type a number from 2 to 100.

commands.speak: Here are averages of {n_choice} students. Compare the bracket with its width at four.
Its width follows one rule: the class's spread, about 2.1 points, divided by the square root of the sample size.
Now drag n yourself. Try to halve the bracket you chose, and see how many more students it costs.
Every size keeps the same centre. A bigger sample doesn't move the average; it only stops it wandering.
The same square root is why a poll of a thousand people has a margin of error near three points, and four thousand only halve it.

quiz.question: Averages of 25 students miss by about ± 0.42. What do averages of 100 miss by?
quiz.right: About ± 0.21: four times the students, and the square root of four is two, so the miss halves.

request: Where does a market settle after demand rises? Let me click the new equilibrium on the figure.

commands.speak: When demand rises, where does a market end up? You'll find it yourself on this figure. The market: bicycles in one city, month by month.
Demand slopes down: cheaper bikes, more buyers.
Supply slopes up: a better price brings more bikes to the shops.
Today they cross here: four hundred dollars a bike, a thousand sold a month.
Then the city paints new bike lanes. At every price, people now want five hundred more bikes: demand steps right.
At the old four hundred dollars, buyers now want fifteen hundred bikes. Shops still offer a thousand.
And here the new demand curve crosses supply.

ask.question: Click where the market settles after the shift.
ask.right: Here, where new demand meets supply: the price climbs until buyers want just as many bikes as sellers offer.
ask.wrong: At four hundred dollars, sellers still offer only a thousand bikes.

commands.speak: The fifteen hundred was only a wish: at that price, five hundred buyers would leave empty-handed.
So they bid the price up, to about four hundred and ninety dollars, with some twelve hundred and fifty bikes sold.
That is what makes it an equilibrium: every buyer willing to pay the price gets a bike, and no shop is left with one unsold.
Antoine Augustin Cournot drew the first demand curve in 1838. It took half a century before Alfred Marshall crossed it with supply.

quiz.question: Why doesn't the price stop at $400 once demand has risen?
choices: Buyers who find no bike bid it up
quiz.right: At four hundred dollars, five hundred buyers find no bike, and they bid the price up until demand and supply match again.

request: What makes a chord major — and can I find the third myself?

commands.speak: What makes C, E and G a major chord? The gaps between them — counted on every key, the black ones included.
A chord is built up from its root: here, C.
Then E. Count the keys from C: C sharp, D, D sharp, E — four half steps. That gap is a major third.
Three more half steps up to G, the fifth — seven above the root.
Together: bright and settled. That is C major.
Now move the middle note down one key, to E flat: three half steps instead of four.
Same root, same fifth, and the chord turns sad: C minor. One key made the difference.
So the third decides the mood; the root and the fifth are shared by both.
A major chord, from any root: up four half steps, then three more.
A piano's E is a shade higher than a perfectly pure third. The tuning gives that up so every key sounds equally in tune.

ask.intro: Your turn, from a new root.
ask.question: G is the root. Press the third that makes G major.
ask.right: B — four half steps above G: G sharp, A, A sharp, B.
ask.wrong: Count every key up from G, black ones too, and stop at four.

commands.speak: The same four half steps from any key make a major third — your fingers can now build a major chord anywhere.

request: Can I find the checkmate in Scholar's Mate myself?
title: Deliver the mate

commands.speak: A puzzle: White has one move that ends this game at once. After three moves each, Black has just played knight to f6.
White's queen stands on h5, and that knight is attacking her.
White's bishop on c4 has been waiting since move three, aimed along the diagonal toward Black's king.
Most players look first at the queen in danger. Look at the king instead: which square beside him does nobody else defend?

ask.question: One move wins the game. Click the queen, then the square she takes.
ask.right: Queen takes f7: the queen and the bishop both hit it, and only the king defends it.
ask.wrong: Saving the queen isn't the point. Count the attackers on each square next to Black's king.

commands.speak: Checkmate. The king cannot take the queen, because the bishop guards her.
And he cannot run: the queen covers e7, and his own pieces fill his other squares.
Two lines meeting on a square only the king guards: that is the pattern to spot, from either side of the board.
The knight's attack on the queen was real, and it didn't matter. A threat of mate outranks a threat to a piece.
German players call it the [german:Schäfermatt], the shepherd's mate.

quiz.question: Rewind one move: Black to play after Qh5. Which move keeps f7?
quiz.right: g6: it stands between the queen and f7, so only the bishop still attacks the square, and the king holds it.

request: What is the Italian Game, and why is it a good first opening?
title: The Italian Game — your move

openings.name: Italian Game
openings.idea: The bishop aims at f7, and White can castle next move.

openings.name: Ruy Lopez
openings.idea: The bishop pressures the knight that guards e5.

openings.name: Scotch Game
openings.idea: White opens the centre at once.

commands.speak: The Italian Game is one of the oldest chess openings, and a good first one to learn. Why? Every move in it does real work.
Both sides stake the centre at once: pawn to e4, pawn to e5.
White's queen could leap out to h5 now. But Black's knights would chase her, and every retreat is a move thrown away.
So the queen stays home, and the lighter pieces come first.
Knight to f3 develops a piece and attacks the pawn on e5.
So Black's reply is forced to be useful too: knight to c6, developing and defending.
Then the Italian move itself: bishop to c4.
It aims at f7, the one square near Black's king that only the king defends.
And look at what the knight and bishop left behind.
Two empty squares between king and rook: White can castle next move and tuck the king away.
Three moves: the centre claimed, two pieces out, a target chosen, and the king ready to hide. None of them wasted.
If Black answers bishop to c5, it becomes the [italian:Giuoco Piano], Italian for the quiet game.

quiz.question: Why not bring the queen out on move two?
choices: Black's pieces chase her and gain moves
The queen may not move before castling
quiz.right: Black's pieces chase her and gain moves: each attack also develops a black piece, while White spends the move retreating.

request: Why are most published research findings false? Show the base-rate arithmetic, and put the paper itself on the slide: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.0020124
title: Most findings are false

spec.title: Why most published findings are false

commands.speak: How can most published findings be false when nobody cheats? Sort a thousand hypotheses a field might test: true or false, significant or not.
Say a hundred of the thousand are really true. That share, the prior, is the number no single study reports.
Studies with eighty percent power find eighty of the hundred true effects, and miss twenty.
The nine hundred false hypotheses face a five percent threshold, so forty-five come out significant anyway, by chance.
Journals print the significant column: a hundred and twenty-five findings.
Forty-five of them are false: more than one in three, though every study followed the rules.
Now make the studies small, with twenty percent power. Only twenty true effects surface, but the forty-five false ones stay.
Two in three significant findings are now false. Low power doesn't just miss effects; it makes the effects you do find less believable.
And a field chasing long shots, where one hypothesis in a hundred is true, is mostly false even with good power.
John Ioannidis set out this arithmetic in 2005, in a paper whose title makes the claim outright.
So a significant result is only as believable as its field's prior and its study's power, and a p-value reports neither.

quiz.question: Mostly long shots, large studies: its significant findings are…
choices: Mostly true: the power is high
Mostly false: few hypotheses are true
quiz.right: Mostly false: when true hypotheses are rare, the five percent of false ones that slip through outnumber the real finds, whatever the power.

request: What can attention do that recurrence could not? Quote the paper's own sentence for it: https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762
title: Attention, in the paper's words

elements.quote: dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely

commands.speak: What could attention do that recurrence couldn't? Take a sentence: 'Anna told Ben she left.' To understand 'she', a network must find Anna.
A recurrent network reads in order, carrying a running memory from word to word. Anna reaches 'she' only by passing through 'told' and 'Ben'.
And each step waits for the one before, so a thousand-word text is a thousand steps in a row that no chip can share out.
Attention drops the queue: 'she' looks directly at the other words and scores how relevant each one is.
Anna scores highest, so her meaning flows straight into 'she': one hop, however far back she was named.
Every word does this at the same time, so the whole sentence is computed in one parallel pass instead of a queue.
The 2017 paper that made this the standard design said it in one line of its abstract:
dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely.
Attention itself wasn't new: it already helped recurrent translators. The bold step was removing the recurrence around it.
The payoff was speed. The paper's largest model trained in three and a half days on eight GPUs, and its design became the T in GPT.
So the gift was less attention than parallelism: a model that reads a whole text at once can learn from vastly more of it.

quiz.question: What did dropping recurrence buy the Transformer, above all?
choices: Every word processed at once, in parallel
Attention, which did not exist before
quiz.right: Parallelism: with no word-by-word queue, every position is computed at the same time, so training on huge amounts of text became fast.

request: Why did Malthus think population growth must end in famine, and was he right?
title: Malthus's two lines

elements.of: An Essay on the Principle of Population

commands.speak: In 1798 Thomas Malthus argued that famine was not bad luck but arithmetic.
Was he right? His Essay on the Principle of Population rests on two lines.
People grow by multiplication. The American colonies had been doubling every twenty-five years: two, four, eight, sixteen.
Food, he argued, grows only by addition: clear another field, drain another marsh. The same amount more each generation.
Start them level, and the gap opens and never closes. Everyone above the food line must go without.
After a century, sixteen times the people and five times the food. After two, his own figures: 256 to 9.
Any doubling, however slow, overtakes any straight line, however steep. So famine, or late marriage and fewer births, had to hold people back.
The arithmetic holds. What broke was the straight line.
Fertiliser, new crops and machines made food multiply too, and faster than people.
Since 1800 the world has grown from one billion people to eight, and food per head has still gone up.
His other line bent as well: as people grew richer, they chose smaller families, and world population growth has been slowing since the late 1960s.
The essay had one reader Malthus never expected: in 1838 Charles Darwin read it, and saw in its struggle for food the engine of natural selection.

quiz.question: Suppose food rose by twice as much each generation, still by addition. Would that avoid Malthus's gap forever?
quiz.right: No: a steeper straight line only moves the crossing later, because a doubling curve overtakes any line. Only food that multiplies keeps up.

request: What is a derivative, really? Link Grant Sanderson's calculus video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WUvTyaaNkzM
title: The derivative is a limit of slopes

commands.speak: A derivative is the rate of change at one instant — which sounds impossible. Take a dropped stone: after t seconds it has fallen five t squared metres.
Two seconds in, it has fallen twenty metres. How fast is it moving at exactly that moment?
Speed needs two moments. At four seconds it has fallen eighty metres, and the line through both points has a slope…
…of sixty metres fallen over two seconds…
…which is thirty metres a second, on average.
But the stone kept speeding up after two seconds, so thirty is too fast for the moment we asked about.
Close the gap to one second: twenty-five metres more, so twenty-five metres a second.
Shrink it further — a tenth, a hundredth of a second — and the slope stops changing, closing in on twenty.
That limit is the derivative: twenty metres a second, the slope of the tangent — the line that just grazes the curve at two seconds.
Why not set the gap to zero? Then the stone falls zero metres in zero seconds, and zero over zero says nothing.
So the derivative is not a slope measured at one point, but the number the slopes head for as the gap shrinks.
A speedometer shows exactly this: never distance over a whole trip, only where that ratio is heading right now.
Newton wrote a dot over the letter, Leibniz wrote d y over d x, and this prime is Lagrange's — three names for one limit.
Click this label for Grant Sanderson's video, which builds the same limit from scratch.

quiz.question: From 2 s to 4 s the stone averages 30 m/s. Its speed at exactly 2 s is…
choices: zero — an instant has no speed
quiz.right: Less — twenty metres a second: the stone speeds up, so any stretch after two seconds averages more than its speed at two.

request: A disease hits 1 in 10,000. The test catches 90% of cases and false-alarms only 1% of the time. I tested positive — should I panic? Add 3Blue1Brown's Bayes video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HZGCoVF3YvM
title: Positive on a very good test

spec.title: A very good test, a very rare disease

card.title: A good test, a rare disease

commands.speak: Should a positive on a very good test make you panic? It depends on how rare the disease is. Follow a hundred thousand people instead of percentages.
The disease hits one in ten thousand: ten of them have it, and ninety-nine thousand nine hundred and ninety do not.
The test catches ninety percent of real cases: nine of the ten test positive, and one is missed.
It false-alarms one time in a hundred. Small — but one percent of almost a hundred thousand is a thousand people.
A thousand healthy people are told they might be sick.
Everyone with a positive result stands in one of these two boxes: nine sick, a thousand healthy.
So a positive puts you among one thousand and nine people, of whom nine are sick. Under one percent.
The test didn't fail. Your chance rose about ninety-fold, from one in ten thousand to nearly one in a hundred. It just started very low.
Now say you went to the doctor with symptoms, and one in a hundred people like you has the disease. Same test.
Nine hundred true positives now face nine hundred and ninety false ones. The same positive means nearly even odds.
Back to one in ten thousand. What a positive result means depends on who takes the test.
When Gerd Gigerenzer gave doctors counts like these instead of percentages, far more of them got this question right.
Click this label for 3Blue1Brown's picture of why.

quiz.question: With this 1-in-10,000 disease, you test positive on two independent tests. Roughly what is your chance now?
quiz.right: Close to half: after one positive you are one of 1,009 with nine sick; a second test keeps about eight of them against ten false alarms.

request: How can a drug help every group of patients yet look harmful overall? Link the article: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simpson%27s_paradox
title: When the trend reverses

commands.speak: How can a drug help every group of patients, yet look harmful when you add them up? That's Simpson's paradox. Here, ten patients: dose against recovery.
Five mild cases got low doses. Among them, every extra ten milligrams bought about four points of recovery.
Five severe cases got high doses. They start lower, because they are sicker, but gain the same four points per ten milligrams.
Now ignore who was sick and fit one line through all ten. It slopes down: more drug, worse recovery.
Nothing in the data changed. This line compares low-dose mild patients with high-dose severe ones.
The drop from one cloud to the other is severity, not dose. Doctors gave the sickest the most drug, and the pooled line blames the drug.
Which to believe? The numbers can't say. The story of how doses were chosen says compare like with like: within each group, the drug helps.
It happens with real data: in a 1986 study of kidney-stone surgery, open surgery did better on small stones and on large ones, yet worse overall.
It had been given more of the hard cases. Click the pooled line for the article.
An average over a mix of patients answers a question about the mix, not about the drug.

quiz.question: Sicker patients get more of a drug, and pooled data show high doses doing worse. What should you check first?
choices: The dose effect within each severity group
Whether the pooled line is steep
quiz.right: Compare like with like: within each severity group, higher doses did better. The pooled slope mixes the drug's effect with how sick people were.

request: How can two sounds add up to silence? Put 3Blue1Brown's Fourier video on the slide: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=spUNpyF58BY
title: Waves that cancel

card.title: How can two sounds make silence?

commands.speak: How can two sounds add up to silence? Noise-cancelling headphones do it. Here is a steady hum: air pressure rising and falling, a hundred times a second.
The headphones play a second wave of their own. Suppose it is an exact copy, in step with the hum.
Sound waves add point by point: crest on crest, trough on trough. The sum swings twice as far — louder, not quieter.
Now delay the copy by half a wave. For a hundred-hertz hum that is five thousandths of a second.
Every crest now meets a trough of the same size, and the sum is flat: the air at your ear barely moves.
Here the hum pushes the air up, and at the same instant the copy pulls it down by exactly as much.
Real headphones flip the sound upside down rather than delay it: a microphone hears the hum, and the speaker plays its mirror image.
That works best on steady, low sounds like an engine's drone — a voice changes too fast to be matched in time.
Any sound is a sum of simple waves like these — Fourier's idea. 3Blue1Brown's video shows how to take a sound apart into them.
Click the still to watch it.

quiz.question: A delay of 5 thousandths of a second silences a 100 Hz hum. What does the same delay do to a 200 Hz hum?
quiz.right: Louder: at 200 hertz, five thousandths of a second is a whole wave, so crest lands on crest again.

commands.speak: How many random draws before their average can be trusted? This Python simulation runs for real, in your browser.
Two knobs: how many draws to take, and a button that throws a fresh batch.
Every draw comes from a bell curve centred on zero, so the true average is exactly zero.
The script prints the sample's average, the number we hope lands on zero.
Beside it, how far such an average typically misses: one over the square root of the number of draws.
Then a histogram of the draws, with the true bell curve drawn over it to compare.
Two hundred draws: the average is 0.016, and the typical miss is 0.071. This batch landed closer than most.
Now twenty draws, then two hundred, then two thousand. The typical miss falls from 0.22 to 0.07 to 0.02.
A hundred times the draws bought only ten times the precision. The miss shrinks with the square root, not with the count.
That the average must settle at all was proved by Jacob Bernoulli; his proof appeared in 1713, eight years after his death.
Drag the draws yourself and press Draw again: at twenty the average jumps about, at two thousand it barely stirs.

quiz.question: An average of 500 draws typically misses by 0.045. How many draws to halve that miss?
quiz.right: Two thousand: the miss shrinks with the square root of the draws, so halving it takes four times as many.

On a ruler from 0.40 to 0.60, our coin lands a hair left of the middle.
Landing exactly on half is not even likely: the script puts the chance of precisely 250 heads under four percent.
What is normal is a wobble of about 0.022 either way. Nineteen fair coins in twenty land inside this band, 0.455 to 0.545.
Three hundred heads would sit at 0.60, far outside it. That coin you should stop trusting.
The band narrows with more flips. Interned in Denmark in the war, John Kerrich flipped a coin ten thousand times and got 5,067 heads.
So a fair coin is not one that lands on half. It is one that lands inside the band.

quiz.right: No: 0.54 is still inside the band where nineteen fair coins in twenty land, so 500 flips cannot convict it.

commands.speak: Why does compound growth curve upward when the rate never changes? A hundred dollars over fifty years, computed in Python.
Two rates, two percent and seven, and the same chart drawn twice.
The only difference between the two charts is how the vertical axis is ruled.
Then the two totals, and what seven percent earns in the first year and in the last.
On an ordinary axis, two percent looks almost straight, and seven percent bends sharply upward.
Two hundred and sixty-nine against 2,946. And the yearly gain grows from seven dollars to a hundred and ninety-three.
That is the bend: seven percent every year, but of an ever bigger pile. Each year's gain is proportional to what is already there.
Now rule the axis by multiples instead: each gridline ten times the one below.
Both curves turn into straight lines. A steady percentage is a steady slope; seven percent just climbs steeper.
So the rate never speeds up. The bend is what steady percentage growth looks like on an axis that counts in dollars.
Logarithms, which John Napier published in 1614, turn multiplying into adding. That is exactly what this axis does to growth.

quiz.question: On a log-scale chart, how does a fund growing a steady 7 % a year look?
quiz.right: A straight line: each year multiplies by the same 1.07, and on a log axis equal multiples are equal steps.

request: Why do the primes thin out? Count them in Python below 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50, adding the bars as you go

elements.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
def is_prime(k):
    divisors = range(2, int(k ** 0.5) + 1)
    return k > 1 and all(k % d for d in divisors)
limits = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
counts = [sum(is_prime(k) for k in range(n)) for n in limits]
for stage in (2, 4, 5):
    plt.figure()
    plt.bar([str(n) for n in limits[:stage]], counts[:stage])
    plt.xlim(-0.6, 4.6)
    plt.ylim(0, 16)
print("share below 50:", counts[-1] / 50)
print("primes below 1000:", sum(is_prime(k) for k in range(1000)))

commands.speak: Why do prime numbers get rarer as numbers grow? We'll count them in Python: below ten, below twenty, and on to fifty.
A number is prime if nothing from two upward divides it evenly.
Only up to its square root: any bigger divisor comes paired with a smaller one, already tried.
Five limits, and for each, the count of primes below it.
The chart grows in three stages, on axes that already leave room for all five bars.
And two numbers to print, for the end.
Four primes below ten, eight below twenty: doubling, so far.
But thirty and forty add only two each: ten, then twelve.
Fifteen below fifty. Still growing, but more and more slowly.
The reason is in the test. Near ten a number only has to dodge two and three; near fifty, five and seven as well.
So the share keeps falling: three in ten below fifty, and below a thousand only 168, about one in six.
As a teenager, Gauss guessed the rule: near a number N, about one in every log of N is prime. Near a thousand, one in seven.
Thinner and thinner, but never gone: Euclid proved there is no largest prime.

quiz.question: Roughly what share of the numbers below a million are prime?
quiz.right: About eight percent, 78,498 of them: the bigger the numbers, the more primes each must dodge, so the share keeps falling.

request: Did Norway get poorer between 2010 and 2020, as its GDP per head in dollars suggests?

commands.speak: Did Norway get poorer between 2010 and 2020? A chart of GDP per person seems to say so. In 2010, Norway: ninety thousand dollars a head.
Sweden fifty-three thousand, Denmark fifty-eight. World Bank figures: each country's output per person, converted into US dollars.
Now 2020. Sweden holds, Denmark creeps up, and Norway drops to seventy-one thousand: a fifth gone.
But the bar is a dollar figure. Norway's output is counted in kroner, then converted at that year's exchange rate.
In 2010 a dollar cost six kroner; in 2020 over nine. The same kroner bought about a third fewer dollars.
Oil went from over a hundred dollars a barrel in 2014 to under thirty in early 2016, and the krone fell with it.
Counted in kroner and corrected for prices, output per Norwegian rose about five percent over the decade. The yardstick shrank, not the economy.
The same chart can mislead a second way. Start the axis at fifty thousand instead of zero.
Now Norway's bar looks seven times Sweden's, though its number is only a third larger.
A bar's length is read as its value, so bars start at zero. Back at zero, the three are close neighbours.

request: How did China overtake Japan and Germany between 1990 and 2020?

commands.speak: How did China go from last of today's four biggest economies to second, in thirty years? Nineteen ninety, in trillions of dollars.
China's economy was under half a trillion, smaller than Italy's then. America's was six trillion, about fifteen times bigger.
Through the nineties China triples. America grows by only about seventy percent.
Yet the gap in dollars widens, from under six trillion to nine. Seventy percent of a big economy is more dollars than tripling a small one.
The next decade China grows fivefold. It passes Germany, then Japan: by 2010 it is the second-largest economy in the world.
By 2020 China reaches fourteen point seven trillion, and the gap to America is down to about six.
Japan's bar even shrank this decade, from 5.7 to 5 trillion: a slow economy, and a weaker yen, counted in dollars.
Now read the top two as a ratio: fifteen times, then eight and a half, then two and a half, then one and a half.
The ratio fell every decade; the dollar gap only began to close once China was big. A faster grower wins the ratio first, the dollars last.

quiz.question: In the 1990s China's economy tripled while America's grew about 70 %. What happened to the dollar gap between them?
quiz.right: It widened, from about 5.6 to 9 trillion: seventy percent of six trillion adds far more dollars than tripling 0.4 trillion.

request: When 100 grows at 2 percent and at 7 percent, how fast does the gap between them grow?

commands.speak: How fast does the gap between two interest rates grow? A hundred at two percent and at seven, one decade per row.
After ten years: a hundred and twenty-two against a hundred and ninety-seven. A gap of seventy-five, and seven percent holds 1.61 times as much.
The rates differ by five points, so you might expect the gap to grow by the same seventy-five every decade.
After twenty years the gap is two hundred and thirty-eight, more than three times as big. The ratio is 2.60.
After thirty, a gap of five hundred and eighty, and seven percent holds 4.20 times as much.
Read down the last column: 1.61, 2.60, 4.20. Each is roughly the one above it, times 1.61.
Divide one growth path by the other, and the ratio is a growth path too: 1.07 over 1.02, about 4.9 percent a year.
So the lead itself compounds, doubling about every fourteen and a half years.
Simon Stevin printed tables like this in 1582, so merchants could look up interest instead of working it out.
So compare two growth rates by their ratio, not their difference: the difference hides that the lead grows by a percentage.

quiz.question: What will the 7 % ÷ 2 % ratio be after forty years?
quiz.right: About 6.8: each decade multiplies the ratio by 1.61, and 4.20 times 1.61 is 6.8. Adding 1.6 would give only 5.8.

Current dollars ask what a year's output would fetch in dollars that year. Constant dollars ask whether the country made more.
Simon Kuznets, who built America's national accounts in the 1930s, warned Congress that such a number is not a measure of welfare either.

commands.speak: Why does seven percent interest end with eleven times as much as two percent, not three and a half? Six checkpoints, a decade apart.
First a hundred dollars at two percent, each year's interest added to the pot.
The bars barely lean: a hundred becomes two hundred and sixty-nine in fifty years.
Now the intuition most people carry: seven percent of the original hundred, seven dollars every year. That is simple interest.
Equal steps, seventy dollars a decade: four hundred and fifty after fifty years. Only about three and a half times the gain.
Real compounding pays seven percent on the whole pot, interest included.
The steps stop being equal. Each bar is roughly double the one before it.
About two hundred, four hundred, eight hundred: the ratio between decades stays fixed, so the gaps keep growing.
Two thousand nine hundred and forty-six against two hundred and sixty-nine: three and a half times the rate, eleven times the money.
The rule of 72: seventy-two divided by the rate is the doubling time. At seven percent, about ten years.
The rule is old.
It already appears in Luca Pacioli's arithmetic book of 1494.
Anything that grows on itself behaves like this: savings, debts, populations. Read such a chart by the doubling, not the step.

request: Why does averaging dice produce a bell curve?

spec.title: Where the bell curve comes from

elements.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
edges = np.linspace(1, 6, 12)
def shares(n):
    means = rng.integers(1, 7, size=(20000, n)).mean(axis=1)
    counts, _ = np.histogram(means, bins=edges)
    return [round(float(c) / 20000, 3) for c in counts]
frames = [shares(1), shares(2), shares(10)]

card.title: Where the bell curve comes from

commands.speak: Why does the bell curve turn up everywhere, even from dice? Roll one die twenty thousand times: each face comes up a sixth of the time.
Six equal spikes. Nothing about one die is bell-shaped.
Now roll two dice and plot their average. The half-steps fill in, and the middle rises.
An average of one needs a double one: one way out of thirty-six.
An average of three and a half has six ways: one and six, two and five, three and four, each either way round.
Average ten dice, and the triangle melts into a bell.
It narrows too. An extreme average needs all ten dice to agree, and that almost never happens.
A third of all averages now land in this one middle bar.
Abraham de Moivre found this curve in 1733, counting heads in long runs of coin tosses.
The dice never changed: each still shows any face a sixth of the time. The bell belongs to the average, not the die.
That is the central limit theorem: add many independent bits of chance, and a bell appears whatever each bit looked like.

quiz.question: After averaging ten dice thousands of times, what is the chance a single die shows a six?
quiz.right: Still one in six: each die is as flat as ever. Only the average of many dice is bell-shaped.

request: How can a kidney-stone treatment win on small stones and on large stones, yet lose overall?

spec.title: Better in each group, worse in total

card.title: Better in each group, worse in total

commands.speak: How can a treatment win in every group yet lose overall? Kidney-stone data from a 1986 British study: open surgery, A, against a keyhole method, B.
Overall, B wins: eighty-three percent of its patients treated successfully, against seventy-eight for A.
Now split the same patients by stone size. On small stones, A wins: ninety-three percent against eighty-seven.
On large stones, A wins again: seventy-three against sixty-nine. Better in both groups, worse in total.
The answer is in the counts. Three quarters of A's patients had large stones; under a quarter of B's did.
Large stones are harder to treat by any method, and the hard cases had mostly gone to open surgery.
Each total is an average of the two rows, weighted by how many patients sit in each. Here is A's.
Three quarters of the weight falls on large stones, so A's total is dragged down towards seventy-three. B's leans the other way, towards eighty-seven.
So the totals compare the mix of patients as much as the treatments. The rows compare like with like.
Edward Simpson described the effect in 1951, but Udny Yule had spotted it about fifty years earlier.

quiz.question: If each treatment had been given to equal numbers of small and large stones, which would have done better overall?
quiz.right: A: half and half gives A about eighty-three percent and B about seventy-eight. With the mix equal, winning in each group wins overall.

The same hundred dollars, grown at two percent and at seven.
The rate sits in the exponent: fifty multiplications by 1.07, each on top of the last year's total.
At two percent the curve looks almost straight: two hundred and sixty-nine after fifty years.
For contrast, simply adding seven dollars a year, never earning on the gains.
That is a straight line to four hundred and fifty: seven a year, fifty times, no surprises.
Compounding at seven bends away from it, to 2,946. The whole gap between the two lines is interest earned on interest.
Read it decade by decade: 197, 387, 761, 1,497, 2,946. Every ten years, roughly double.
So the last decade alone adds 1,450 dollars: more than the first forty years together.
Don't misread the flat-looking line: two percent also doubles, just every thirty-five years. On this scale the big numbers squash the small ones.
The shortcut — seventy-two divided by the rate gives the doubling time — is already in Luca Pacioli's arithmetic book of 1494.

quiz.question: At 7 %, how long does 1,500 dollars take to grow to 3,000?
quiz.right: About ten years: at seven percent every doubling takes ten years, whether it starts from 100 dollars or from 1,500.

request: What does 'flattening the curve' actually change in an epidemic?

elements.code:
def sir(r0, days=300, gamma=0.1):
    s, i, out = 0.999, 0.001, []
    for d in range(days):
        out.append(round(i, 4))
        new = r0 * gamma * s * i
        s, i = s - new, i + new - gamma * i
    return out
days = list(range(300))
frames = [sir(2.5), sir(1.4)]
limit = [0.1] * 300

commands.speak: What does flattening the curve actually change? The same virus in the same town, simulated with the simplest epidemic model there is.
When each case infects two and a half others, the wave peaks on day 51 with a quarter of the town ill at once.
Read the height carefully: it counts people ill on that day, not people who have ever been ill.
Now a line for what the hospitals can handle: one person in ten ill at once, a made-up level for the picture.
The tall wave stays above it for more than five weeks: more patients than beds, and people who could have been treated are not.
The area under the curve counts all the sickness: in this wave, ninety percent of the town falls ill at some point.
Cut contacts until each case infects 1.4 others. The same wave comes later, lower and longer.
Its peak is under five percent, on day 133, and it never crosses the line.
Its area shrank too: about half the town is infected in the slow wave, against ninety percent in the fast one.
But half the town is still susceptible, so lifting the distancing too early can start a second wave.
In 1918 Philadelphia held a war-bond parade while St. Louis closed its schools and theatres; Philadelphia's death rate peaked far higher.

quiz.question: What does the height of this curve show on day 60?
choices: How many have ever been ill
How many are ill that day
How many new cases that day
quiz.right: How many are ill that day: the height is people ill at once, which is what hospitals must cope with; the total is the area.

request: Why look at a scatter plot when the summary statistics already agree? Anscombe's quartet

commands.speak: Why plot data when the summary numbers already agree?
Eleven points, from a paper the statistician Francis Anscombe published in 1973.
The least-squares line: y equals three plus half of x. The correlation is 0.82, a respectable trend.
Read it as the line intends: a noisy cloud, points scattered evenly above and below.
Now the points move to Anscombe's second set. Same means, same line, same correlation, to two decimals.
But there is no noise at all: the points lie on a smooth arch that rises and falls.
A straight line is simply the wrong shape here: too low in the middle, too high at both ends.
The third set: ten points on an exact straight line, and one far above it, at x equals thirteen.
That single point tilts the fit. Without it, the other ten give a slope of 0.35, not 0.5.
A noisy trend, a curve, an outlier: the summary numbers cannot tell them apart. The picture can.
Anscombe had a fourth set: ten points stacked at one x, and a single point far to the right that makes the whole slope.

quiz.question: Two datasets share the same means, fitted line and correlation. What do you know about their shape?
quiz.right: Nothing yet: Anscombe's sets share all those numbers while one is a curve and one has an outlier. Only the plot shows the shape.

request: If students who study more score higher, does studying cause the higher scores? A simulation in Python

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
hours = np.arange(1, 13)
# world A: each hour adds 4 points
a = 40 + 4 * hours + rng.normal(0, 6, 12)
# world B: keenness drives hours AND scores
keen = hours + rng.normal(0, 1.5, 12)
b = 40 + 4 * keen + rng.normal(0, 6, 12)
scores = [a.round(1).tolist(), b.round(1).tolist()]

commands.speak: Students who study more score higher, but does the studying cause it? Twelve made-up students, one to twelve hours each.
In world A we build the answer in: each hour adds four points, plus noise, because nobody's brain is a formula.
One dot per student. The trend is clear, and so is the scatter around it.
Two lines of numpy fit the least-squares line and hand its slope and intercept to the chart.
The slope is the reading: about four points per extra hour, close to the four we built in.
World B is different. Keen students both study more and score higher; the hours themselves add nothing.
The four points now ride on keenness; hours merely travel along with it.
Both worlds go to the chart as two stages.
Here is world B. The dots move, but the cloud tells the same story.
The world A line still runs right through it. From the dots alone you cannot tell which world you are in.
Only an experiment settles it: assign some students extra hours at random, and see whether their scores move.

quiz.question: In world B, a student is made to study two extra hours. What happens to their expected score?
quiz.right: No change: in world B keenness drives both, so forcing extra hours leaves the score where it was, although the chart shows the same slope.

request: How do you read a correlation matrix, and what do its warm and cool cells mean?

commands.speak: How do you read a correlation matrix? Four health measures in illustrative numbers, blood pressure as BP, each paired with every other: one cell per pair.
Each cell runs from minus one to one. Warm: the two rise together. Cool: one falls as the other rises.
Age first. Against itself it is exactly one, as every cell on the diagonal is, so the diagonal carries no news.
Age against blood pressure reads 0.51, the deepest warm cell off the diagonal: older people here tend to have higher pressure.
Income is the cool row: minus 0.12 with age, minus 0.21 with blood pressure.
Colour gives the sign, depth gives the strength. Minus 0.21 is exactly as strong as plus 0.21, only pointing the other way.
BMI and blood pressure complete the grid, and the lower half mirrors the upper: 0.51 appears twice.
Every pair is printed twice, so papers often blank one triangle. Nothing is lost.
The palest cell, BMI against income at 0.08, means no straight-line link. It does not mean no link at all.
A U-shape, high at both ends and low in the middle, can score a correlation of zero: r only sees straight lines.
Francis Galton coined 'co-relation' in 1888, comparing people's height with the length of their forearms.

quiz.question: A cell in a correlation matrix reads −0.6, a deep cool blue. What does it say?
choices: A strong link, pointing opposite ways
quiz.right: A strong link: as one rises the other tends to fall. The minus sign gives the direction; 0.6 gives the strength, deeper than any warm cell here.

request: Does a strong correlation mean a big effect? A correlation matrix computed with pandas

commands.speak: Does a strong correlation mean a big effect? Four hundred simulated people, seeded, so we know exactly how every number was made.
Ages spread around fifty, give or take twelve years; BMI drifts up a little with age.
Systolic blood pressure is built from both, plus noise.
Each point of BMI adds 1.1 to the pressure…
…while each year of age adds only 0.45. Per unit, BMI is the bigger push.
pandas builds the frame, and one call to corr computes every pairwise correlation for the grid.
The same three variables down the side and along the top; warm means rising together, deeper means tighter.
Every cell is warm, and the diagonal is one: each variable matches itself.
Yet age against blood pressure reads 0.57, and BMI only 0.36. The smaller push has the bigger correlation.
The reason is spread. Ages vary by about eleven years, and eleven times 0.45 moves the pressure five points.
BMI varies by only two and a half units here: times 1.1, under three points.
A correlation measures how much of the variation a variable accounts for in this sample, not how hard each unit of it pushes.
Karl Pearson gave the coefficient its modern formula in 1896, which is why it is called Pearson's r.

quiz.question: Rerun this with only people aged 49 to 51. What happens to the age–pressure correlation?
quiz.right: It falls towards zero: age barely varies, so it moves the pressure by under a point against eight points of noise, though each year still adds 0.45.

commands.speak: Why do most people earn less than the average? Two hundred made-up incomes in R will show it, seeded so they come out the same every time.
Each income starts at forty thousand dollars and is multiplied by a random factor, the way raises and setbacks come as percentages.
The factor is e to a bell-curve draw: good luck can multiply an income by four, bad luck only shrinks it towards zero.
Two ways to name a typical income: the mean, the total shared out equally, and the median, the person in the middle.
Then the share of people who earn less than the mean.
And a histogram, with the mean as a red line and the median as a blue one.
The mean is 54.7 thousand, the median 46.5. Sixty percent of these people earn less than the average.
The histogram is lopsided: a crowd between twenty and sixty thousand, and a thin tail running out past two hundred.
The median only asks who stands in the middle. The mean adds up every dollar, so the few big incomes drag it to the right.
Add random amounts instead of multiplying, and the bell stays symmetric: mean and median sit together, and half earn below average.
In 1931 the French engineer Robert Gibrat argued that growth in proportion to size makes incomes and firms lopsided in just this way.
So below average is where most people are, wherever luck comes as percentages.

quiz.question: In a lopsided income distribution like this one, what share of people earn less than the average?
quiz.right: More than half: the few large incomes in the tail pull the mean above the median, and the median is where half the people are.

card.title: A few items carry the shop

commands.speak: What does a sorted sales table show that the raw one hides? pandas and plotly express, in a Python light enough to load in a second.
A small bakery's week, in made-up numbers: six items, a thousand dollars of sales, listed alphabetically.
Into a table, one row per item.
Each item's share of the week: its sales divided by the total.
Then sort from the best seller down. The alphabet hid the pattern; this order asks where the money comes from.
A running share adds the shares as we go down the list: how much of the week do the top items bring?
Print the table, and chart the shares as bars.
Cake alone is half the sales. Cake and pies together, two items of six, bring in seventy-five percent.
The other four, two thirds of the menu, share the last quarter. Tarts bring three percent.
If every item pulled equal weight, each bar would stand at seventeen percent, and the running share would climb in even steps.
Joseph Juran called this lopsidedness the Pareto principle, after Vilfredo Pareto, who found most of Italy's land owned by a small share of its people.
Sort, then add up: two lines of pandas find where the weight sits in any list.

quiz.question: Four of the six items are two thirds of the menu. What share of the week's sales do they bring?
quiz.right: About a quarter: the running share is already 0.75 after cake and pies, so the other four together bring the last 0.25.

request: In minimal Python (MicroPython): if interest is added more and more often, does a year's growth grow without limit?

commands.speak: If interest is added more and more often, does money grow without limit? One dollar at a hundred percent a year, in a Python of half a megabyte.
Split the year into n pieces: once, twice, quarterly, monthly, weekly, daily.
Each piece earns a hundred percent divided by n, and each piece's interest earns interest in all the pieces after it.
Print what the dollar has become by the end of the year.
The last line is left bare, so its value shows: a number we will need in a moment.
Once a year, the dollar becomes two. Twice a year, 2.25. Monthly, 2.61. Daily, 2.7146.
Each step gains less than the one before. Going from monthly to daily, thirty times as often, adds barely ten cents.
The tempting guess is that twice as often means twice the bonus, without end. Instead the gains shrink towards a ceiling.
The ceiling is e, 2.71828. Interest added every instant still turns one dollar into less than 2.72.
More pieces mean more interest on interest, but each piece earns less; the two effects balance ever more closely, and the total levels off.
Jacob Bernoulli asked this very question about a sum lent at full interest in 1683, and so found the number now called e.
At five percent a year, daily adding pays 5.13 percent instead of 5: the rate matters far more than how often it is added.

quiz.question: A bank adds the 100 % interest every second instead of every day. What does the dollar become in a year?
quiz.right: About 2.72: daily adding already reaches 2.7146, and every second only closes the last cents to the ceiling, e.

request: Why is the cutoff for a two-sided test at five percent 1.96, not 1.645? The critical values computed in Python

commands.speak: Why does a test at five percent reject beyond 1.96 standard errors, and not some other number? This curve is what chance alone produces.
It is centred on zero, the result a treatment with no effect would give on average.
Each rung is one standard error: how far a result wobbles by chance alone.
The test sets aside the five percent of results least likely under no effect. Two-sided, that five percent is split: 2.5 in each tail.
Python's inverse normal found the point with exactly 2.5 percent beyond it: 1.96 standard errors.
Put all five percent in the right tail instead, and the cutoff moves in, to 1.645. A one-sided test is easier to pass.
So a result 1.8 standard errors above zero passes the one-sided test and fails the two-sided one. Same data, different verdict.
That is why the side is chosen before the data arrive. Picking it after seeing which way the result fell doubles the false alarms, to ten percent.
Two-sided, the cutoff stays at 1.96.
The same 1.96 builds the 95 percent confidence interval, estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors. The test rejects exactly when that interval misses zero.
Abraham de Moivre found this curve in 1733, as a shortcut for adding up the chances of long runs of coin tosses.

quiz.question: A trial's result lies 1.8 standard errors above zero. Is it significant at 5 %?
choices: No test could call it significant
quiz.right: Only one-sided, chosen in advance: 1.8 clears the one-tail cutoff of 1.645, but not 1.96, where a two-sided test splits its five percent.

request: What should a meta-analysis do when its trials disagree? Four trials pooled in Python, with and without random effects

elements.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import chi2
est = np.array([0.82, 0.71, 1.12, 0.55])
lo = np.array([0.63, 0.55, 0.90, 0.42])
hi = np.array([1.07, 0.92, 1.39, 0.72])
y = np.log(est)
se = (np.log(hi) - np.log(lo)) / (2 * 1.96)
w = 1 / se ** 2
fixed = (w * y).sum() / w.sum()
q = (w * (y - fixed) ** 2).sum()
df = len(y) - 1
p_het = round(float(chi2.sf(q, df)), 4)
i2 = round(max(0.0, (q - df) / q), 2)
tau2 = max(0.0, (q - df) / (w.sum() - (w ** 2).sum() / w.sum()))
wr = 1 / (se ** 2 + tau2)
mu = (wr * y).sum() / wr.sum()
half = 1.96 / np.sqrt(wr.sum())
pooled = {k: round(float(np.exp(v)), 3) for k, v in
          [("est", mu), ("lo", mu - half), ("hi", mu + half)]}

commands.speak: A meta-analysis pools trials into one estimate. But what if the trials disagree? Four trials of a drug against relapse; a risk ratio below 1 means it helps.
Anderson finds 0.82 and Bianchi 0.71: both lean towards benefit.
Carter finds 1.12: if anything, more relapses on the drug.
Diallo finds 0.55, a large benefit. Its interval and Carter's do not even overlap.
The simple pooled average, weighting each trial by its precision, gives 0.81, from 0.71 to 0.91: a confident benefit.
But that average assumes one true effect, with trials differing only by chance. Trials this far apart would arise by chance less than once in a thousand.
The measure I-squared puts it in one number: eighty-three percent of the spread between these trials is real difference, not noise.
So Python pools with random effects: each trial has its own true effect, and the diamond estimates their average: 0.78, from 0.58 to 1.05.
The diamond is wider, and it now crosses 1. The confident answer came from pretending the trials agreed.
The better question is no longer the average, but why Carter and Diallo differ: other patients, other doses, other follow-up.
I-squared is young: Julian Higgins and Simon Thompson proposed it in 2002, and most meta-analyses now report it.

quiz.question: The trials disagree far more than chance allows. How does the random-effects diamond compare with the fixed-effect one?
quiz.right: Wider: it must cover how much the true effect varies from trial to trial, not only each trial's sampling error.

request: What does 'median survival not reached' mean, and what can a survival curve say instead? Kaplan-Meier computed from the death counts

def km(at_risk, deaths):
    s, out = 1.0, []
    for d in deaths:
        s *= 1 - d / at_risk
        at_risk -= d
        out.append(round(s, 3))
    return out

treated = km(120, [0, 9, 11, 10, 7, 6])
control = km(118, [0, 18, 20, 15, 12, 9])
# area under each curve over months 0-5
rmst = [round(sum(a[:5]), 2) for a in (treated, control)]

commands.speak: How much longer does a treatment keep patients alive? Trials usually answer with the median, and sometimes the median cannot be found. One trial, month by month.
Standard care: 118 patients. Eighteen die in month one, twenty in month two; after five months forty-four are alive, thirty-seven percent.
Treatment: 120 patients and fewer deaths every month. After five months seventy-seven are alive, sixty-four percent.
Median survival is where a curve falls to one half. On standard care that happens in month four.
The treated curve never gets there: most are still alive when follow-up ends. The report says 'median not reached', and the comparison has no number.
The area under each curve still gives one. It counts the months lived, on average, within the five months followed.
Under standard care, 3.5 of the first five months. Under treatment, 4.2.
The shaded gap between the staircases is the gain: two-thirds of a month per patient, about three weeks, on average.
A median reads one height on one curve. The area uses every month, so early deaths and late ones all count.
Its name is the restricted mean survival time: restricted, because it stops where follow-up stops, and says nothing about month six.
Told in 1982 that his cancer's median survival was eight months, Stephen Jay Gould wrote 'The Median Isn't the Message'. He lived twenty more years.

quiz.question: Two drugs have the same median survival, 12 months. Can their mean survival differ?
choices: No, same median means same survival
Yes, the areas under the curves can differ
Only if the trials differ in size
quiz.right: Yes: the median reads one point on each curve, while the area adds up every month, so what happens before and after the halfway point still counts.

request: Why is a cost-effectiveness acceptability curve a slope and not a yes-or-no?

elements.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
cost = rng.normal(9000, 3000, 4000)
qaly = rng.normal(0.22, 0.09, 4000)
icer = round(cost.mean() / qaly.mean() / 1000, 1)
wtp = np.arange(1, 101)
p = np.array([(1000 * w * qaly - cost > 0).mean() for w in wtp])
mid = float(wtp[np.abs(p - 0.5).argmin()])
width = round(float(10 / (4 * (p[int(mid) + 4] - p[int(mid) - 6]))), 1)

commands.speak: Why is an acceptability curve a gentle slope, not a yes or no? Along the bottom: what we would pay for one QALY, in thousands of dollars.
Suppose we knew a new drug adds exactly 0.22 QALYs for 9,000 dollars more. Then the answer would be a step.
Nine thousand over 0.22 is about forty-one thousand per QALY, the ICER. Below it the drug never pays its way; above it, it always does.
But both numbers are uncertain. The script draws four thousand plausible pairs, cost give or take 3,000, gain give or take 0.09, and at each price counts the drug's wins.
Standard care is the mirror image: in every draw, exactly one of the two comes out ahead.
The step has been smeared into a slope, centred where the step stood. How wide the smear is, is how much we don't know.
At thirty thousand the step said never. Yet the drug wins in just over a quarter of the draws: those where it works better than the mean.
At fifty thousand the step said always, and the drug wins in only about two draws of three.
So the curve holds two things at once: where the ICER lies, and how sure we are of it.
Pinning that second thing down is why England's NICE has asked for probabilistic analysis like this since its 2004 methods guide.

quiz.question: A larger trial halves the uncertainty about the drug's effect. At $30,000 per QALY, the chance it is cost-effective…
quiz.right: It falls. Less uncertainty steepens the curve around the same crossing, near forty-one thousand, so below it the drug wins in fewer draws.

card.title: Did the minimum wage cost jobs?

commands.speak: Did New Jersey's minimum-wage rise, from $4.25 to $5.05 in April 1992, cost jobs? Difference-in-differences answers by comparing with a neighbour that stood still.
Card and Krueger surveyed fast-food restaurants in February and again in November. In New Jersey, jobs per restaurant went from 20.44 to 21.03.
Jobs means full-time equivalents: full-timers and managers, plus half of each part-timer.
Across the river, eastern Pennsylvania kept its minimum at $4.25. Its restaurants went from 23.33 to 21.17.
Pennsylvania starting higher does not matter: the method compares changes, not levels.
The step to see: had New Jersey changed as Pennsylvania did, it would have fallen 2.16, to 18.28. That third line is borrowed, never observed.
What happened minus what would have: 21.03 minus 18.28, about 2.75 more jobs per restaurant. Not fewer.
Now split that 2.75. New Jersey's own change was only 0.59.
The other 2.16 is Pennsylvania's fall. Most of the estimate comes from the comparison state, so the result rests on believing New Jersey would have fallen too.
That is why the study was fought over for years, with payroll records and new data. It changed how economists argue about minimum wages.
David Card shared the 2021 Nobel prize partly for this work. Alan Krueger, his co-author, had died two years earlier.

quiz.question: Suppose Pennsylvania had held steady at 23.33 jobs per restaurant. What would the estimate be?
quiz.right: +0.59: with a flat comparison, the estimate is just New Jersey's own change. The comparison state's path is half of every difference-in-differences.

commands.speak: Why estimate a reform's effect quarter by quarter, rather than as one before-and-after number? The quarter-by-quarter picture is an event study.
Take a simulated reform: forty hospitals start caring for frail patients at home, each compared with a similar hospital that does not.
Each dot is the gap in emergency admissions per thousand residents, against the quarter just before the reform. Before it, the gaps sit on zero.
The script fits a line through them too: a slope of almost nothing, so the comparison hospitals were moving in step.
In the first quarter after the reform, admissions fall by about half a case per thousand.
Then more each quarter, to nearly two by the fifth. The whiskers, from the script's standard errors, stay well clear of zero.
And the effect is still growing when the data stop.
One before-and-after number averages these five: about 1.2. That is neither where the effect started nor where it ended up.
Worse, it depends on when you stop looking. Two quarters of data would have said 0.7.
When reforms start at different dates and effects grow like this, the usual pooled regression can even get the sign wrong, as Andrew Goodman-Bacon showed in 2021.
So an event study answers two questions a single number merges: was there an effect, and how did it unfold?

quiz.question: A reform's effect grows every quarter. If you pool two years of data instead of one, the single before-and-after estimate will be…
quiz.right: Larger. A pooled number averages a growing effect, so a longer window takes in the bigger later quarters; the quarter-by-quarter dots stay where they are.

request: Why does an epidemic wave turn around before everyone is infected? An SIR model in R

elements.code:
sir <- function(r0, days = 250, gamma = 0.1) {
  s <- 0.999; i <- 0.001
  S <- I <- numeric(days)
  for (d in seq_len(days)) {
    S[d] <- round(s, 4); I[d] <- round(i, 4)
    new <- r0 * gamma * s * i
    s <- s - new
    i <- i + new - gamma * i
  }
  list(S = S, I = I)
}
a <- sir(2.5); b <- sir(1.4)
days <- 0:249
sus <- list(a$S, b$S); ill <- list(a$I, b$I)

commands.speak: Why does an epidemic wave turn around while many people are still uninfected? A model in R: almost everyone starts susceptible, one in a thousand ill.
Each day, new infections are made where the ill meet the susceptible…
…so they grow with both shares at once: fewer susceptibles, fewer new cases, however many are ill.
And a tenth of the ill recover each day, leaving the game.
Run it for 250 days with each case infecting 2.5 others, then with 1.4.
The susceptible share falls, fast at first, as the virus uses people up.
The ill share rises into a wave that peaks on day 51, with nearly a quarter ill at once.
Read the two lines together: at the peak, the susceptible share has fallen to forty percent.
That is one over 2.5. Each case now meets so few susceptibles that it infects exactly one other: fewer than one, and the wave must shrink.
At 1.4 the wave turns much earlier, while seventy-one percent are still susceptible: one over 1.4.
A wave ends not because the virus weakens, but because each case finds too few people left to infect.
Kermack and McKendrick published this model in 1927, with this threshold at its heart.

quiz.question: A virus spreads with each case infecting 4 others. At what susceptible share does its wave peak?
quiz.right: Twenty-five percent: one over four. Below that, each case infects fewer than one other, so the wave shrinks.

commands.speak: How far can a fitted line be trusted? Eleven simulated children, aged two to twelve, each measured once, in R.
Each is built to grow about six centimetres a year, plus a few centimetres of individual difference.
Here they are: a tight, rising cloud, from 87 centimetres at two to 148 at twelve.
lm finds the line that makes the squared vertical gaps from the dots as small as possible.
coef hands its slope and intercept to the chart.
6.29 centimetres a year. Inside the data it is superb: it accounts for 98 percent of the spread.
But the axis runs on to age thirty-two, and the line runs with it. Nothing in it knows where the data stopped.
Now one grown-up, left out of the fit: 170 centimetres at thirty.
The adult lands far below the line.
At thirty the line says 263. It is off by almost a metre, though it fitted the children nearly perfectly.
It fails backwards too: at age zero it says 74.5 centimetres, where a newborn is about 50.
Forwards, by about thirty-one it passes 2.72 metres, the height of Robert Wadlow, the tallest person on record.
Nothing in these eleven dots could warn us: they never saw growth stop. A fit describes the range it was given, and only that.

quiz.right: Little: children from two to twelve cannot show growth stopping, so the line's 200 centimetres at twenty is a guess dressed as a fit.

Twelve made-up runners: kilometres trained per week, and minutes over ten kilometres.
More training, faster times, but with plenty of scatter.
The simplest forecast ignores training: everyone gets the average, 52.9 minutes. The dots miss it by 5.7 minutes, typically.
An OLS formula, time against kilometres, finds the line with the smallest squared misses.
About sixteen seconds faster for every extra weekly kilometre.

Yet here is Ada, forty kilometres a week, nearly six minutes slower than the line says.
Seventy percent sounds like near certainty, but the misses that remain are still about three minutes, runner to runner.

card.title: How many draws make a bell

commands.speak: Why does a histogram of a hundred random draws look so lumpy, and how many draws does it take to show the bell they came from?
First the true bell itself, computed point by point, so every histogram has the right answer drawn over it.
Two sample sizes, a hundred and ten thousand, both drawn from that same bell.
Each gets its own histogram. Density scaling puts both on one scale, so their shapes can be compared directly.
The bell on top, fixed axes, a title, and show it: two figures from one script.
A hundred draws: ragged bars, some well above the curve, some well below. Yet every one of them came from a perfect bell.
A bar that should hold ten draws typically gets seven to thirteen: chance moves it by about a third of its height.
Ten thousand draws, and the bars hug the curve.
A bar that should hold a thousand gets between 970 and 1030: three percent. A hundred times the data, ten times smoother.
The wobble shrinks with the square root of the count, not with the count: to halve it, you need four times the draws.
The same square root sets a poll's margin: a thousand people give about three points either way, whatever the size of the country.
So a lumpy small sample is no evidence against the bell: a shape can only be judged once there are draws enough to show it.

quiz.question: To make each bar's chance wobble half as big, how many draws do you need?
quiz.right: Four times as many: the wobble shrinks with the square root of the count, and the square root of four is two.

commands.speak: Why do neighbouring Fibonacci numbers settle into one odd ratio, 1.618? Two ones to start, in MicroPython, a Python small enough for a microcontroller.
Each step slides the pair along: one and two, two and three, three and five, the new number always the sum of the last two.
And it records the new number divided by the one before.
The ratios: two, then one and a half, 1.67, 1.6, 1.625. They jump above and below, closing in.
Mind the axis: it starts at 1.4, not zero, so the wobble looks big. By the tenth step it is in the fourth decimal.
Why the zigzag? The next ratio is b plus a, over b: one plus one over the last ratio.
A ratio that is too big makes one over it too small, so the next ratio undershoots, and each miss is smaller than the last.
The zigzag stops only at a number the rule gives back unchanged.
Multiply through and phi squared equals phi plus one, whose positive root is one plus root five, over two: the golden ratio.
Fibonacci posed the sequence in 1202 as a puzzle about breeding rabbits; the golden ratio hiding in it was noticed only centuries later.

quiz.question: Start with 3 and 10 instead of 1 and 1. Where does the ratio settle?
quiz.right: At 1.618: the rule, one plus one over the last ratio, never looks at the starting pair, so every start zigzags to the same number.

card.title: What a positive test is worth

commands.speak: How likely is a positive screening test to be right? Take a test that catches ninety percent of the sick and clears ninety-five percent of the healthy.
A small function: true positives, the sick it catches, against false positives, the healthy it wrongly flags.
Three groups to screen: one person in a thousand ill, one in a hundred, and one in ten.
For each, the chance after one positive, and after a second positive on another test.
The second test starts from the first answer: the people it sees have already tested positive once.
The rows go in as a list of lists, because MicroPython's dictionaries do not keep their order, and the columns would shuffle.
One in a thousand ill: a positive is right less than two percent of the time. One in ten: two times in three.
Picture a thousand people at one in a thousand: one is sick and caught, while five percent of the other 999, about fifty, get false alarms.
A second positive lifts the first row from 1.8 to 24.5 percent: the first test did the work of picking a high-risk group.
The test is the same in every row; only who was tested changed. Prevalence decides what a positive is worth.
That second step assumes the two tests err independently, which is why a positive HIV screen is confirmed with a different kind of test.

quiz.question: One person in a thousand is ill, and your screening test is positive. A second, different test is positive too. The chance you are ill is about…
quiz.right: About a quarter: the first positive raised the odds from one in a thousand to about two in a hundred, and the second test starts from there.

Five years in, Delta has led four years running, on a hundred and fifty-one. Only the top five stand on the board.
A record like that would sell itself. But Delta had no edge at all: the same dice as everyone else.
By 2015 Delta has slipped to fourth, and Alfa leads on two hundred and six.

The one-percent bar now fills less than a fifth of the plot, though it has grown by a third.

Month twenty-two. The view starts at month ten, and Nord's fifty percent, the tallest peak of the whole epidemic, has scrolled off the left.

commands.speak: Why do five identical urns end up so unequal? Each starts with five balls, and each new ball joins an urn in proportion to what it already holds.
Sixty-five balls in, the shares already differ: Urn C holds twenty-nine percent, Urn B under fourteen.
Nothing sets the urns apart but luck: an urn that wins an early ball becomes likelier to win the next.
By a hundred and eighty-five balls, Urn E leads on thirty percent, and Urn B has fallen under eight.
By four hundred and twenty-five, the fan has stopped opening: E on thirty-two, B on six and a half.
Why it freezes: with twenty-five balls, one more moves an urn's share by three points. With eight hundred, by less than a tenth of a point.
Eight hundred and twenty-five balls. E holds about a third, B about a sixteenth, and E has led at every count since ball one-eighty-five.
Choose the urns evenly instead, and every share would settle near twenty percent. The inequality comes from the rule, not from the urns.
Rerun it with another seed and a different urn wins.
George Pólya studied this urn in 1923: each share settles, but where it settles is chance.
So Urn B was never worse at anything. It lost a few early draws, and under this rule the early draws are the ones that count.
