Every cell is an estimate, and at twenty people the estimates are poor.
Fifty draws. B against C falls to 0.54, but the noise column still finds correlations near 0.2 where there are none.
Two hundred draws: 0.44, and the noise has cooled to almost nothing.

For pure noise, a sample correlation wanders by about one over the square root of n: 0.22 at twenty people, 0.03 at a thousand.
So a pale-warm 0.2 from twenty people is exactly what noise produces. From a thousand, it would be a real signal.
Ronald Fisher worked out in 1915 how sample correlations scatter around the truth, which is how we know how many people a study needs.

quiz.right: About 0.1: one over the square root of a hundred. A correlation of 0.1 from a hundred people is no evidence of anything.

commands.speak: Does a fair coin even out: after a run of heads, do the tails catch up? Five hundred flips in light Python, typed as we go.
Seeded, so the same flips come back every time, and three tallies: heads so far, the share of heads, and the gap.
Five hundred flips, each adding a head or nothing.
After every flip, store the share of heads, and heads minus tails.
Print both after ten flips and after all five hundred.
The first plot: the share, with a flat line at one half.
The second: heads minus tails, with a line at zero.
Run it. The share of heads is seventy percent after ten flips, fifty-two after five hundred.
Plotted, the share swings wildly over the first flips, then settles close to a half: the law of large numbers.
But heads minus tails does not shrink. Heads led by four after ten flips, and by twenty after five hundred.
The coin has no memory: after a run of heads, the next flip is still fifty-fifty, so nothing pulls the count back.
The share settles anyway, because a gap of twenty is large among twenty flips and tiny among five hundred: it is swamped, not repaid.
Believing the tails are due is the gambler's fallacy; at Monte Carlo in 1913, black came up twenty-six times in a row while players bet on red.
Change the seed and run it yourself: the share always settles, the gap goes wherever it likes.

commands.speak: How do you study the wages of Norway's women when you may never see a single person's record? On microdata.no, you write a script.
The registers cover everyone living in Norway. The first line names the database to ask, the second opens an empty dataset of your own.
Then you pull in a variable for the whole population: sex, which the register stores as a code, one or two.
And wage income, read at a date. A register variable always belongs to a moment, so the script has to say which.
Keep only the women: code two.
The step that feels odd: you never look at a row and pick it. You describe the rows you want, and the server picks.
Now summarise. One word, and the counting happens on the server, not on your computer.
Back comes a table: how many, the mean, the spread. Here the data are synthetic, so no real person is behind these numbers.
That is the whole bargain. The statistics come out; the individuals never leave the wall.
Change the year, or keep the men instead, and run it yourself.

quiz.question: What does the summarize line send back to you?
choices: Every woman's wage, row by row
Statistics about all of them together
A random sample of rows to check
quiz.right: Statistics about the whole group: count, mean, spread. On microdata.no the rows stay on the server, and only aggregates come back.

request: Why did the Commodore 64 outsell every other computer model?

commands.speak: Why did the Commodore 64 outsell every other computer model? Start with the machine: a keyboard box you plugged into the family television.
In 1982 it cost five hundred and ninety-five dollars, with sixty-four kilobytes of memory, a lot for a home machine then.
For contrast, the IBM PC, a year older, started at fifteen hundred and sixty-five dollars.
The real advantage was underneath. Commodore owned MOS Technology, the firm that made its processor, its graphics chip and its sound chip.
So it could cut the price again and again. By the middle of 1983 a C64 sold for about three hundred dollars.
Rivals who bought their chips from others could not follow that far. Texas Instruments gave up on home computers late in 1983.
It was sold where families already shopped, in department and toy stores, not only by computer dealers.
And for that price it was a real games machine: moving sprites, and the SID, a three-voice synthesiser chip.
So it did not win by being the best computer. It won by being the cheapest good one, cheap because Commodore made its own parts.
Jack Tramiel, Commodore's founder, had a slogan for it: computers for the masses, not the classes.
Here is what most of them were bought for. Find your way out of the maze, then close the emulator.
Guinness World Records lists it as the best-selling single computer model; estimates run from twelve and a half to seventeen million.

quiz.question: Why could Commodore keep cutting the C64's price when its rivals could not?
choices: It had less memory than rivals
Shops sold it at a loss
quiz.right: It made its own chips: owning MOS Technology meant no supplier's margin, so each price cut cost Commodore less than it cost its rivals.

request: How do you write your first program on a Commodore 64?

elements.code:
10 PRINT CHR$(147)
20 FOR I=1 TO 5
30 PRINT "HELLO, WORLD"
40 NEXT I
50 POKE 53280,0
60 POKE 53281,0

commands.speak: How do you write a program on a Commodore 64? You switch it on and start typing: it boots straight into BASIC.
The number in front is what makes this a program. The machine stores the line instead of doing it, and waits for RUN.
The line itself clears the screen. Character one hundred and forty-seven is the clear-screen key, so printing it wipes the screen.
A loop: FOR I equals one TO five, print, NEXT. Three lines, and the middle one runs five times.
Two POKEs. Address fifty-three thousand two hundred and eighty is the border colour, eighty-one the background. Zero is black.
A POKE writes one byte straight into a chip. This BASIC had no commands for graphics or sound, so POKE was how everyone reached the chips.
RUN. The screen clears, five greetings, and the colours go black. Then READY: the program is still stored, ready to run again.
Why count in tens? Lines run in number order, not typing order, so a line 25 typed tomorrow slots in between 20 and 30.
Numbering in tens was the habit that left room for second thoughts.
Now a lunar lander someone wrote in ten lines of this same BASIC. Land softly, then close the emulator.

quiz.question: You finish the program, then type a new line 35 at the end. When does it run?
quiz.right: Between 30 and 40: the machine runs lines in number order, whatever order you typed them in, so line 35 lands inside the loop.

request: What is immediate mode on a Commodore 64, and how is it different from a program?

elements.code:
PRINT 2+2
P=595
PRINT P/2
POKE 53280,0
POKE 53281,0
PRINT CHR$(158);"HELLO"

commands.speak: What is immediate mode? It is a Commodore 64 doing each line the moment you press RETURN, with no program at all.
Type PRINT two plus two, and press RETURN.
Four, with a space in front where a minus sign would go. Then READY: the machine has finished, and says so.
P equals five hundred and ninety-five. Nothing is printed, but the machine now remembers P.
So PRINT P over two answers two hundred and ninety-seven point five. The lines are gone, the variable stays.
POKE writes one byte straight into the video chip. Fifty-three thousand two hundred and eighty is the border: zero, black.
And eighty-one is the background.
Colours are characters too: character one hundred and fifty-eight switches the ink to yellow before the word.
Every line was done at once and then dropped. The machine kept only what the lines changed: P, and the colours.
Now put a number in front. Press RETURN, and nothing happens: the line is stored as part of a program, waiting for RUN.
That is the whole difference. Immediate mode and a program speak the same BASIC; a line number just says: not now, later.
That BASIC came from Microsoft: Commodore licensed it, and close cousins of it ran on the Apple II and many other machines of the time.

quiz.question: You type 10 PRINT 2+2 and press RETURN. What appears?
quiz.right: Nothing: a line number tells the machine to store the line in its program and wait for RUN, instead of doing it now.

request: Where exactly is the liver?

commands.speak: Where exactly is the liver? Higher, and further to one side, than most people point. Here is a torso facing you, the way a doctor sees a patient.
The chest first: the windpipe, two lungs, and the heart between them, tipped toward the body's left.
This is the RIGHT lung, although it sits on your left: the body faces you, so its right is your left. Every anatomy picture works this way.
Below the chest, the organs of the belly — none of them named yet.
One is the stomach, high on the body's left, just below the heart and tucked under the lower ribs.

ask.question: Click on the liver.
ask.intro: The liver lies opposite the stomach.
ask.right: The liver: the big wedge under the body's right ribs, which is your left as you face it.
ask.wrong: It sits directly under the right lung — the one on your left.

commands.speak: It is the heaviest organ inside you, about one and a half kilos, and its top rises under the ribs to about the fifth rib.
Only the thin dome of the diaphragm separates it from the right lung, so each deep breath pushes it down, and a doctor can feel its edge.
Most people point here, above the navel. That is small intestine: the liver sits higher, almost all of it hidden behind the ribs.
It is also the organ that grows back: remove up to two thirds, and the rest regrows to nearly full size within months.

quiz.question: A patient facing you says it hurts under her right ribs. On which side of YOUR view is that?
quiz.right: Your left: she faces you, so her right side is on your left — and under those ribs lies her liver.

request: Hva ligger egentlig inne i buken?

commands.speak: Hva ligger egentlig i buken? Mest fordøyelse — og hvor hvert organ ligger, avgjør hvor det gjør vondt. Vi zoomer inn under ribbeina.
Øverst på kroppens høyre side, til venstre for deg, ligger leveren: omtrent halvannen kilo, det største organet i buken.
Under den henger galleblæren, som samler galle til neste fete måltid.
Magesekken ligger oppunder ribbeina på venstre side — mye høyere enn der folk tar seg til magen.
Bak og til venstre for den ligger milten, omtrent på størrelse med en knyttneve, skjermet av de nederste ribbeina.
Bukspyttkjertelen ligger på tvers helt bakerst, stiplet fordi magesekken skjuler den.
Tynntarmen fyller midten: flere meter lagt i slynger, og her tas det meste av næringen opp.
Tykktarmen går rundt den som en ramme: opp på høyre side, tvers over, og ned på venstre.
Så «vondt i magen» rett over navlen er sjelden magesekken. Der ligger tarmene.
Bukspyttkjertelen ligger så skjult at sykdom der ofte merkes sent — og smerten kjennes gjerne i ryggen.

quiz.question: Hvilket av disse organene ligger nærmest ryggen?
quiz.right: Bukspyttkjertelen: den ligger bakerst, bak magesekken — derfor er den stiplet, og derfor stråler smerten ofte mot ryggen.

request: Why is a broken thigh bone so serious?

commands.speak: Why is a broken thigh bone an emergency? Start with a skeleton from the front: skull, spine, rib cage and pelvis.
The arms hang from the shoulder girdle.
The legs stand on the pelvis. Each thigh holds one bone, the femur — the longest in the body, about a quarter of your height.
In this skeleton, one bone is broken.

ask.question: Click on the broken bone.
ask.right: The left femur: a jagged break runs straight across the middle of its shaft.
ask.wrong: Look for the jagged red line — it is on one of the legs.

commands.speak: It is the body's left thigh, on your right. Snapping the shaft of the strongest bone takes great force: a car crash, a fall from a height.
And the thigh hides blood: a broken shaft can bleed a litre or more into the muscle, with no wound on the skin.
The big thigh muscles then pull the two ends past each other, so the leg looks shorter — which is why a traction splint pulls it back out to length.
Far more often the femur breaks up here instead, at its neck just below the hip: the broken hip of an older person after a simple fall.
So a broken hip is usually not the pelvis at all. It is the top of the thigh bone, thinned by osteoporosis.

quiz.question: An 85-year-old falls and breaks her hip. Which bone is usually broken?
quiz.right: The femur: a broken hip is usually a break in the neck of the thigh bone, just below the ball of the hip joint.

request: Which joints does the leg bend at, and which bones meet in each?

commands.speak: The leg bends at three joints, and each is built for a different job. Here is the left leg from the hip down; first the thigh bone, the femur.
Below it, two bones: the thick tibia, the shin, on the inside, and the thin fibula along the outside.
In front of the knee rides the kneecap, the patella — a bone that grows inside the tendon of the thigh muscle.
Then the foot: seven tarsal bones, the five long metatarsals, and the toes.
Three joints join these bones, ringed in red. Which is which?

ask.question: Click on the knee.
ask.right: The knee: the rounded end of the femur rolls on the flat top of the tibia, with the patella gliding in front.
ask.wrong: It is the joint the kneecap sits in front of.

ask.question: Click on the ankle.
ask.right: The ankle: the tibia and the fibula grip the talus, the top bone of the foot, from both sides.
ask.wrong: It joins the leg to the foot.

ask.question: Click on the hip.
ask.right: The hip: the ball at the top of the femur sits deep in a socket of the pelvis, so the thigh can swing every way.

commands.speak: The fibula stops just below the knee: it takes no part in the knee joint, and carries only a small share of the weight.
At the ankle it matters: its lower end is the knob on the outside of your ankle, the tibia's is the knob on the inside.
Because it carries so little, surgeons can take a length of fibula to rebuild a jaw, and the patient still walks.

quiz.question: Which bone of the lower leg takes no part in the knee joint?
quiz.right: The fibula: it ends just below the knee and joins in only at the ankle, as the outer ankle bone.

request: What are the main organs, and where does each one sit?

commands.speak: Which organs fill the body, and where does each one sit? A body facing you, so its right is your left — and at the top, the brain.
The chest is mostly lung: the windpipe splits in two to feed a right and a left lung.
Between them, the heart, tipped toward the body's left — which is why the left lung is the smaller of the two.
Under the ribs on the body's right, the liver, the largest organ inside you.
Opposite it, the stomach, and further back the spleen, which filters worn-out red cells from the blood.
Below, the gut: the small intestine coiled in the middle, the large intestine framing it on three sides.
Behind the gut, dashed because they are hidden: the pancreas lying across, and a kidney on each side of the spine.
At the bottom, the bladder, which collects what the kidneys make.
Those two small kidneys filter about 180 litres of fluid out of the blood every day, and return all but a litre or two.
So a front view is a stack: the organs you see first sit in front, and some of the busiest ones hide behind them.

quiz.question: Which lung is the smaller one?
quiz.right: The left: the heart leans toward the body's left and takes up room, so the left lung has two lobes to the right's three.

request: What lies behind the intestines?

commands.speak: What lies behind the intestines? A second, hidden layer of organs — which is why kidney pain is felt in the back. A torso, facing you.
In front, filling the belly: the liver, the stomach, the coils of the gut, and the bladder low down.
Behind them, dashed because hidden: a kidney on each side of the spine, each capped by a small adrenal gland.
Also at the back: the pancreas lying across, the aorta running down the middle, and the spleen, far back on the left.
Lift the front layer away, and the hidden layer lies flat against the back wall of the belly.
These lie behind the belly's lining, the peritoneum — retroperitoneal — so a surgeon can reach a kidney from the back without opening the belly.

ask.question: Click on the left kidney.
ask.right: The body's left kidney — on your right, because the body faces you.
ask.wrong: The body's left is on your right.

commands.speak: The right kidney sits a little lower than the left: the liver, above it, takes the room.
The spleen lies just as far back, but inside the lining, tethered to the stomach — so it is not one of them.
Put the front layer back, and the kidneys vanish behind the gut. A doctor checks them by tapping the back, just below the lowest ribs.

quiz.question: Where is kidney pain usually felt?
choices: In the back, below the ribs
Low in the front of the belly
quiz.right: In the back, below the ribs: the kidneys lie behind the gut, against the back wall, either side of the spine.

request: Hva heter knoklene i beinet på latin, og hva betyr navnene?

commands.speak: Leger over hele verden bruker de latinske navnene på knoklene i beinet, og de fleste er små bilder. Øverst: os femoris.
Os betyr knokkel, femur betyr lår, og sinister betyr venstre. Lårbeinet er kroppens lengste knokkel, omtrent en firedel av høyden din.
Foran kneet ligger patella, «den lille skåla» — nøyaktig samme bilde som det norske ordet kneskål.
Skinnebeinet heter tibia, og det bærer nesten hele vekten din ned mot foten. På latin betyr tibia også fløyte.
Ved siden av ligger fibula, det tynne leggbeinet. Fibula betyr spenne: det ligger langs tibia som nåla i en romersk brosje.
Fibula bærer lite vekt. Den holder fast muskler, og nederst danner den yttersiden av ankelen.
I foten: ossa tarsi, sju fotrotsbein. Det største av dem er hælbeinet.
Så ossa metatarsi, fem mellomfotsbein. Meta betyr bortenfor — bortenfor fotroten.
Ytterst phalanges, fjorten tåbein. En falanks var en gresk slaglinje, soldater på rad — slik tærne står.
Tell sammen: fire lange knokler, sju, fem og fjorten. Tretti knokler i hvert bein, fra hofta og ned.
Navnene er altså ikke pugg, men beskrivelser: lår, liten skål, fløyte, spenne og slaglinje.

ask.question: Hva heter skinnebeinet på latin?
ask.right: Tibia — det samme ordet som fløyte.

quiz.question: Hvilken av de to knoklene i leggen bærer vekten din?
quiz.right: Tibia: den tykke skinnebeinsknokkelen bærer nesten alt, mens den tynne fibula mest holder muskler og ankelen.

request: Where are the 206 bones of the skeleton?

commands.speak: An adult skeleton has 206 bones, and this drawcast asks where they are. At the top, the skull, with the lower jaw hinged beneath it.
Down the middle runs the spine: seven neck vertebrae, twelve in the chest, five in the lower back, then the sacrum.
Twelve pairs of ribs hang from the chest vertebrae, and most of them meet in front at the breastbone, the sternum.
That central column is the axial skeleton: eighty bones that protect the brain, the spinal cord and the heart.
The arms hang from a ring of four bones: two collarbones in front, two shoulder blades behind.
One bone in the upper arm, two in the forearm — so the forearm can twist.
The legs hang from the pelvis in the same pattern: one thigh bone, then two in the lower leg.
Now the hands. Each one holds 27 bones: eight in the wrist, five in the palm, fourteen in the fingers.
And each foot holds 26, built on the same plan.
A newborn has around 300 bones; many fuse as it grows. This sacrum began as five separate vertebrae.

ask.question: Click on the bone where the ribs meet in front.
ask.right: The sternum, the breastbone: the upper ribs join it through cartilage.

quiz.question: Roughly what share of the 206 bones sit in the hands and feet?
quiz.right: More than half: 27 in each hand and 26 in each foot make 106 of the 206.

request: Hvorfor har hånden så mange knokler?

commands.speak: Hånden har 27 knokler, og her ser vi hvorfor den trenger så mange. Nærmest armen: åtte små håndrotsbein i to rader.
De glir mot hverandre, så håndleddet kan bøye seg i alle retninger. Båtbeinet her er det som oftest brekker når man tar seg for.
Så fem mellomhåndsbein, ett for hver finger. Sammen danner de håndflaten.
Ytterst fingerbeina: tre i hver finger, men bare to i tommelen. Fjorten til sammen.
Åtte, fem og fjorten: 27. De to hendene har altså over en firedel av kroppens 206 knokler.
Hvert fingerbein er et ledd til. Derfor kan hånden forme seg rundt en blyant, en ball eller et håndtak.
Foten har nesten like mange knokler, men kan ikke gripe. Forskjellen sitter ved roten av tommelen.
Tommelens mellomhåndsbein møter håndroten i et sadelledd, som lar tommelen dreie over og møte hver fingertupp.

ask.question: Klikk på knoklene der båtbeinet sitter.
ask.right: Håndrotsbeina, i håndleddet mellom underarmen og mellomhånden. Båtbeinet er ett av de åtte.

quiz.question: Hvor sitter bevegelsen som lar tommelen møte lillefingeren?
choices: Ved roten, mellom håndrot og mellomhånd
quiz.right: Ved roten: tommelens mellomhåndsbein sitter i et sadelledd mot håndroten og kan dreie tommelen inn mot fingrene.

request: What's where inside the body?

commands.speak: Your organs are packed in layers, front to back, and this drawcast maps where each one sits. The brain has the skull to itself.
In the chest, the windpipe comes down the middle and branches into two lungs, which fill most of the rib cage.
The heart sits between them, behind the breastbone, its tip pointing to the left.
Below the lungs, a sheet of muscle, the diaphragm, closes off the chest. Right under it, on the body's right, lies the liver.
On the left, the stomach, and tucked behind it, against the ribs, the spleen.
Dashed lines mean further back. The pancreas lies behind the stomach, and the kidneys sit against the back wall, either side of the spine.
In front of them all hangs the gut: the coiled small intestine, framed on three sides by the large intestine.
And lowest of all, behind the pubic bone, the bladder.
The kidneys sit higher than most people guess: under the lowest ribs, the right one a little lower, pushed down by the liver.
Hidden back there, the two of them filter about 180 litres of blood plasma a day.
Now click any organ to zoom in and see its name, and use the crumbs to come back. Press Continue when you are done.

quiz.question: Where do the kidneys sit?
choices: Low in the belly, near the hips
At the back, under the lowest ribs
quiz.right: At the back, under the lowest ribs — behind the gut, one either side of the spine.

request: Where exactly does the heart sit in the chest?

commands.speak: Where in the chest is the heart? Start with the two lungs that flank it, filling most of the rib cage.
The windpipe comes down the midline and splits into one branch for each lung.
Between the lungs, right behind the breastbone, sits the heart — not on the left, but in the middle.
It is tipped: its broad base up and to the right, its tip down and to the left. About two thirds of it lies left of the midline.
That tip, low on the left, is where you feel it beat — which is why the heart seems to be on the left.
The left lung makes room for it: a notch is carved out for the heart, and it has two lobes to the right lung's three.
Dashed, because they lie behind: the gullet, and the aorta, which arches over and runs down along the spine.
So the heart is a middle organ that leans left, and the lungs are shaped around that lean.
In roughly one person in ten thousand the whole picture is mirrored, and the heart points right. That is called dextrocardia.

quiz.question: Where is the heart?
choices: On the left side of the chest
In the middle, tipped to the left
quiz.right: In the middle, behind the breastbone, with its tip turned left — about two thirds of it left of the midline.

commands.speak: The 3D button under the figure turns this chest round and peels it layer by layer, so the heart's lean shows from the side.

request: Where do the heart, liver and stomach sit?

commands.speak: Where do the heart, the liver and the stomach sit? You will place them yourself, and the bones of the trunk are your map.
Look how low the rib cage reaches: its lower edge arches well below the chest, over the top of the belly.
The lungs fill the upper part of the cage, one on each side of the windpipe.
Between them, behind the breastbone, a space is left open.
Below the ribs the gut fills the belly: the coiled small intestine, framed on three sides by the large intestine.

ask.question: Drag each organ to where it belongs.
ask.right: The heart between the lungs, tipped to the body's left; the liver under the body's right ribs; the stomach under its left ribs, just below the heart.
ask.wrong: Use the ribs: all three sit behind them.

commands.speak: Liver and stomach both sit mostly inside the rib cage. The ribs guard the top floor of the belly, not only the lungs.
Dashed, further back: the gullet and the aorta, the pancreas, and the spleen against the left ribs. The gallbladder hangs under the liver.
That protection has a price: a broken lower rib can tear the liver on the right, or the spleen on the left.

quiz.question: When you point to your 'stomach' at the navel, what is mostly there?
quiz.right: Mostly small intestine — the stomach itself sits higher, under the left ribs.

request: How do you tell the Nordic countries apart on a map?

commands.speak: How do you tell the four Nordic countries apart on a blank map? Each outline has one clue that gives it away.
Norway is the long strip facing the Atlantic: from Lindesnes in the south to the North Cape is about 1,700 kilometres in a straight line.
Its coast is frayed by fjords, and in the far north it wraps over the top of its neighbours.
The islands up in the Arctic are Norway's too: Svalbard. That is why the map reaches so far north.
Sweden is the long one beside it, facing east onto the Baltic: the biggest of the four, about ten times the size of Denmark.
Across the Gulf of Bothnia lies Finland, the one that reaches farthest east, to the Russian border.
Its north-western wedge is called [finnish:Käsivarsi], “the arm”: Finns see a maiden with a raised arm in the outline.
And Denmark is the small one in the south: the Jutland peninsula pointing up at Norway, with its islands.
It is the only one of the four joined by land to the rest of Europe, at its border with Germany.
Four clues: the Atlantic strip, the Baltic side, the arm in the east, the peninsula in the south.

ask.question: Drag each name onto its country.
ask.right: Norway along the Atlantic, Sweden beside it on the Baltic, Finland to the east with its arm, and Denmark on the peninsula in the south.
ask.wrong: Start with the easy two: the long Atlantic strip, and the small peninsula in the south.

request: How do you find C, E and G on a piano keyboard?

commands.speak: How do you find C, E and G on a keyboard with no names on it? The black keys are the map.
They come in groups: two, then three, then two and three again, all the way up.
C is the white key just left of each group of two.
E is just right of that pair, so the two black keys sit between C and E.
G sits inside the group of three, just left of its middle black key.
Together, C major: take a white key, skip one, take one, skip one, take one.
The pattern repeats every octave, so this next pair marks the next C up.
A full piano has 88 keys, 52 white and 36 black, and each of its eight Cs sits just left of a pair.

ask.question: Now the upper octave: drag C, E and G onto their keys.
ask.right: C just left of the pair, E just right of it, and G inside the three, left of its middle key.
ask.wrong: Find the pair of black keys first: C and E stand on either side of it.

commands.speak: C, E, G one octave higher: the same shape on the keys, the same chord.

quiz.question: Which white key sits left of the group of three?
quiz.right: F: the three black keys sit between F and B, just as the pair sits between C and E.

request: Why is the periodic table shaped the way it is?

spec.title: Why the table has that shape

card.title: Why the table has that shape

commands.speak: The periodic table's odd shape, with towers at the sides, a dip in the middle and two rows set apart, comes from how electrons fill in.
One box per element, in order of protons: hydrogen has one, helium two, and each step to the right adds one more.
Helium, with only two, already sits at the far right. The first shell around a nucleus holds just two electrons, so row one ends there.
Lithium's third electron has to start a new shell, so lithium starts a new row. Each row, a period, is one more shell.
Each shell fills in parts. First an s orbital, with room for two electrons: two columns, the red s-block.
Helium turns red too. It is an s element, parked over the noble gases because, like them, its shell is full.
Then the p orbitals, with room for six: six columns, the blue p-block. Two plus six, so rows two and three are eight long.
Row three stops at argon, although its shell has room for ten more electrons.
Those ten are the d orbitals, and they fill late, only after the next shell's s. So the ten-wide d-block drops in from row four.
Row four: two, then ten, then six. Eighteen elements.
From row six, fourteen f places open as well. That strip is so wide it is cut out and printed below, or the table would not fit a page.
So the row lengths, two, eight, eight, eighteen, eighteen, thirty-two, thirty-two, are just the room in the orbitals added up.
Mendeleev found this pattern in 1869, twenty-eight years before anyone found the electron. He left gaps, and gallium turned up to fill one in 1875.

quiz.question: Row four holds 18 elements, row three only 8. Why?
quiz.right: Ten d places fill in row four: two s, ten d and six p make eighteen.

request: Hvorfor heter jern Fe?

commands.speak: Hvorfor heter jern Fe, når ingen av bokstavene står i ordet? Svaret står på selve kortet for jern.
Under symbolet står navnet på latin: ferrum. Fe er de to første bokstavene.
Norsk sier jern, engelsk iron, tysk Eisen. Det ser ut som tre ord, men det er ett gammelt germansk ord i tre drakter.
Latin gikk en helt annen vei: ferrum. Og det var latin kjemikerne bygde symbolene på, tidlig på 1800-tallet.
Symbolet forkorter altså ikke ordet på ditt språk. Det forkorter det latinske, og derfor er det likt over hele verden.
Det som gjør jern til jern, er tallet i hjørnet: 26 protoner i hver kjerne. Navnet er bare en merkelapp.
Noen ganger treffer latinen norsk: natrium blir Na og kalium blir K, fordi vi har tatt de latinske navnene.
På engelsk heter de sodium og potassium, navn Humphry Davy ga dem i 1807. Der passer symbolene ikke i det hele tatt.

quiz.question: Kobber har symbolet Cu. Hvor kommer det fra?
quiz.right: Fra latin cuprum: symbolene bygger på latin, ikke på språket du snakker, selv når copper og Kupfer ligner.

request: Which one is Mars?

commands.speak: Which of the planets is Mars? Count outward from the Sun. Here are all eight orbits seen from above, evenly spaced — not to scale.
Four small rocky planets keep close: the nearest circles 58 million kilometres from the Sun, the fourth 228 million.
Then four giants, far out: Jupiter at 778 million kilometres, Neptune at four and a half billion.
We live on the third. Every planet sits where it really was on the sixth of September 2026.

ask.question: Which one is Mars?
ask.right: Mars is the fourth out, on the orbit just outside ours — the last of the small rocky planets.
ask.wrong: Count out from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth — then one more.

commands.speak: Mars is about half Earth's width, and red because its dust is rich in iron oxide — rust.
Its orbit lies outside ours. So when Earth passes between the Sun and Mars, Mars stands opposite the Sun, up all night.
Venus, inside our orbit, can never do that: seen from Earth it always stays near the Sun.

quiz.question: Which planet can you see high in the south at midnight?
quiz.right: Mars: its orbit is outside ours, so it can stand opposite the Sun. Venus, inside, is only ever an evening or a morning star.

request: How big is Jupiter?

commands.speak: How big is Jupiter, really? Here the planets are drawn at their true sizes — and the Sun is so large that only its edge fits.
Earth: 12,700 kilometres across, a dot beside a Sun that is 109 Earths wide.
The other rocky planets are smaller still: Venus nearly Earth's twin, Mars half as wide, Mercury less.
Jupiter: 143,000 kilometres across — eleven Earths side by side.
Eleven times wider is also eleven times taller and eleven times deeper, so about 1,300 Earths would fit inside it.
Yet it weighs only 318 Earths. It is mostly hydrogen and helium, a quarter as dense as our rock and iron.
Even so, it is two and a half times as heavy as all the other planets put together.
Saturn, nine and a half Earths across, is lighter still — less dense than water.
Then the two ice giants, Uranus and Neptune, each about four Earths across.

quiz.question: Uranus is four Earths across. About how many Earths would fit inside it?
quiz.right: About 64: four times wider, four times taller and four times deeper — four cubed.

request: Why are the inner planets small and the outer ones huge?

spec.title: Rock near the Sun, giants far out

card.title: Rock near the Sun, giants far out

commands.speak: Why are the four planets nearest the Sun small, and the four beyond them giants? Here they are in a row, closest first, sizes squeezed to fit.

ask.question: Drag each name onto its planet.
ask.right: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, then Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
ask.wrong: The four small ones come first; Saturn is the one with the ring.

commands.speak: Earth is the heaviest of the inner four. Jupiter weighs 318 Earths, and even the lightest giant, Uranus, weighs about fifteen.
The split is about temperature. In the young Sun's disc of gas and dust, beyond about here it was cold enough for water to freeze.
Inside that line only rock and metal could be solid, and there was little of either. The planets built from them stayed small.
Outside it, ice joined the rock, and there was more ice than rock. Solid cores grew to around ten Earths.
A core that heavy pulls in the hydrogen and helium around it — ninety-eight percent of the disc. That is how the giants got huge.
Other stars break the pattern: the first planet found round a Sun-like star, in 1995, is a giant orbiting far closer in than Mercury.
It most likely formed out past its star's frost line, then drifted inward.

quiz.question: Why couldn't a giant grow where Earth is?
choices: Too little solid material for a big core
There was no gas that close to the Sun
The Sun's gravity tore big planets apart
quiz.right: Too little solid stuff: inside the frost line only rock and metal were solid — never enough for a core that could grab the gas.

request: Why does Earth catch up with Mars only every two years?

commands.speak: Mars comes close to Earth only once every two years or so. Why so rarely? Here are the four inner orbits, with their distances to scale.
The sixteenth of January 2025: Earth passes between the Sun and Mars, and Mars is near its closest and at its brightest.
Earth goes round the Sun in 365 days.
Mars, half as far out again, has a longer track and moves slower along it: one lap takes 687 days.
Run one year. Earth is back where it started — but Mars has gone only a little over halfway round.
So Earth has to chase it round the far side. It catches up thirteen months later, on the nineteenth of February 2027.
On average the chase takes 780 days, two years and two months — which is why missions to Mars launch in windows 26 months apart.

quiz.question: Jupiter takes twelve years to go round. How often does Earth catch up with it?
quiz.right: Just over once a year: Jupiter barely moves in a year, so Earth needs only 399 days to lap it. The slower the planet, the sooner we catch it.

request: How did Jupiter's moons show the Earth is not the centre?

spec.title: The four that go round something else

card.title: Four moons that don't circle us

commands.speak: How did four small moons of Jupiter shake the idea that everything circles the Earth? In January 1610 Galileo turned his new telescope on Jupiter.
Beside it he saw small lights that shifted from night to night. The nearest, Io, goes round Jupiter in 1.8 days.
Europa, further out, takes 3.6 days.
Ganymede takes 7.2 days — the largest moon in the solar system, wider than the planet Mercury.
Callisto, the outermost, takes almost 17 days, nearly two million kilometres from Jupiter.
Run one week: Ganymede goes round once, Europa twice, Io four times — the three are locked in step.
The old picture put Earth at the centre of every motion in the sky. Here were four bodies plainly circling something else.
They also answered an objection: if the Earth moved, wouldn't it leave its Moon behind? Jupiter moves, and keeps all four.
Click any moon to look closer, use the crumbs to come back out, and try the scale and date buttons. Press Continue when you are done.

quiz.question: What did Jupiter's moons prove?
choices: That the Earth goes round the Sun
That not everything goes round the Earth
That Jupiter is bigger than the Earth
quiz.right: Not everything goes round the Earth: four moons plainly circle Jupiter. That broke the old picture, without yet proving the Earth moves.

request: Why does the sky turn?

spec.title: The sky turns because we do

commands.speak: Why does the whole sky wheel round during the night? First, a chart of it: the rim is your horizon all round, the middle straight overhead.
North is at the top and east on the left, because this is a chart held over your head, not a map of the ground.
Oslo on a September evening: every star you could see from a dark spot, where it really was — and low in the east, Saturn.
One star barely moves: Polaris, less than a degree from the point in the sky that Earth's axis aims at.
It stands as high above your horizon as you are north of the equator: sixty degrees up, here in Oslo.
Near it, the Great Bear, whose seven brightest stars make the Plough.
Now let six hours run. Nothing out there moves: the ground under you turns fifteen degrees an hour, and carries you round.
Saturn has crossed to the south, and in the east the Moon, Mars and Jupiter have come up.
The whole sky wheels about the pole. The Plough is so close to it that from Oslo it never sets — it circles all night, every night.
Polaris won't always be the pole star: Earth's axis slowly wobbles, and in about 12,000 years it will point near Vega.

quiz.question: From the equator, where would Polaris be?
quiz.right: On the horizon: the pole star stands as many degrees up as you are north, and at the equator that is none.

request: Why can't I see the winter stars in summer?

spec.title: Half a year, the other half of the sky

commands.speak: Why do the winter constellations vanish from summer nights? Here is the sky over Oslo on a December evening, the night before the winter solstice.
Every star above the horizon, the constellation shapes traced in, and the Moon and three planets among them.
Low in the south-east, Orion: three stars in a row for a belt, one bright star above it and one below.
Keep the clock at the same hour and let a month pass. Orion has swung round towards the south: the whole sky is running two hours ahead.
Each day Earth moves a degree along its orbit, so the stars come round about four minutes earlier every night — two hours a month.
Now half a year: twelve hours ahead. By this hour in June Orion has already set: it is up only while the Sun is.
And a June night in Oslo barely gets dark at all: at midnight the Sun is less than seven degrees below the horizon.

quiz.question: Why is Orion missing from the June night sky?
choices: It has moved to another part of space
It is above the horizon only in daytime
It is too faint in summer
quiz.right: It is up in the daytime. Nothing out there moved: Earth went half way round the Sun, and our night now faces the other way.

request: Are the stars of a constellation really close together?

spec.title: The W is a trick of direction

card.title: Is the W a real group?

commands.speak: Are the stars of a constellation really close together? Take five bright stars of the northern sky, magnified.
Joined up they make a W: Cassiopeia, the queen, flat as a pattern on a ceiling.
But the sky shows only directions. Turn the view on its side: us at the bottom, distance going up.
Caph, at one end of the W, is about 55 light-years away: the light we see left it in the early 1970s.
Ruchbah is nearly twice as far, about 100 light-years.
Shedar is about 230, and Segin, the faint end of the W, about 410.
And Navi, the middle star, about 550: ten times farther than Caph.
Yet Navi looks as bright as Caph. Ten times the distance means it must give out roughly a hundred times the light.
So the W is not a group at all: five stars hundreds of light-years apart that happen to lie in one direction from us.
Seen from anywhere else in the galaxy, the same five would make some other shape, and no W.
This patch of sky has a famous history: in 1572 Tycho Brahe saw a new star flare up in Cassiopeia, and showed that the heavens could change.

quiz.question: Two stars sit side by side in a constellation. What does that say about their distance from us?
choices: Nothing: one may be ten times farther
quiz.right: Nothing: they only share a direction. Caph and Navi sit in one W, yet Navi is ten times farther away and just as bright.

request: Er Karlsvogna et eget stjernebilde?

spec.title: Karlsvogna er bare en del av bjørnen

commands.speak: Er Karlsvogna et eget stjernebilde? Her er et utsnitt av himmelen mot nord en desemberkveld, forstørret: tjue stjerner.
Sju av dem kjenner du: firkanten og hanken, Karlsvogna.
Men streken går videre, gjennom alle tjue: en hel bjørn, med hode, rygg, lang hale og fire bein.
Stjernebildet er Store bjørn, på latin Ursa Major. Karlsvogna er bare kroppen og halen: et mønster inni stjernebildet, ikke et eget.
Megrez, der kroppen møter halen, er tydelig svakere enn de seks andre i vogna, og derfor ser firkanten litt skjev ut.
Dubhe og Merak, ytterst i firkanten, er pekerne: en linje gjennom dem, fem ganger så lang, treffer polarstjernen — og dermed nord.
Og fem av de sju hører virkelig sammen: de er rundt 80 lysår unna og driver samme vei gjennom rommet.
Dubhe og Alkaid, i hver sin ende, går sin egen vei. Om noen titusener av år er vogna trukket ut av form.

quiz.question: Hva er Karlsvogna?
choices: En del av stjernebildet Store bjørn
quiz.right: En del av Store bjørn: de sju stjernene er bare kroppen og halen på bjørnen, og to av dem hører ikke engang til gruppen.

request: Do I know Orion well enough to draw it?

spec.title: The shield and the club this atlas draws

commands.speak: Can you draw Orion from memory? Here are the twenty-three stars this atlas uses for it, on a January evening, with no lines yet.
Start where the eye does: three stars in a short straight row, the belt.
Four bright stars box it in: Betelgeuse and Bellatrix are the shoulders, Saiph and Rigel the feet.
Their colours differ: Betelgeuse is an orange-red supergiant, cool for its size, while Rigel, at the opposite corner, burns blue-white and hot.
Joined up, the belt and the four corners make the hourglass most people know. This atlas draws more: a head, a raised club and a shield.
Twenty-four lines in all. To draw it back, go in the eye's order: belt first, then the corners, then head, club and shield.
In early 2020 Betelgeuse faded to about a third of its usual brightness: a cloud of dust it had thrown off, not an explosion.

ask.question: Draw Orion.
ask.right: That's Orion — belt, shoulders, feet, head, club and shield: all twenty-four lines of this atlas's own figure.

request: Hvordan kjenner jeg igjen Kassiopeia?

commands.speak: Hvordan kjenner du igjen Kassiopeia? Her er himmelen høyt mot nord en desemberettermiddag, forstørret.
Fire streker gjør fem av dem til en sikksakk: Kassiopeia, dronningen. Tidlig på kvelden står den nesten på høykant.
Men himmelen dreier rundt polarstjernen hele natten. Seks timer senere, sent på kvelden, ligger sikksakken ned.
Etter tolv timer, mot morgenen, står den på høykant igjen, men snudd opp ned.
Mot nord ser du en W når hun står under polarstjernen, og en M når hun står over. Se etter sikksakken, ikke etter bokstaven.
Den midterste, Navi, er alltid spissen som sikksakken bøyer seg rundt.
I norsk himmel går Kassiopeia aldri ned: hun sirkler rundt polen natten gjennom, hele året.
Grekerne forklarte det med en straff: dronningen skrøt av sin skjønnhet, og ble satt på himmelen for å henge opp ned halve tiden.

ask.question: Tegn Kassiopeia slik hun står nå.
ask.right: Der er hun: fem stjerner og fire streker — samme sikksakk, uansett hvilken vei den vender.

request: Why doesn't Jupiter twinkle when the stars do?

spec.title: A point twinkles, a disc does not

commands.speak: Why do stars twinkle while a planet shines steadily? A February evening over Oslo, and one of these bright lights is not a star.
Sirius, low in the south, is the brightest star in the night sky, and on a cold night it flickers hard.
It is so far away that its disc spans only a few thousandths of an arcsecond: its light arrives as a single point.
On the way down, pockets of warmer and cooler air bend that one thin beam this way and that, many times a second — and the point flickers.
Jupiter, in the south-east, is close enough to show a disc about 45 arcseconds wide — thousands of times wider than Sirius.
Every point of that disc flickers too, but out of step with the rest. Averaged over the whole disc, the flicker cancels and the light holds steady.
Height matters as well. Capella, high in the west, twinkles far less than Sirius does.
From Oslo Sirius never climbs above about thirteen degrees, so its light crosses about four times as much air as Capella's, and flashes red, green and blue.
So the rule is about size, not about planets: a point twinkles, a disc does not — and even Venus twinkles when it sits right on the horizon.

ask.question: Click the light that twinkles most tonight.
ask.right: Sirius: a single point of light, and the lowest of the three, so its light crosses the most air.
ask.wrong: A disc holds steady. Of the two points, which is lower in the sky?

request: Why does a small rear cog make pedalling harder but faster, and a big one easier but slower?

commands.speak: Why does a small rear cog make pedalling hard but fast, and a big one easy but slow? Start at the pedals: a chainring with fifty-two teeth.
Your foot turns it with the crank, and legs like one steady pace: about ninety turns a minute.
At the back, a sixteen-tooth cog, bolted to the rear wheel.
The chain joins them, and it keeps strict books: every tooth of chain that leaves the front must pass round the back.
So one pedal turn feeds fifty-two teeth of chain round a cog of only sixteen.
Fifty-two over sixteen is 3.25: the wheel turns three and a quarter times for every turn of your legs.
A road wheel is about 2.1 metres round, so each pedal turn rolls you nearly seven metres: thirty-seven kilometres an hour at ninety turns.
The price is force. Your foot circles about one metre while the bike rolls seven, so it must push about six times harder than the road resists.
Now shift onto the big twenty-eight-tooth cog, the one you reach for at the foot of a hill.
Fifty-two over twenty-eight is about 1.86: under four metres per pedal turn, and twenty-one kilometres an hour at the same ninety.
But your foot's one metre now buys only four metres of road, so the push falls from six times the road's resistance to under four.
A gear makes no energy. Force times distance is the same at the pedal and at the road; the gear only chooses the split.
Before chains, pedals turned the front wheel directly, so a faster bike needed a bigger wheel: the penny-farthing.
Cyclists still rate gears in 'gear inches': the diameter of the penny-farthing wheel that would roll as far per pedal turn.

quiz.question: Same hill, 28-tooth cog instead of 16. The total work your legs do…
quiz.right: It stays about the same: the hill needs the same energy, and the big cog only spreads it over more, lighter pedal strokes.

request: Does a violin's sound come from its strings or from its wooden body?

spec.title: Why a violin needs its box

card.title: Why a violin needs its box

commands.speak: Does a violin's sound come from its strings or from its wooden body? Here is everything but the body: pegs, fingerboard and tailpiece.
Between them run four strings, tuned G, D, A and E. The A string vibrates four hundred and forty times a second.
Rosin on the bow's hair makes it grip the string, drag it sideways and let it snap back, once for every vibration.
Yet a string on its own is almost silent. It is under a millimetre thick, so the air slips round it instead of being pushed.
The strings press down on this small maple bridge, and it rocks with them, four hundred and forty times a second.
Its feet rock the belly, a thin spruce plate. The whole plate moves, and a plate that wide pushes a lot of air: it is the loudspeaker.
The f-holes let the air inside breathe in and out, and that air resonates too, strengthening the lowest notes.
The bouts give the plate its area; the narrow waist is cut in so the bow can reach the outer strings.
So the string sets the pitch, but the bridge and the body make the sound you hear.
An electric violin shows it: a slim frame with no hollow body, it is barely audible across a room until it is plugged in.
One part does nothing for the tone: the chin rest, invented by the violinist Louis Spohr around 1820 to hold the instrument steady.

quiz.question: A practice mute is a small weight clipped onto the bridge. Why does it make the violin quieter?
choices: Less vibration gets through the bridge into the body
quiz.right: The heavier bridge moves less, so less of the strings' vibration reaches the belly, and the belly is what makes the sound.

request: Why is rain fresh when most of it starts in the salty sea?

commands.speak: Most rain starts in the salty sea, yet it falls fresh. Why? Follow one drop round the water cycle, from the ocean to the mountain and back.
The engine is the sun. Its warmth pulls water off the sea surface as invisible vapour.
That is evaporation, and only the water goes. The salt cannot evaporate, so it stays behind in the sea.
The sun is a still the size of the oceans: over four hundred thousand cubic kilometres of fresh water rise off them each year.
Rising air cools, and the vapour condenses on specks of dust as tiny droplets: a cloud.
Wind carries it inland, over the high ground, where the droplets merge and grow.
Once they are too heavy for the rising air to hold, they fall: precipitation. A water molecule stays up there only about nine days.
On the slope the rain gathers into streams and a river, running back toward the sea.
Some soaks into the ground instead, filling the pores of the rock below the water table.
That groundwater creeps seaward too, over years or even centuries.
Together they return about forty thousand cubic kilometres a year: the surplus the wind carried in over the land.
But rivers also carry a little salt, dissolved out of the rocks. Evaporation never lifts it back, so over ages the sea grew salty.
One cycle does both jobs: it hands the land fresh water, and it leaves the sea its salt.

quiz.question: Rain over the ocean comes from salty seawater. Why is it fresh?
choices: Only the water evaporates; the salt stays behind
The salt drops out as the droplets cool
quiz.right: Only the water evaporates. The salt cannot go with it, so the vapour, and the rain it becomes, are fresh.

request: How does pollination turn a flower into a seed?

spec.title: How a flower makes a seed

card.title: How a flower makes a seed

commands.speak: How does pollination turn a flower into a seed? Here is one cut down the middle, starting with the green sepals that wrapped the bud.
The petals are advertising: colour and scent, paid for by the plant to bring in a courier.
On slender filaments sit the anthers, the flower's pollen factories.
In the middle stands the pistil: a sticky stigma on a hollow stalk called the style.
At its base, the ovary holds the ovules. Each ovule carries an egg cell, and each can become one seed.
Everything else in the flower exists to get pollen down to these.
Enter the courier: a bee after nectar, dusted with pollen from another flower.
Grains rub off and stick to the stigma. That is pollination, and it is only the delivery.
Each grain then grows a tube, tunnelling down through the style toward one ovule.
Two sperm cells travel down that tube, so fertilisation happens here, inside the ovary, not up on the stigma.
One sperm joins the egg to make the embryo. The other makes its food store, the endosperm, which is most of a grain of wheat.
The fertilised ovule becomes a seed, and the ovary swells around it into the fruit.
So every seed marks one grain's journey: a pea pod with six peas was reached by at least six pollen tubes.

quiz.question: A bee has just left pollen on the stigma. Where does fertilisation happen?
quiz.right: Inside the ovary: pollination only delivers the grain, and its tube carries the sperm down the style to an ovule.

request: How can a small push on a hydraulic press lift a heavy load?

spec.title: How a small push lifts a car

card.title: How a small push lifts a car

commands.speak: How can one hand lift a car? A hydraulic jack does it with two cylinders joined at the bottom.
They are filled with oil, which, unlike air, cannot be squeezed into less space.
On the left, a narrow piston: say five square centimetres.
On the right, a wide one of twenty square centimetres, four times the area.
Push down on the narrow piston with a hundred newtons, about the weight of ten kilograms.
That push becomes pressure, force per area: a hundred newtons on five square centimetres is twenty newtons on each one.
Blaise Pascal saw in the 1650s that a closed fluid passes a rise in pressure to every part of it, undiminished.
So the wide piston feels the same twenty newtons on each of its twenty square centimetres.
Twenty times twenty: four hundred newtons pushing up. The oil only passes the pressure on; the area does the multiplying.
Make the big piston fifty square centimetres, ten times the small one, and the same hand lifts a thousand newtons.
The catch: oil pushed out of the narrow cylinder spreads thin under the wide one. Press ten centimetres down, and the load rises one.
A hundred newtons over ten centimetres is the same work as a thousand over one. The press buys force with distance.
Swap the oil for air and the push goes into squeezing the air first, which is why air in car brakes makes the pedal feel spongy.

quiz.question: Compared with the oil under the small piston, the pressure under the big piston is…
quiz.right: The same: the oil passes the pressure on unchanged, and the ten times larger area is what makes the force ten times larger.

request: Hvorfor er det samme π i omkretsen 2πr og i arealet πr²?

commands.speak: π står både i omkretsen, 2πr, og i arealet, πr². Hvorfor akkurat det samme tallet? Ta et rundt teppe.
Radien er én meter. Rundt kanten er det 2π meter, litt over seks: det er slik π er definert.
Et kvadratisk teppe rundt det er to ganger to meter, fire kvadratmeter. Sirkelen er mindre.
Kvadratet med hjørnene på kanten har bare to kvadratmeter. Sirkelen ligger et sted mellom to og fire.
Klipp teppet i tolv stykker og legg dem om, annenhvert snudd: halve kanten havner oppe, halve nede.
Langs toppen ligger altså halve omkretsen: π meter, omtrent 3,14.
Høyden er ett stykke fra spissen til kanten: radien, én meter.
Kanten er bulkete, men med førti-åtte stykker er den nesten rett. Arealet endrer seg aldri, bare formen.
Et rektangel er grunnlinje ganger høyde: π r ganger r.
Der er svaret: π kommer inn i arealet fordi grunnlinjen ER halve omkretsen. Arealet er bygget av kanten.
For teppet: 3,14 kvadratmeter, midt mellom kvadratenes to og fire.
Arkimedes klemte π på samme måte, med mangekanter inni og utenpå sirkelen. Med nittiseks kanter fikk han π mellom 3,1408 og 3,1429.

quiz.question: En sirkel har omkrets 10 m og radius 1,6 m. Hva er arealet?
quiz.right: 8 kvadratmeter: halve omkretsen, 5 meter, ganger radien 1,6. Du trenger ikke π når du kjenner omkretsen.

request: Hvordan kan kakestykker vise at arealet av en sirkel er πr²?

commands.speak: Hvorfor er arealet av en sirkel pi r i andre? Et rektangel måler vi med lengde ganger bredde, men en sirkel har ingen rette sider.
Så skjær den opp og legg bitene om. Med fire store stykker blir det bare en bølgete klump.
Skjær i stedet i tolv like stykker, som en pizza.
Pizzaen har radius 10 centimeter, fra midten ut til skorpa.
Skorpa rundt er omkretsen, 2 pi r: omtrent 62,8 centimeter.
Skygg annethvert stykke lysere. Halve skorpa sitter på de mørke stykkene, halve på de lyse.
Snu de lyse stykkene på hodet, og skyv alle sammen som tennene i en glidelås.
Langs toppen ligger skorpa fra de mørke stykkene: halve omkretsen, pi r, omtrent 31,4 centimeter.
Høyden er ett stykke fra spissen til skorpa: radien, 10 centimeter.
Et rektangel er grunnlinje ganger høyde: pi r ganger r.
Altså pi r i andre. For pizzaen: 3,14 ganger 100, omtrent 314 kvadratcentimeter.
Kantene er fortsatt litt bølgete. Men jo tynnere stykker, jo rettere blir de, og arealet var hele tiden det samme.
Arkimedes viste det samme for over 2200 år siden: sirkelen er like stor som en trekant med omkretsen som grunnlinje og radien som høyde.

quiz.question: Hvor lang er den lange siden i rektangelet?
quiz.right: Halve omkretsen, pi r: bare de mørke stykkene har skorpa langs toppen; den andre halvdelen ligger langs bunnen.

request: Hvorfor er arealet av et parallellogram grunnlinje ganger høyde?

commands.speak: Hvorfor er arealet av et parallellogram grunnlinje ganger høyde, og ikke bare de to sidene ganget sammen?
Dette har grunnlinje 6 centimeter.
Den skrå siden er 5 centimeter. Er arealet da 6 ganger 5, altså 30?
Vipp det som et hengsel: sidene er fortsatt 6 og 5, men flaten krymper mot null.
Så sidene alene kan ikke bestemme arealet. Det som krympet, var høyden.
Høyden er 4 centimeter: avstanden rett opp fra grunnlinja, ikke langs den skrå siden.
Klipp langs høyden. Da faller en trekant av på venstre side.
Skyv den over til høyre. Den passer nøyaktig, fordi de to skrå sidene er like lange og like skrå.
Nå er det et rektangel, 6 ganger 4: 24 kvadratcentimeter. Ingenting kom til, ingenting forsvant.

commands.speak: Hva skjer egentlig med en figur når den speiles? Det overraskende er ikke hvor den havner, men at den snus. Her er en speilingsakse.

request: Hva er egentlig et integral?

Del tiden i fire biter, og regn farten som fast innenfor hver bit. Fire rektangler gir 18,5 meter.

Summen er fortsatt for liten: hver søyle leser farten i starten av biten sin, og bilen var raskere resten av biten.
Førti smale søyler gir 22,4 meter. Skivene som mangler, blir tynnere for hver deling.

Et integral er altså ingen formel, men en sum av uendelig mange små biter: her fart ganger tid, lagt sammen til en strekning.

request: Hva er den deriverte?

spec.title: Den deriverte: stigningen i ett punkt

Mindre og mindre h: 2,1, så 2,01. Tallene nærmer seg 2.

Men hvorfor akkurat 2? Stigningen mellom de to punktene er endringen i f delt på h.

request: Hvorfor er arealet av en sirkel πr²? Et bevis med ringer

commands.speak: Hvorfor er arealet av en sirkel pi r i annen? Her er et bevis uten kakestykker: skjær sirkelen i tynne ringer, som årringer i en stamme.

Trappa er ikke helt rett. Men jo tynnere ringer, desto mindre trappetrinn, og i grensen forsvinner de.
Arealet av en trekant er en halv ganger grunnlinje ganger høyde: en halv ganger 2 pi r ganger r.
Halvdelen og totallet går opp mot hverandre, og igjen står pi r i annen: omtrent 314 kvadratcentimeter.
Arkimedes beviste dette for over 2200 år siden: en sirkel har samme areal som en trekant med omkretsen som grunnlinje og radien som høyde.

quiz.question: Radien dobles fra 10 til 20 centimeter. Hvor mye større blir arealet?
quiz.right: Fire ganger: både grunnlinja, omkretsen, og høyden, radien, dobles, så trekanten blir to ganger to så stor.

request: Hvorfor er arealet av en regulær mangekant halve omkretsen ganger apotemet?

commands.speak: Hvorfor er arealet av en regulær mangekant halve omkretsen ganger apotemet? Ta en sekskant, delt fra sentrum i seks like trekanter.
Hver trekant har en av sekskantens sider som grunnlinje: 10 centimeter.
Høyden, fra sentrum rett ut til midten av siden, heter apotemet, a: omtrent 8,7 centimeter.
Seks trekanter, hver en halv ganger grunnlinje ganger høyde.
Men seks sider er hele omkretsen, O. Så arealet er en halv ganger omkretsen ganger apotemet.
Det kan også sees. Behold sekskanten der den står.
Legg trekantene annenhver opp og ned. De glir sammen til et parallellogram.
Høyden i parallellogrammet er høyden i hver trekant: apotemet.
Tre trekanter har grunnlinja si nederst, tre øverst. Bunnen er derfor halve omkretsen: 30 centimeter.
Arealet er 30 ganger 8,7: omtrent 260 kvadratcentimeter.
Regelen gjelder for alle regulære mangekanter. Med flere og flere sider blir apotemet til radien og omkretsen til 2 pi r.
Da sier formelen en halv ganger 2 pi r ganger r: sirkelens pi r i annen.
Bier bygger sekskanter.
Av alle måter å dele et plan i like store celler, bruker sekskanter minst vegg: det beviste Thomas Hales i 1999.

quiz.question: En regulær åttekant har omkrets 40 cm og apotem 6 cm. Hva er arealet?
quiz.right: 120 kvadratcentimeter: halve omkretsen, 20, ganger apotemet, 6.

commands.speak: Hvordan kan uendelig mange tall legges sammen og bli nøyaktig 1? Ta et kvadrat med areal 1.
Fyll halvparten. Halvparten står fortsatt tom.
Fyll så halvparten av det som er igjen, en firedel. Nå står en firedel tom.
En åttedel til, og en åttedel står tom.
En sekstendel, en trettitodel, en sekstifiredel. Hver bit tar halvparten av hullet, og hullet halveres.
Hullet er alltid like stort som den siste biten: her en sekstifiredel.
Summen er derfor alltid 1 minus hullet. Hullet kan bli så lite du vil, men aldri null.
Med uendelig mange ledd blir summen nøyaktig 1: den kommer forbi ethvert tall under 1, men aldri over.
Zenon, en gresk filosof, hevdet at du aldri når døra: først halve veien, så halvparten av resten, i det uendelige. Summen viser at du kommer fram.
Men det holder ikke at leddene krymper. En halv pluss en tredel pluss en firedel, og så videre, vokser forbi ethvert tall.
Forskjellen: her tar hvert ledd bare halvparten av det som er igjen, så summen kan aldri passere 1.

quiz.question: Hvor mye mangler på 1 etter 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/16?
quiz.right: En sekstendel: hullet er alltid like stort som den siste biten som ble lagt til.

request: Hva skjer med arealet når sidene dobles?

commands.speak: Hva skjer med arealet når alle sidene dobles? Start med et kvadrat med side 2 meter.
Arealet er 2 ganger 2: 4 kvadratmeter.
Doble først bare bredden. Nå er arealet dobbelt så stort, 8, og der stopper de fleste gjetninger.
Men høyden skal også dobles, og den doblingen dobler arealet en gang til: 16 kvadratmeter.
Fire ganger så stort, ikke to. Hvorfor?
Det store kvadratet rommer fire kopier av det gamle, to i hver retning.
Areal har to retninger, og hver av dem ble doblet: to ganger to er fire.
Et volum har tre. Dobler du alle mål på en kube, blir volumet to ganger to ganger to: åtte ganger så stort.
Galilei brukte dette i 1638: et dyr dobbelt så høyt veier åtte ganger mer, men beina blir bare fire ganger tykkere. Derfor har elefanter så tykke bein.

quiz.question: En pizza på 40 cm mot en på 20 cm. Hvor mye mer pizza får du?
quiz.right: Fire ganger så mye: diameteren dobles, og en flat pizza vokser i to retninger, to ganger to.

request: Hvorfor er en ytre vinkel lik summen av de to motstående indre?

commands.speak: Hvorfor er en ytre vinkel i en trekant lik summen av de to motstående indre? Ta trekanten A B C.
Vinkelen ved A er 45 grader.
Vinkelen ved C er 75 grader.
Forleng siden A B forbi B. Vinkelen mellom forlengelsen og siden B C er den ytre vinkelen ved B: 120 grader.
Påstanden er at den alltid er summen av de to langt borte, 45 pluss 75. Hvorfor skulle de bestemme den?
Den indre vinkelen ved B er 60 grader. Den og den ytre ligger langs samme rette linje, så de utgjør 180 sammen.
Men de tre vinklene i trekanten utgjør også 180.
Og B pluss den ytre, y, er 180.
B må fylle det samme hullet opp til 180 i begge. Det som er igjen, må være likt: y er A pluss C.
Det finnes også et bilde. Trekk en linje gjennom B, parallell med A C.
Vinkelen ved A glir langs grunnlinja til B. Den parallelle linja skjærer grunnlinja i den samme vinkelen.
Vinkelen ved C, snudd en halv omdreining, passer mellom parallellen og B C: en Z-vinkel mellom to parallelle linjer.
Sammen fyller de nøyaktig den ytre vinkelen: 45 pluss 75 er 120.
Euklid beviste akkurat dette i Elementene, bok én, setning 32, og fikk vinkelsummen på 180 grader med på kjøpet.

quiz.question: En trekant har 30° ved A og 50° ved C. Hva er den ytre vinkelen ved B?
quiz.right: 80 grader: den ytre vinkelen er summen av de to motstående, 30 pluss 50.
quiz.wrong: 100 grader er den indre vinkelen ved B. Den ytre ligger på den andre siden av linja.

request: Hva er en ellipse?

commands.speak: En ellipse ser ut som en klemt sirkel, men hva er den egentlig? Start med to knappenåler, 400 fra hverandre.
Knyt en tråd på 500 mellom dem, og hold den stram med en blyant: 250 til hver nål.
Før blyanten rundt med tråden stram. Den ene biten vokser, og den andre krymper like mye.
Ved enden er bitene 450 og 50. Summen er fortsatt 500, for tråden er den samme.
Sporet blyanten følger, er ellipsen: alle punkter der de to avstandene til nålene har samme sum.
Nålene heter brennpunkter og ligger på den lange aksen. Den er nøyaktig like lang som tråden: ved enden ligger begge bitene langs den.
Skyv nålene sammen, og ellipsen runder seg til en sirkel. En sirkel er en ellipse der de to brennpunktene faller sammen.
Jo lenger fra hverandre nålene står, jo flatere blir ellipsen.
Kepler viste i 1609 at Mars går i en ellipse rundt sola, med sola i det ene brennpunktet, ikke i midten.

quiz.question: Tråden er 500. Et punkt på ellipsen ligger 100 fra det ene brennpunktet. Hvor langt er det til det andre?
quiz.right: 400: avstandene til de to brennpunktene er alltid til sammen trådens lengde, 500.

request: Hvordan lager en symaskin et sting når nåla aldri slipper tråden?
title: Symaskinen: to tråder, én knute

commands.speak: Hvordan lager en symaskin et sting, når nåla aldri slipper tråden og aldri går helt gjennom stoffet? Svaret ligger i noen få deler.
Overtråden går fra snella på toppen, gjennom trådgiveren og ned til nåla.
Syr du for hånd, stikker du hele nåla gjennom stoffet, med øyet bakerst og tråden etter.
Det kan ikke maskinnåla: den sitter fast i maskinen. Derfor sitter øyet helt nederst, ved spissen.
Og derfor trengs en tråd til. Under stoffet ligger spolen med undertråden, som aldri kommer opp.
Trykkfoten holder stoffet nede mens nåla går ned og opp.
Idet nåla snur og løfter seg litt, henger overtråden igjen under stoffet som en liten løkke.
Griperen snapper løkka og drar den rundt hele spolen.
Når løkka har gått rundt, ligger undertråden inni den.
Så rykker trådgiveren overtråden opp igjen, og løkka strammes rundt undertråden.
Krysset mellom de to trådene havner midt inne i stoffet.
Det er hele stinget: ingen knute, bare to tråder som låser hverandre. Derfor ser sømmen lik ut på begge sider.
Så mates stoffet fram rundt to og en halv millimeter, og nåla stikker ned igjen.
Én runde på håndhjulet er ett sting. En søm på femti centimeter er to hundre runder.
Med rundt åtte hundre sting i minuttet er den sydd på femten sekunder.
Øyet i spissen og to tråder som låser hverandre: det fikk amerikaneren Elias Howe patent på i 1846.

quiz.question: Hva skjer hvis undertråden er brukt opp?
quiz.right: Det blir ingen sting: løkka av overtråd har ingen undertråd å låse seg rundt, og trådgiveren drar den bare opp igjen.

request: How does a lock and key open a door?
title: The shear line

spec.title: A pin tumbler lock, in section

card.title: How a key opens a lock

commands.speak: How does a key open a lock? A front-door lock is a plug that must turn inside a fixed housing, and between them runs a thin gap.
Across that gap sit stacks of pins, brass below and steel above. Springs push them down, so each steel pin straddles the gap and pins the plug.
A key is not a code the lock reads. It is just a row of heights.
Slide in a key with one cut a step too deep.
Two stacks split exactly at the line, but the middle one is lifted too little.
Its steel pin still crosses the gap, and the plug will not budge. The lock never rejects a key; one pin simply stays in the way.
The right key has the right height under every stack.
It slides in, and each cut lifts its own stack by its own amount.
Every joint between brass and steel arrives at the line at the same moment.
Now nothing crosses the gap.
Seen from the front, the plug is a cylinder, and the joint between the pins sits exactly on its edge.
So the plug turns, carrying the brass pins with it, and pulls back the bolt.
This drawing has three stacks; a front door has five or six. With six depths per cut, five stacks already allow 7,776 different keys.
It also explains lock picking: twist the plug gently, and the pins bind one at a time, so each can be pushed to the line on its own.

quiz.question: One cut on a key is a step too deep. What happens?
quiz.right: It stays locked: that stack is lifted too little, so its steel pin still straddles the shear line.

request: Hvorfor blir bremselengden fire ganger så lang når farten dobles?
title: Bremselengden vokser med kvadratet

commands.speak: Hvorfor blir bremselengden fire ganger så lang når farten dobles? Det avgjør om bilen stanser foran et barn i veien, eller ikke.
De fleste gjetter en rett linje: dobbel fart, dobbel bremselengde.
En bil som bremser hardt på tørr asfalt i femti kilometer i timen, står etter tolv meter.
I hundre trengs førtiåtte meter: fire ganger så langt, ikke to.
Formelen viser hvorfor: bremselengden er farten i annen, delt på to ganger bremsingen.
Bremsene tar bort like mye bevegelsesenergi for hver meter, og energien vokser med kvadratet av farten.
Med god bremsing, åtte meter per sekund i annen, gir femti kilometer i timen tolv meter.
Men før bremsene tar, går det gjerne et sekund der du ser faren og flytter foten. I femti kjører du fjorten meter.
I hundre kjører du tjueåtte meter før du i det hele tatt har begynt å bremse.
Legg de to sammen, og bilen i femti står etter tjueseks meter.
Bilen i hundre trenger syttiseks.
Står et barn tjueseks meter foran, stanser bilen i femti rett foran det.
Bilen i hundre har ikke engang begynt å bremse der. Den treffer i full fart.
Et sammenstøt i hundre har samme energi som et fall fra nesten førti meters høyde.

quiz.question: Farten øker fra 30 til 60 km/t. Hva skjer med bremselengden?
quiz.right: Den firedobles: bremselengden følger farten i annen, og to i annen er fire.

request: What does E = mc² actually say? Show me the curve it comes from.
title: The energy of standing still

commands.speak: What does E = mc² actually say? It is one point on a curve: the energy an object carries, plotted against its speed.
Push a ball faster and faster and its energy climbs, gently at first, then without limit as it nears light speed.
The whole curve is one formula: mass times light speed squared, divided by a square root.
The root shrinks as v approaches c. At ninety per cent of light speed it is about 0.44.
So at 0.9 c the ball carries 2.3 times mc².
Now slow the ball down. The root grows back towards one, and the energy falls with it…
…but not to zero. At rest the curve lands here, on E = mc².
So the famous equation is not about speed at all. It is the energy a thing has for sitting still.
Newton's formula adds half m v squared on top of that, and tracks the curve closely up to about half light speed.
Then it falls hopelessly behind: at 0.9 c Newton says 1.4, the real value is 2.3.
And because the curve has no top, no amount of energy pushes a thing with mass all the way to light speed.
Einstein's 1905 paper put it as a question: does the inertia of a body depend on its energy content?

quiz.question: In E = mc², how fast is the object moving?
choices: Not at all: it is at rest
quiz.right: At rest: mc² is where the energy curve meets the axis, and c is only the conversion rate.

request: Hvorfor er nordlyset grønt?
title: Fargen forteller høyden

commands.speak: Hvorfor er nordlyset nesten alltid grønt? Fargen er ikke tilfeldig: den forteller hvilket stoff som lyser, og hvor høyt oppe.
Fra bakken ser det slik ut: et grønt teppe, ofte med en svak rød rand øverst.
Elektroner, satt i fart av solvinden og jordas magnetfelt, stuper ned i lufta og støter borti atomene der.
Mellom hundre og to hundre og femti kilometer er mye av lufta enkle oksygenatomer. Et støt gir atomet litt ekstra energi.
Den energien sender atomet ut igjen som lys med én bestemt bølgelengde: 557,7 nanometer. Det er grønt.
Men atomet bruker nesten et sekund på å gi fra seg lyset. Så lenge må det være i fred, ellers tar et nytt støt energien.
Oksygen kan også lyse rødt, men da må atomet være i fred i nesten to minutter.
Det skjer bare over to hundre og femti kilometer, der lufta er så tynn at støtene nesten aldri kommer.
Under hundre kilometer er lufta for tett også for det grønne. Der lyser nitrogen, blått og fiolett.
Og grønt vinner fordi de fleste elektronene stanses nettopp i denne høyden, der det grønne lyset får tid.
Den grønne linja var lenge en gåte. Først i 1925 viste John McLennan i Toronto at den kom fra oksygen.
Så fargene er en høydemåler: rødt øverst, grønt i midten, og blått bare når elektronene når uvanlig langt ned.

quiz.question: Hvorfor lyser ikke oksygenet rødt i hundre kilometers høyde?
choices: Atomet blir truffet før det rekker å lyse rødt
quiz.right: Det røde lyset tar nesten to minutter, og så lavt blir atomet truffet av andre og mister energien før det lyser.

request: Why is the Eiffel Tower shaped like that?
title: The wind curve

elements.text: all the wind above the cut

commands.speak: Why is the Eiffel Tower shaped like that? Its flare looks like decoration, but it is a calculation: the shape the wind demands.
Three hundred metres of open iron, finished in 1889. Its engineers feared the wind far more than the tower's own weight.
A straight shaft that tall would be a lever: wind pushing all the way up, and one narrow foot to hold it.
Wind presses on every level, and the higher it presses, the longer its lever over the ground.
Cut the tower at any height, here at the second platform. Everything above the cut is trying to tip over it.
All the wind above the cut adds up to one push, acting at one height.
Eiffel's rule: at every height, the legs lean so that their lines meet right there, where that push acts.
Then the wind's push runs along the iron, as a pull in one leg and a squeeze in the other, instead of bending it.
Move the cut down, and more tower and more wind stand above it, on a longer lever.
So the legs splay wider and wider towards the ground, where the base is 125 metres across.
Near the top there is little above to catch the wind, and the legs close in, almost upright.
The shape is so sparing that its seven thousand tonnes of iron, melted down, would fill its square base only about six centimetres deep.

quiz.question: Where must the tower be widest, and why?
choices: At the base: most wind above, longest lever
At the top: the wind is strongest there
In the middle: it is heaviest there
quiz.right: At the base: each cut lower down has more tower, and more wind, pushing on a longer lever above it.

request: Hvorfor har Stortinget en rund bue midt på fasaden?

commands.speak: Stortingsbygningen har en rund bue midt på fasaden. Hvorfor? Se huset ovenfra: to fløyer i gul tegl langs Karl Johans gate.
Midt på buler bygget ut mot gata, som en halv sirkel.
Innenfor ligger stortingssalen, og benkeradene følger nøyaktig den samme buen.
I sentrum, ved den rette veggen, sitter presidenten. Alle 169 representantene vender seg mot det samme punktet.
Buen i fasaden er altså ikke pynt. Den er salen selv, sett utenfra: huset er formet innenfra og ut.
Representantene sitter ikke partivis, men etter valgdistrikt: hvert fylke samlet i sin kile av halvsirkelen.
Det britiske Underhuset er bygget annerledes: to rette benker vendt mot hverandre, regjering mot opposisjon.
Der står man i to fronter. I en halvsirkel ser alle mot midten, og partifellene sitter spredt mellom hverandre.
Tegningene er av den svenske arkitekten Emil Victor Langlet, og huset stod ferdig i 1866.
Så neste gang du ser buen fra Karl Johan, ser du rett inn i salen der lovene vedtas.

quiz.question: Hvorfor buler Stortinget ut mot Karl Johan?
choices: Det er et tårn med utsikt
quiz.right: Stortingssalen er et amfi formet som en halvsirkel, og ytterveggen følger benkeradene.

request: Hvorfor blir renters rente så stor?
title: Årene står i eksponenten

commands.speak: Hvorfor blir renters rente så stor? Svaret står i formelen: årene havner i eksponenten. Ta 10 000 kroner til sju prosent i året.
Med enkel rente får du 700 kroner hvert år, alltid regnet av startbeløpet. Beløpet vokser i en rett linje.
Her står antall år, n, som en faktor: ti år gir ti ganger 700 kroner.
Med renters rente ganges hele beløpet med 1,07 hvert år. Etter ett år har du 10 700.
Året etter ganges 10 700 med 1,07 igjen, så også fjorårets 700 kroner gir rente.
Etter n år har du ganget med 1,07 n ganger. Da står n i eksponenten.
Og en eksponent bøyer kurven oppover, selv om renten aldri endres.
Etter ti år skiller det lite: 17 000 mot 19 700, knapt 2 700 kroner.
Pengene har nesten doblet seg, som regelen om 72 sier: 72 delt på sju er omtrent ti år.
Etter tretti år står det 31 000 på den ene kontoen og 76 000 på den andre.
De ti siste årene alene gir 37 000 kroner, mer enn de tjue første årene til sammen.
Renten ble aldri høyere. Det er beløpet den regnes av som vokser, fordi årene står i eksponenten.

quiz.question: Hva gir mest etter 30 år?
quiz.right: Sju prosent renters rente: 76 000 mot 52 000 kroner. Dobbel rente som faktor slår ikke årene i eksponenten.

request: Hvorfor har en bikube sekskanter? Vis et ekte bilde og skissen.

elements.credit: Merdal at Turkish Wikipedia · CC BY-SA 3.0

commands.speak: Hvorfor er cellene i en bikube sekskanter? Se på et ekte bilde: hver celle er en sekskant, og de står vegg i vegg.
Voks er dyrt: bia må spise flere gram honning for hvert gram voks. Bygget hver for seg trenger sju celler 42 vegger.
Skyv dem sammen, og naboer deler vegg.
Nå holder 30 vegger for de samme sju cellene.
Cellen i midten eier ikke en eneste vegg alene: alle seks deler den med en nabo.
I en stor kake deles hver vegg av to celler. Da betaler hver celle bare for tre vegger av seks: halvparten.
Sirkler kan ikke dele vegg. De berører hverandre i ett punkt, så hver trenger sin egen hele vegg, og mellom dem blir det hull.
Kvadrater deler vegger like godt. Men med samme plass til honning trenger et kvadrat omtrent sju prosent mer vegg enn en sekskant.
Så det meste av sparingen kommer av å dele vegger. Sekskanten legger bare de siste prosentene på toppen.
Charles Darwin kalte bikaka helt perfekt til å spare arbeid og voks.

quiz.question: Hva sparer biene mest voks på?
