quiz.right: Delte vegger halverer voksen: hver vegg tjener to celler. Sekskantformen sparer bare omtrent sju prosent i tillegg.

request: Hvorfor ligger de gamle fabrikkene ved elva?

commands.speak: Hvorfor ligger de gamle fabrikkene langs elvene? Fordi kraften en gang ikke kunne flytte seg. Ei elv faller, meter for meter, mot havet.
Der fallet er brattest, setter noen et hjul i vannet, og fallet gjør arbeidet.
En kubikkmeter vann i sekundet som faller ti meter, gir rundt hundre kilowatt. Jo høyere fall, jo mer kraft.
Fabrikken bygges tett inntil hjulet. Kraften kom ut som en roterende aksel, og aksler og reimer rakk bare gjennom én bygning.
Arbeiderne måtte bo der maskinene stod, så boligene fulgte etter. Slik vokste hele bydeler fram rundt ett fall.
I Oslo faller Akerselva 149 meter på åtte kilometer, og langs den lå fabrikk ved fabrikk: spinnerier, veverier og møller.
Så kom strømmen. En generator ved fossen gjør fallet om til strøm, og en ledning bærer den ti mil nesten like lett som ti meter.
Fra da av kunne fabrikken ligge hvor som helst: ved jernbanen, ved havna, der arbeidsfolket bodde.
De gamle fabrikkene står der ennå, ved fossene. De ble bygget da kraften ikke kunne flytte seg, så fabrikken måtte flytte til kraften.

quiz.question: Hvorfor lå fabrikken tett inntil vannhjulet?
choices: Aksler og reimer rakk bare noen meter
Elva var eneste vei for varene
quiz.right: Kraften gikk gjennom aksler og reimer, som bare rakk gjennom én bygning. Først strømmen kunne bære den langt.

request: Why does a vaccine protect people who never got it?

commands.speak: A vaccine can protect people who never got it, like a baby too young for the shot. The reason is the road a virus travels.
A virus has no legs of its own: it moves only from one person to the next. Here each sick person passes it to two.
Two become four.
Four become eight, and one of the eight is a three-week-old baby. She was simply next in line.
Now run it again, but first vaccinate just two of these fourteen people.
The virus still reaches both of them, and there it stops: in this simple picture, a vaccinated person passes nothing on.
Behind them whole branches never catch it: eight people who never got a vaccine, the baby among them.
Nothing changed inside the baby. She is as susceptible as before; what changed is that no chain of infection reaches her.
So every dose protects twice: the body that got it, and everyone down the chains that would have run through it. That is herd immunity.
Doctors use this on purpose. To shield newborns from whooping cough, they vaccinate the parents and siblings around them. It is called cocooning.

quiz.question: How does the vaccine protect the unvaccinated baby?
choices: It breaks the chains that reach her
Antibodies spread to her from others
quiz.right: It breaks chains: vaccinated people stop passing the virus on, so no chain reaches her. Her own body is unchanged.

request: Why does a higher frequency squeeze the wave?

commands.speak: Why does a higher frequency squeeze a wave? Because frequency is a count: how many times each second the air at your ear is pushed and released.
This is the pressure at your ear from a thin beep of one kilohertz: a thousand pushes a second.
So one push and release lasts a thousandth of a second: one millisecond, trough to trough.
In this first millisecond exactly one cycle fits.
Raise the frequency to four kilohertz, and the same millisecond must hold four cycles, so each one is squeezed.
Nothing about the wave changed but the count.
Frequency and period are one fact read two ways: four thousand cycles a second, a quarter of a millisecond each.
The period is one over the frequency: four times the count, a quarter of the time.
Now follow your eardrum through time. It is this dot, pushed in and out with the air.
In just over a millisecond it swings in and out five times: four thousand times a second.
Squeezing time is also how a recording plays higher: at double speed every period halves, and every note jumps an octave.
A siren coming towards you squeezes its waves the same way.
Buys Ballot tested it in 1845, with horn players on a moving train.

quiz.question: A note's period is 4 milliseconds. What is its frequency?
quiz.right: 250 hertz: a second holds a thousand milliseconds, and cycles four milliseconds long fit into it 250 times.

request: What is the tangent at a point, and how does it turn as the point slides?

spec.title: The tangent turns with the point

commands.speak: What is the tangent at a point, and what does its tilt tell you as the point slides? Take the sine curve, rising and falling forever.
Put a point on it at x = 0.
The tangent there is the straight line that leans exactly as the curve leans. Here it climbs one for every one across: slope one.
Record that slope as a height: a second dot, straight above, at height one.
Slide to the crest. The tangent flattens, and the slope dot falls to zero.
Past the crest the tangent tips downhill. At pi it is steepest, slope minus one, and the dot bottoms out.
Here the tangent even cuts through the curve. It need not stay on one side; it only has to match the lean.
Keep sliding. Uphill, the dot rises above zero; downhill, it sinks below. Its trail is a whole new curve.
It is the cosine: the same wave, shifted a quarter turn to the left. The slope of sine is cosine.
That is why a swinging pendulum is fastest at the bottom: where its position crosses zero, its rate of change peaks.
So the derivative is not one number but a second curve: the tangent's tilt, written down at every point.

quiz.question: Where is the sine curve's slope at its lowest?
quiz.right: Where it falls through zero, at pi: that is where it runs steepest downhill, slope minus one. At the trough the slope is zero.

request: Does the equilibrium follow when demand shifts?

card.title: How the price finds its way

commands.speak: When demand shifts, does a market really move to the new equilibrium, and how? Take strawberries at one market: crates a day, and the price of a crate.
Growers bring more crates, the better the price.
Buyers take fewer, the dearer they are.
They meet at fifty dollars and thirty crates, and that is where the market price sits.
Then a heat wave: at every price, buyers want twenty more crates, and demand slides right.
Nobody can see the new crossing. What everyone sees is this: at fifty dollars, buyers want fifty crates and growers bring thirty.
Stalls sell out by noon, and buyers ask for more. The shortage is the signal.
So sellers ask more. Each step up brings more crates in and talks some buyers out of it, until the gap is gone.
It closes at the new crossing: sixty dollars, forty crates. Nobody had to find it; the shortage led there.
But that assumes growers can answer at once. Strawberries are planted a season ahead, on last season's price.
Fifty dollars brings only thirty crates, so buyers bid them up to seventy. Seventy brings fifty crates, a glut, and the price falls back to fifty.
And round again. With these curves the price never settles: it jumps between fifty and seventy, circling the sixty it never reaches.
Arthur Hanau found such swings in German pig prices in 1928. Economists still call it the hog cycle.
This wedge is what buyers and growers gain from trading. It is largest at the crossing, so every lap of the cycle wastes some of it.
So the equilibrium does pull the price, through shortage and glut. Whether the price arrives depends on how fast supply can answer.

quiz.question: What if growers reacted to price less strongly than buyers?
quiz.right: They die out: each crop overshoots less than the last, so the price spirals in to the crossing.

request: What happens to the angle when one arm turns?

commands.speak: What happens to an angle when one arm turns? An angle measures turning: how far one arm has swung from the other. This arm stays put.
This one starts thirty degrees round from it.
The angle is the opening between them, and it writes its own size: thirty degrees.
Turn the arm sixty degrees more, and the arc widens with it: ninety, a quarter turn, the right angle.
Now make the fixed arm much longer. The angle stays at ninety: an arm's length is no part of it.
Draw the corner mark bigger, and it is still ninety. The size of the drawing never counts, only the turn.
Turn on another sixty, and the opening grows to a hundred and fifty degrees: wider than a right angle, an obtuse one.
Every change in the number came from turning the arm, and from nothing else.
Why three hundred and sixty for a full turn? Dividing the circle into 360 degrees comes from Babylonian astronomy, which counted in sixties.

quiz.question: Double the length of both arms. The angle…
quiz.right: It stays the same: an angle measures the turn between the arms, not how long they are.

request: How do you solve 2x + 3 = 11?

commands.speak: How do you solve 2x + 3 = 11? The rule is to do the same to both sides, and a balance scale shows why that works.
On the left pan: two boxes, each holding the unknown x, and three one-kilo weights.
On the right: eleven kilos. The scale balances, which is exactly what the equals sign says.
To get the boxes alone, the three kilos must go.
Take them off the left pan only…
…and the scale tips. The two sides are no longer equal.
Take three off the right as well…
…and it balances again. The same change on both sides keeps the balance.
Write that down on a new line. Two boxes weigh eight kilos: 2x = 8.
Share the eight between the two boxes, and each box balances four.
Dividing both sides by two says the same: x = 4.
Check it in the first line: two fours and three make eleven.
The equals sign itself was invented in 1557 by Robert Recorde: two parallel lines, because no two things could be more equal.

quiz.question: In 3x + 5 = 20, what must happen to the 20?
quiz.right: Subtract 5: whatever leaves the left pan must leave the right, so 3x = 15 and x = 5.

request: What does the ICER compare?

commands.speak: The ICER is how agencies judge a new drug's price, and it compares less than you'd think. The new drug costs thirty thousand dollars per patient; the old, twenty.
Patients on the old drug live 4.0 quality-adjusted life years, QALYs; on the new one, 4.2.
The tempting sum divides the new drug's cost by its QALYs: about seven thousand dollars each. That sounds like a bargain.
But four of those years came with the old drug too. The new drug didn't buy them, so they can't be on its bill.
What the new drug did buy sits on top. Ten thousand dollars of extra cost, in red…
…for this thin sliver of extra health: 0.2 QALYs, in blue. That sliver is all the drug adds.
The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio divides one difference by the other.
Extra cost on top: new minus old.
Extra health below, measured against the same comparator.
Ten thousand over 0.2: fifty thousand dollars for each QALY the new drug adds, seven times the tempting figure.
Small slivers make big ratios. A drug that is only a little better has to be only a little dearer.
And the ratio always answers 'compared with what?'. Swap the old drug for a different comparator and the ratio changes, though the new drug has not.
This incremental logic was set out for medicine by Milton Weinstein and William Stason in 1977, and every agency's ratio still follows it.

quiz.question: A third drug costs $31,000 and gives 4.21 QALYs. Its ICER against the new drug?
quiz.right: A hundred thousand dollars per QALY: one thousand dollars more, for one hundredth of a QALY more. Only the differences count.

request: Why do cos and sin draw a circle?

spec.title: Why cos and sin draw a circle

card.title: Why cos and sin make a circle

commands.speak: Why do cos and sin draw a circle? In school they are ratios in a right triangle, so the circle needs a reason.
Start with an arm of length one, from the centre, turned sixty degrees up from the x axis.
Its shadow across is cos sixty: one half. With a hypotenuse of one, the ratio is simply the length.
Its height is sin sixty: 0.87.
So the tip of the arm sits at the point cos t, sin t.
The legs change as the arm turns, but they always make a right triangle whose long side is one.
So Pythagoras holds at every angle: 0.5 squared plus 0.87 squared, 0.25 plus 0.75, is exactly one.
Every point one unit from the centre: that is what a circle is.
Sweep a full turn and the tip traces it. Past ninety degrees the shadow points left: cos is negative, but squared it counts the same.
Trigonometry in fact began on the circle: Hipparchus, around 140 BC, made the first known table, of chords in a circle.
So cos and sin are not two separate things: they are the two coordinates of one turning arm.

quiz.question: If sin t = 0.6, what can cos t be?
quiz.right: 0.8 or minus 0.8: cos squared must be one minus 0.36, which is 0.64.

request: Why is a life-year gained in thirty years worth so little today?

commands.speak: Why does a year of health thirty years away count for so little today? Across: years from now. Up: the weight that year gets in a cost-effectiveness sum.
With no discounting, the weight is flat at one: a year is a year, whenever it arrives.
Discounting bends that line with one rule: a year t years away counts one over one plus r, to the power t.
The rate r starts at zero, so the power does nothing yet.
Turn r up to three and a half percent, England's rate for costs and health alike. The line sags, and sags more every year.
Read off year thirty.
One point oh three five, multiplied by itself thirty times, is about 2.8. So that year counts as 0.36 of a year lived today.
Nearly two thirds gone, from a rate that sounds tiny. Each year shrinks what the year before it left, so the losses compound.
Now add up a benefit that lasts forever, year after year. Shade its first twenty years.
And shade the rest: year twenty to sixty, plus a thin tail that runs off the chart and never quite stops.
The two areas are equal. At three and a half percent, half the value of an everlasting benefit arrives in its first twenty years.
Now one and a half percent, the lower rate some guidelines allow for benefits that last for decades. The whole curve lifts.
Year thirty now keeps 0.64 of its weight. Two points off the rate, and the distant year's loss is nearly halved.
For a benefit that lies decades away, the choice of r can matter more than the clinical evidence, which is why it is argued over so hard.

quiz.question: At 3.5 %, year 30 counts 0.36. What does year 60 count?
quiz.right: About 0.13: thirty more years multiply the weight by 0.36 again, and 0.36 times 0.36 is 0.13. Discounting divides; it never runs out.

request: Do people live longer if the cancer is found earlier?

commands.speak: Do people live longer when a cancer is found earlier? Survival figures say yes, loudly. Follow one life to see what they measure. The tumour starts in year two.
In year eight it causes symptoms, and that is the day of diagnosis.
In year eleven the patient dies of it.
Survival runs from diagnosis to death: three years. That is the number the statistics collect.
Now the same life again, in a country that screens. Same tumour, same year, and so far the same day of death.
Before the scan is switched on, it is found by symptoms in year eight, and the ruler reads three years again.
Switch the screening on. The scan finds the tumour in year four, four years before any symptom.
Survival more than doubles, three years to seven. Yet the death did not move: the ruler simply starts further left. That head start is lead time.
Five-year survival goes from zero to a hundred percent, without one day of life added.
Now suppose early treatment really works, and pushes death two years later, to year thirteen.
Survival reads nine years. Of the six extra, four are still lead time; only the two the death moved are life.
So survival rises whether screening works or not. The honest yardstick is where death falls: deaths per hundred thousand people, screened or not.
In 2000, Gilbert Welch and colleagues compared twenty cancers over four decades: gains in five-year survival bore no relation to changes in death rates.

quiz.question: Screening raises five-year survival from 40 % to 70 %. What have we learned?
quiz.right: Nothing yet: an earlier diagnosis lengthens survival even when death does not move. Only fewer deaths in a trial shows that lives were saved.

request: How can a calculator work out sin(1.2) with nothing but plus and times?

spec.title: A polynomial learns the sine curve

commands.speak: How can a calculator give the sine of 1.2 when all it can do is add and multiply? One way: a polynomial that imitates this curve.
Here is the number we want: at 1.2 the curve stands at 0.9320.
Start as simply as possible: P of x equals x, a straight line. At 1.2 it says 1.2, far too high.
But near zero, line and curve agree: the sine of a hundredth is a hundredth, to six decimal places.
So add a correction that matters only further out: minus x cubed over six.
The line bends over and follows the curve past the first crest. At 1.2 it now says 0.912.
Next, plus x to the fifth over a hundred and twenty.
Now 0.9327 at 1.2, and the agreement reaches further out.
One more term.
0.93203: right to four decimals. Four terms of pure arithmetic now hold a whole hump of the curve.
The denominators, six, a hundred and twenty, five thousand and forty, are factorials: three times two times one, and so on.
They come from how sine bends at zero alone. The recipe never looks at the curve out at three, yet follows it there.
That is a Taylor series: what a function does at one point, spent on the whole neighbourhood around it.
But the fit only grows outward from that point. Far enough away the polynomial always runs off, and more terms just push that edge further out.
So real maths libraries first fold any angle into a small range near zero, where a few terms are enough.

quiz.question: Which would these four terms get least accurately?
quiz.right: sin 5: the fit spreads outward from zero, and at five the polynomial has already begun to run away.

request: How could anyone see whether two tones were in tune, a century before electronic tuners?

spec.title: Tuning with a beam of light

card.title: Tuning with a beam of light

commands.speak: How could anyone see that two tones were in tune, long before electronic tuners?
In 1857 Jules Lissajous turned the question into a picture.
He glued a small mirror to a tuning fork and bounced a beam of light off it. Fork A swings the spot side to side.
A second fork, turned at right angles, swings it up and down. Sounding together, the spot has to obey both at once.
Start with both forks at the same pitch: a ratio of one to one.
A quarter cycle apart, the spot runs round one closed loop, a circle, again and again.
Now raise fork B an octave: exactly twice the frequency.
A figure of eight. It touches the top twice for every once it touches the side: two to one, read straight off the screen.
A perfect fifth is three to two. Now the spot needs two full sideways swings before the pattern closes.
Three touches along the top, two down the side. The interval is read without knowing a single frequency.
Now put fork B a hair out of tune. A slightly wrong frequency is a phase that keeps creeping, so the whole figure starts to roll.
The speed of the roll is the error: one roll a minute means fork B is off by one vibration a minute.
It is the same drift you hear as beats. To tune, you turned the peg until the picture stood still.
The curves themselves were not new: Nathaniel Bowditch had drawn them with a swinging pendulum in 1815. Lissajous made them out of sound.

quiz.question: Turning the peg makes the figure roll faster. Meaning?
choices: You are moving away from the pitch
quiz.right: Further away: the rolling speed is the size of the error, and a figure standing still means an exact ratio.

request: Can a treatment be better for mild cases, better for severe cases, and still lose overall?

elements.x_label: Share of the drug's patients who were severe (%)

commands.speak: Can a drug win for mild cases and for severe cases, yet lose overall? It can, and one picture shows where the reversal comes from.
Drug A cures ninety percent of mild cases, sixty percent of severe ones. Overall, it depends on the mix: all mild at the left, all severe at the right.
Drug B cures eighty-five and fifty-five. Its line runs five points below A's, whatever the mix.
So among mild cases, A wins by five.
Among severe cases, A wins by five again.
A drug's overall rate is a dot on its own line, at the share of severe patients it was given. With the same mix, A's dot sits right above B's.
But suppose doctors saved drug A for the hardest cases: eighty percent of its patients were severe, and only twenty percent of B's.
Pooled, A cures sixty-six percent and B seventy-nine. B wins by thirteen, though it lost both comparisons.
Neither line moved. The dots slid along them: A's pooled rate is mostly a severe-case rate, B's mostly a mild-case rate.
The honest comparison puts both dots on one vertical line: the same mix of patients.
Give both drugs half mild and half severe, and A leads by five, as it did in each group.
A randomised trial does this for you: chance, not a doctor, picks who gets which drug, so both get the same mix on average.
The 1948 British trial of streptomycin for tuberculosis is often called the first to assign patients by random numbers.

quiz.question: In a randomised trial, where would the two dots sit?
quiz.right: On one vertical line: chance gives both drugs the same mix of patients on average, so only the gap between the lines shows.

request: The test is 99% accurate and mine came back positive. Am I probably ill?

commands.speak: Does a positive on a ninety-nine percent accurate test mean you are probably ill? First, what that one number hides. Here are a hundred people like you.
Say one person in a hundred has the disease. Just this one.
A test that tells everyone they are healthy is right about ninety-nine of these hundred. Ninety-nine percent accurate, and useless.
So accuracy alone says little. A test has two numbers: how often it catches the sick, and how often it wrongly flags the healthy.
A good test catches ninety-nine percent of the sick, so this person tests positive.
It also flags one healthy person in a hundred. Among ninety-nine healthy people that is about one: this person, perfectly well.
Two positive results, and only one of them is ill. Your positive is a coin flip.
Weigh the two ways to get a positive: one sick person, caught, against ninety-nine healthy people, times a one percent slip.
When the false-alarm rate is as large as the share who are ill, a positive is even odds, however good the test sounds.
Now retest just these two, with a second test whose mistakes are independent. In this new crowd, one in two is ill.
The healthy crowd has shrunk from ninety-nine to one. A second positive means ninety-nine to one: ninety-nine percent.
The first positive didn't settle it. It picked out a smaller crowd, in which the same kind of test is finally convincing.
Thomas Bayes worked out this kind of updating; his essay was published in 1763, two years after his death, by his friend Richard Price.

quiz.question: Disease: 1 in 50. False alarms: 1 in 50. A positive means…
quiz.right: About even odds: the share who are ill equals the false-alarm rate, so a positive is as likely a slip as a real case.

request: Why is the production possibilities frontier bowed outward and not a straight line?

commands.speak: Why does a production frontier bow outward instead of running straight? Take a small country with three regions, making bread and steel.
The simple guess is a fixed swap. All bread gives 120, all steel gives 70, and a straight line joins them.
But the regions differ. Start with all bread, and move the mill town into steel first: its 40 bread become 40 tonnes, one loaf a tonne.
Next the plains: their 40 bread make only 20 tonnes, so each tonne now costs two loaves.
Last the farm valley: 40 bread for just 10 tonnes, four loaves a tonne. The line keeps getting steeper.
And at forty tonnes it sits far above the guess: eighty bread, where the straight line promised about fifty.
A straight line only fits a country whose regions are all alike.
A real country has thousands of different farms, mills and workers, each a tiny segment. The corners blur into a smooth bow.
So the bow is not a law of nature. It is the fact that resources differ, and each is moved in the order of what it does best.
David Ricardo made the same point about countries in 1817: England's cloth and Portugal's wine.

quiz.question: What if all three regions were equally good at steel?
quiz.right: Straight: every tonne would cost the same bread, whichever region made it, so the swap never changes.

request: Why can a heat pump deliver more heat than the electricity it uses?
title: Where a heat pump's extra heat comes from

spec.title: Where a heat pump's extra heat comes from

commands.speak: Why can a heat pump deliver more heat than the electricity it uses? It sounds like something for nothing, so follow where the extra comes from.
On a mild day, plus seven outside, one kilowatt-hour of electricity puts about three kilowatt-hours of heat into the house.
The same refrigerant goes round and round these four parts, and the trick is what happens in each one.
Outside, the refrigerant is colder than the air, so heat flows into it. Even air at minus fifteen still has heat to give up.
That is where the missing two kilowatt-hours come from: the outdoor air.
The compressor squeezes the gas, and squeezing a gas makes it hot, hotter than the room. This is the step the electricity pays for.
Now the refrigerant is the hottest thing in the room, so heat flows out of it, into the air you breathe.
The valve lets it expand and turn cold again, ready to go back outside for another load.
Round it goes. The electricity never becomes most of the heat; it pays to carry heat that was already outside.
An electric heater turns one kilowatt-hour into exactly one. It has nothing to carry.
In frost the pump must lift the heat further, from minus fifteen up to room warmth, so each kilowatt-hour carries less.
At minus fifteen a typical air unit gives about two: still double a heater, but no longer three.
Lord Kelvin described such a heat multiplier in 1852, a century before heat pumps warmed ordinary homes.

quiz.question: At minus fifteen, where does the second kilowatt-hour come from?
quiz.right: The outdoor air: minus fifteen is far above absolute zero, and the refrigerant in the coil is colder still, so heat flows in.

request: Why does a bigger sample make a poll more accurate — and why doesn't the size of the country matter?
title: What a poll's margin really depends on

spec.title: What a poll's margin really depends on

commands.speak: Why does asking more people make a poll more accurate, and why doesn't the size of the country matter? A poll asks a thousand, and speaks for millions.
This is how far off a random sample can be, as the number asked grows. It falls steeply, then flattens out.
Ask a hundred people and the answer is give or take ten points: useless for a close race.
Ask four times as many and the margin halves, to five.
Four times again, and it only halves once more. Every halving costs four times the interviews, which is why polls stop near a thousand.
The margin shrinks with the square root of the number asked. Nothing in that curve asks how many people live in the country.
Here is the same poll in a town of five thousand. The two curves agree until you have asked a large share of everyone.
Only out here, asking half the town, does the size of the population help. A thousand is a speck of any country, so Norway and America need the same thousand.
In 1936 the Literary Digest counted over two million mail-in ballots and predicted Roosevelt would lose. Gallup, asking far fewer people, got it right.
The Digest's readers were not a random sample of voters. A big sample shrinks random error; it does nothing for a biased one.

quiz.question: 1,000 Norwegians or 1,000 Americans: which poll has the smaller margin?
quiz.right: The same: the margin depends on how many you asked, not on how many you could have asked.

request: Hvorfor blir ventetiden hos legen så mye lengre når kontoret er nesten fullbooket?
title: Ventetid og slakk

commands.speak: Hvorfor blir ventetiden hos legen så mye lengre når kontoret er nesten fullbooket? Ta et kontor der en konsultasjon tar ti minutter i snitt.
Mange tenker seg at ventetiden vokser jevnt med hvor fullt det er, langs en rett linje som denne.
Men når pasientene kommer når det passer dem, og timene tar ulik tid, ser det slik ut.
Halvt booket venter du ti minutter i snitt, like lenge som en konsultasjon.
Ved åtti prosent venter du førti minutter.
Ved nitti prosent: halvannen time. Ti prosentpoeng til, og ventetiden er mer enn doblet.
Ved nittifem prosent: over tre timer.
Regnestykket er enkelt: ti minutter, ganger hvor fullt det er, delt på det som er igjen.
Det som er igjen, er slakken. Halver slakken, og ventetiden dobles omtrent; går slakken mot null, går ventetiden mot uendelig.
Grunnen er at pasienter klumper seg. Med luft i dagen spises en forsinkelse opp; uten luft arver neste pasient den, og pasienten etter der igjen.
Dette er køteori, og den begynte med den danske ingeniøren Agner Krarup Erlang, som regnet på telefonsentralen i København rundt 1909.
Så ventetid måler ikke hvor hardt de jobber der inne, men hvor lite slakk de har igjen til å ta forsinkelser med.

quiz.question: Kontoret går fra 90 til 95 prosent booket. Ventetiden …
quiz.right: Den blir omtrent doblet: slakken halveres fra ti til fem prosent, og ventetiden går fra halvannen til over tre timer.

request: Why does an epidemic peak and then fade, even when nobody was immune at the start?

commands.speak: Why does an epidemic peak and then fade, even when nobody was immune at the start? Take a virus where each case infects three others.
This is the share of a town ill at once, in the simplest epidemic model. It climbs, peaks near day thirty-eight, and drains away.
On day twenty, a case meets three people it could infect, and nearly all of them are still susceptible.
Three times the share still susceptible, 0.93: about 2.8 new cases for every case. So the wave grows.
At the peak, two of every three people have had it. The same three meetings find only one person who can still catch it.
Three times a third is one. Each case now just replaces itself, which is exactly why the curve stops rising here.
By day fifty-five, nine in ten have had it. Three meetings make about a third of a new case, and the wave drains.
Nothing about the virus changed. It never weakened, and nobody stayed home: three meetings per case, from the first day to the last.
What changed is who it met. The epidemic turns because it is using up its own fuel, making the immunity nobody had at the start.
It even stops short: about six in a hundred never catch it, because by the end there are too few cases left to reach them.
William Farr saw in 1840 that epidemics rise and fall in a regular curve, almost ninety years before this model explained why.

quiz.question: At the peak, why does each case infect only one other?
choices: Two of its three contacts are immune
quiz.right: Two of its three contacts are already immune: the virus spreads as easily as ever, but only a third of the people it meets can still catch it.

request: What does a sampling distribution look like if I only have one sample? Can I bootstrap it in R?

elements.code:
library(ggplot2)
n <- Slider(10, 400, default = 40, label = "Sample size")
replace <- TRUE
resample <- Button("New sample")
set.seed(1 + resample)
x <- rexp(n, rate = 1/4)
means <- round(replicate(2000, mean(sample(x, replace = replace))), 3)
cat("sample mean:", round(mean(x), 2), " bootstrap SE:", round(sd(means), 2), "\n")
ggplot(data.frame(m = means), aes(m)) + geom_histogram(bins = 25) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1, 8))

commands.speak: How can you see a sampling distribution when you only have one sample? The bootstrap builds one, here in R, running live.
The one sample: forty waiting times, averaging about four minutes, from a skewed distribution with a long tail.
Two more knobs: whether to resample with replacement, and a button for a fresh sample.
The trick: draw forty values from the sample itself, with replacement, take their mean, and do it two thousand times.
Then print the spread of those two thousand means, and draw them.
That histogram stands in for the sampling distribution of the mean. Its spread, 0.61, is the standard error.
The textbook formula, the sample's standard deviation over root n, gives 0.61 as well. The bootstrap got there with no formula at all.
Why with replacement? Each resample then repeats some values and drops others, just as a fresh sample from the population would.
Switch replacement off, and every resample is the same forty values, reshuffled.
Every mean is the same, so the histogram collapses to one bar and the standard error to zero. Nothing was learned.
Turn it back on, and let the sample grow to four hundred. The histogram narrows, as a real sampling distribution would.
Bradley Efron published the bootstrap in 1979. The name is from pulling yourself up by your own bootstraps.
Press New sample a few times: the histogram moves with each sample, but its width stays about the same.

quiz.question: Why must the bootstrap resample with replacement?
choices: Otherwise every resample has the same mean
quiz.right: Without replacement every resample is the same values reshuffled, so the means never vary; with it, they vary as fresh samples would.

request: How does a Markov cohort model turn two yearly risks into a picture of a whole population over time?

commands.speak: How does a Markov model turn two yearly risks into a picture of a whole population? It sorts everyone into states: well, sick, or dead.
Each year, one in ten of the well fall sick.
And one in five of the sick die. In this model nobody recovers.
Start a cohort of a thousand people, all well, in year zero.
One year on, a hundred have fallen sick and nine hundred are still well.
Year two: ninety more fall sick, and twenty of the sick die. The same two percentages, applied to the new counts.
That step is the whole model. Repeat it every year, and the shares trace a picture.
The well, in blue, lose a tenth every year, so they shrink quickly at first and ever more slowly.
The dead pile up, since no arrow leaves that state.
And the sick, in red, rise and then fall, though neither risk ever changed.
They peak around year six, at about 27 percent of the cohort.
Why a hump? The sick gain a tenth of the well, a shrinking inflow, and lose a fifth of themselves, a growing outflow.
Jump the counts to year six: 531 well, 269 sick, 200 dead.
Here the two flows balance: a tenth of 531 is 53 falling sick, a fifth of 269 is 54 dying. In equals out, so the sick stop growing.
Robert Beck and Stephen Pauker brought this kind of model into medical prognosis in 1983. It still runs most cost-effectiveness studies.

quiz.question: Both risks stay fixed. Why do the sick decline after year six?
choices: Fewer well people are left to fall ill
The risk of falling ill drops
quiz.right: Fewer well people are left: a tenth of a shrinking group is a shrinking inflow, while a fifth of the sick still leave each year.

request: Why do health economists draw a cloud of dots instead of one number when they compare two treatments?

commands.speak: Why do health economists compare two treatments with a cloud of dots, not one number? Across: the QALYs a new drug adds. Up: what it costs extra.
The trial's best guess: a quarter of a QALY, for twelve thousand dollars more. One dot, one ratio: forty-eight thousand dollars per QALY.
The payer will go up to fifty thousand per QALY. Below this line is good value, so the single dot says yes.
But twelve thousand and a quarter are estimates, and each could easily be a good deal higher or lower.
So the model is run again and again, drawing costs and effects from that uncertainty each time. Every run is one dot: a world that might be ours.
Nineteen of these thirty worlds, in blue, lie below the line. The single number said yes; the cloud says about two chances in three.
Up here the drug costs more and does harm. Its ratio comes out negative, which in a table of ratios looks like the cheapest of all.
Here the gain is nearly zero, so the ratio explodes to almost half a million dollars per QALY.
Ratios break down near zero and flip sign across the axes. So the cloud is read by counting dots on each side of the line, never by averaging ratios.
That count is the chance the drug is good value, and it is what a payer is really deciding under.
William Black drew this plane in 1990, precisely to show what a single ratio hides.

quiz.question: World A: +$12,000 for +0.25 QALYs. World B: −$12,000 for −0.25. Same verdict?
quiz.right: No: A buys health below fifty thousand a QALY, but B gives up a quarter of a QALY to save less than it is worth. Same ratio, opposite verdicts.

request: How much is a health gain worth today if it only arrives decades later?

commands.speak: How much is health worth today if it arrives decades later? It decides real budgets. Take a million dollars: spent treating patients now, it buys ten QALYs this year.
Or it vaccinates twelve-year-olds against a cancer of middle age: twice the health, twenty QALYs, arriving about twenty-five years later.
Counted as they come, undiscounted, the vaccine wins two to one.
Now discount at three and a half percent. Each distant QALY is divided by 1.035 to the twenty-fifth power, about 2.4.
The vaccine's twenty shrink to eight and a half, below the treatment's ten. Treatment wins, with half the health.
The treatment's bar did not move: its QALYs arrive now, and both options are paid for today. Only the waiting benefit is discounted.
At one and a half percent the vaccine is worth almost fourteen, and wins again.
The verdict flips at about 2.8 percent. Below that rate prevention wins; above it, the treatment does.
So the rate is not a technicality. It chooses between the patient in the clinic today and the one a vaccine protects decades from now.
Countries do choose differently: Dutch guidelines discount health at 1.5 percent while discounting costs at 4.

quiz.question: The discount rate rises from 1.5 % to 3.5 %. Which option loses value?
quiz.right: The vaccine: its QALYs are twenty-five years away, so a higher rate shrinks them, while the treatment's arrive today and keep their full weight.

request: How does Morse code spell letters with just two signals — and can I send SOS?

commands.speak: Morse code spells every letter with just two signals, a short dot and a long dash. So which letter gets which pattern?
Each letter gets its own pattern of one to four signals.
E, the commonest letter in English, is a single dot.
T, the second commonest, is a single dash.
Q, which you rarely need, takes four: dash, dash, dot, dash.
The shortest patterns went to the letters used most, so an ordinary message needs far fewer signals than alphabetical order would give.
The red rows are the word we'll send. S is three dots, and O is three dashes.
To send, use the four pads: dot, dash, gap to end a letter, and send. Or hold the space bar, briefly for a dot.
What you send appears as a strip, with the letters it decodes to above it.
A dash lasts three dots, so the ear tells them apart by length alone.
The gap is a signal too: without it, three dots and three dashes are just six sounds the listener must split somewhere.
SOS stands for nothing. It was adopted in 1906 because three dots, three dashes, three dots is easy to send and hard to mistake.

ask.question: Send SOS on the key.
ask.right: Three short, three long, three short: nine signals, each letter closed with a gap.
ask.wrong: End each letter with the gap pad, then press send.

quiz.question: Why is E a single dot?
quiz.right: It is the commonest letter in English: short codes for frequent letters make every message quicker to send.

request: Why does the Tower of Hanoi take 2^n − 1 moves?

commands.speak: The Tower of Hanoi asks how few moves shift a whole tower to the right peg. The rules: one disk at a time, never a larger on a smaller.
Take three disks. Before the biggest can move anywhere, what has to be true?
Both disks above it must be out of the way, stacked on the middle peg. That is a two-disk tower, moved: three moves.
Then the big disk crosses, in one move.
And the two-disk tower moves again, onto it: three more. Three, one, three: seven.
The same holds for any size: to move n disks, move the tower above the biggest twice, plus one move for the biggest.
That twice is the whole story. Each extra disk doubles the work, and adds one.
One, three, seven, fifteen, thirty-one: always one less than a power of two. A guess of two more per disk would say nine for four disks; it takes fifteen.
Édouard Lucas sold the puzzle in 1883 with a legend of monks moving sixty-four disks. At a move a second, that takes about 585 billion years.
Back to the start. Now it's your tower.

ask.question: Move the tower to the right peg. Can you do it in seven?
ask.right: Solved. Seven is the fewest: the small pair aside in three, the big disk over, the pair back on top in three.
ask.wrong: Get the top two onto the middle peg first; that frees the big disk.

quiz.question: Five disks take 31 moves. How many does six take?
quiz.right: 63: the five-disk tower moves twice, 31 moves each, plus one move for the biggest disk.

request: What is an XOR gate for?

spec.title: What an XOR gate is for

card.title: What an XOR gate is for

commands.speak: An XOR gate is the part of a computer that adds. It takes two bits, A and B: two switches, each on or off.
The bulb shows its output. It lights when exactly one switch is on, and stays dark when both are.
An ordinary OR gate would light for both on as well. Exclusive or refuses that one case, and that refusal is the whole point.
Add two one-digit binary numbers. Nought plus nought is nought, and one plus nought is one, either way round.
But one plus one is two, and binary writes two as one, nought.
Read the last digit of the four answers: nought, one, one, nought. That is exactly when the bulb lights.
So XOR computes the ones digit of a sum, which is why every adder in a processor is built around it.
The one that moves left, the carry, needs a second gate, an AND, lit only when both are on. Together they make a half adder.
Chain adders like this column by column, each passing its carry to the left, and a processor adds numbers of any length.
In 1937 a 21-year-old student, Claude Shannon, showed that switches wired like this can carry out any logic, arithmetic included.

ask.question: Light the bulb: find inputs whose sum ends in 1.
ask.right: One switch on, one off: one plus nought is one, so the sum ends in 1.
ask.wrong: Both on is one plus one, and that ends in 0.

quiz.question: Both switches on. What does the half adder give?
quiz.right: One plus one is binary one, nought: XOR gives the digit 0, and AND gives the carry 1.

request: Why do the shorter bars of a xylophone sound higher?

commands.speak: Why does a short xylophone bar ring higher than a long one? Eight bars here, from middle C on the left to the C above.
Strike the longest, and it rings at middle C: about 262 vibrations a second.
The shortest rings an octave higher, exactly twice as fast: 523 a second.
A struck bar bends like a springboard. A shorter bar is stiffer for its weight, so it springs back sooner: more swings every second.
For a guitar string the rule is simple: halve the length and the pitch doubles, one octave up.
A bar is different. Its pitch rises with one over the length squared.
So the octave bar needs about seven tenths of the length, not half. A bar cut to half would ring two octaves up.
Makers also carve an arch under each bar. Thinning the middle lowers its pitch, so the low bars need not be so long.
Your turn. Tap a bar or press its number; done sends the tune.

ask.question: Play the bars from shortest to longest, then press done.
ask.answer: C5 B4 A4 G4 F4 E4 D4 C4
ask.right: Shortest to longest runs highest to lowest: a falling scale, from the top C down to middle C.
ask.wrong: Start at the right-hand end, bar 8, and work left.

quiz.question: A bar cut to half length rings how much higher?
quiz.right: Two octaves: pitch goes with one over length squared, so half the length vibrates four times as fast.

request: Why is bubble sort so slow?

commands.speak: Bubble sort is one of the slowest ways to sort, and six bars show why. Its one rule: only neighbours may swap.
Five stands before two, so they swap. Then it compares the next pair along, and the next, pass after pass.
One pass carries the tallest bar, nine, all the way to the end. Each pass settles just one bar.
Now count the pairs standing in the wrong order. Five stands ahead of three smaller bars: two, one and three.
Two is ahead of one; eight ahead of one and three; nine ahead of three. Seven wrong pairs in all.
A neighbour swap fixes exactly one wrong pair and disturbs no other. So this row needs seven swaps, and bubble sort makes exactly seven.
Worst case, a row in reverse: every pair is wrong. Six bars make fifteen pairs; n bars make n times n minus one, over two.
A thousand bars: half a million swaps. A million bars: five hundred billion.
Faster sorts, like merge sort, compare items far apart. A million items take them about twenty million steps, not five hundred billion.
Donald Knuth judged that bubble sort has nothing to recommend it, except a catchy name.
Now sort these six yourself, one neighbour swap at a time.

ask.question: Sort the bars. Can you do it in seven swaps?
ask.right: Seven swaps, one for each pair that stood in the wrong order.
ask.wrong: Only neighbours may swap: drag a bar onto the one beside it, or click the two in turn.

quiz.question: Ten bars in reverse order. How many swaps?
quiz.right: 45: all ten times nine over two pairs are in the wrong order, and each swap fixes just one.

request: Why does tic-tac-toe always end in a draw?

commands.speak: Tic-tac-toe between two careful players always ends in a draw. Why can't the first player force a win? Watch one game.
X opens in a corner.
O takes the centre, the square on four of the eight lines.
X takes the opposite corner.
O takes another corner. It looks natural, and it loses.
O now threatens the diagonal, so X must block in the bottom corner. And that one block makes two threats.
Up the left side and along the bottom: a fork. O can block only one of them.
O blocks the bottom row.
X completes the left column and wins.
Every win in this game comes from a fork, because a single threat can always be blocked.
So rewind to O's second move.
This time O plays an edge, and makes a threat of its own, down the middle column.
X must block at the bottom. A player busy blocking never gets the free move a fork needs.
Answer threat with threat, and the board fills up with no winner. Every opening goes that way under perfect play.
In 1952 Sandy Douglas put noughts and crosses on Cambridge's EDSAC computer: one of the first video games.
Your board: you are X. The computer plays win, block, centre, then the first free corner: the rule that just lost.

ask.question: Play a game. Hold at least a draw, or find the fork.
ask.right: Held. Against a perfect defender nobody does better than a draw; against this rule, corner then opposite corner wins.
ask.wrong: O got three in a row. Block its threat before building your own.

quiz.question: X holds two opposite corners, O the centre. Where should O play?
quiz.right: An edge: it makes a threat X must block, so X never gets the free move a fork needs.

request: Why does a disease with a higher R0 need so many more people vaccinated before it stops spreading?

elements.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
r0 = Slider(1.2, 18.0, step=0.2, default=2.0, label="R0")
efficacy = Slider(0.5, 1.0, step=0.01, default=0.9, label="Vaccine efficacy")
coverage = Slider(0.0, 1.0, step=0.05, default=0.6, label="Coverage")
r = np.linspace(1.05, 18, 300)
plt.plot(r, 1 - 1 / r, label="share that must be immune")
need = 1 - 1 / r0
plt.scatter([r0], [need], zorder=3)
plt.axhline(coverage * efficacy, color="gray", linestyle="--", label="immune today")
plt.xlabel("R0"); plt.ylabel("share immune"); plt.ylim(0, 1); plt.legend()
print("R0", r0, "needs", round(100 * need), "% immune; today", round(100 * coverage * efficacy), "%")

commands.speak: Why does a more contagious disease need so many more people vaccinated before it stops? The first knob is R0: how many one case infects when nobody is immune.
To stop spreading, each case must infect fewer than one. With a share p immune, a case infects R0 times one minus p.
Solve for p: the immune share must pass one minus one over R0. That is the herd immunity threshold.
The other two knobs belong to the vaccination programme: how well the vaccine protects, and how many people get it.
The curve is that threshold for every R0. At an R0 of two, the dot says half of us must be immune.
The dashed line is who is immune today: sixty percent vaccinated, nine in ten of them protected, so 54 percent. Just past the dot.
Walk R0 up. The share needed leaps from under forty percent to two thirds by an R0 of three, then only crawls: three quarters, four fifths.
So a disease twice as contagious does not need twice the coverage. From an R0 of two to four, the need goes from a half to three quarters.
Now measles, whose R0 is usually put at twelve to eighteen. At twelve, ninety-two percent must be immune.
Here is the catch. With a vaccine that protects nine in ten, even vaccinating everyone leaves us short: past an R0 of ten, it can never be enough.
Two doses of measles vaccine protect about ninety-seven percent. Given to ninety-five percent of children, that just clears the bar.
That is why the World Health Organization asks for ninety-five percent coverage against measles, and why a small dip lets outbreaks back in.
Try it: pick an R0, then find the lowest coverage that clears the dot, first with a weak vaccine, then a strong one.

quiz.question: R0 doubles from 4 to 8. The share that must be immune…
quiz.right: From three quarters to seven eighths: one minus one over R0 flattens, so twice as contagious needs only a little more, though that little may be beyond a vaccine's reach.

request: Hvorfor gir en god test så mange falske alarmer når sykdommen er sjelden?

elements.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
forekomst = Slider(0.001, 0.1, step=0.001, default=0.01, label="Forekomst")
sensitivitet = Slider(0.5, 1.0, step=0.01, default=0.9, label="Sensitivitet")
spesifisitet = Slider(0.9, 1.0, step=0.001, default=0.95, label="Spesifisitet")
n = 100000
syke = n * forekomst
ekte = syke * sensitivitet
falske = (n - syke) * (1 - spesifisitet)
ppv = ekte / (ekte + falske)
plt.bar(["ekte syke", "falske alarmer"], [ekte, falske])
plt.ylabel("positive prøver av 100 000")
plt.ylim(0, 5000)
print("Av de positive er", round(100 * ppv, 1), "% faktisk syke")

commands.speak: Hvorfor gir en god test så mange falske alarmer når sykdommen er sjelden? Svaret ligger i den første knappen: hvor vanlig sykdommen er.
De to andre er testens egne egenskaper: sensitivitet, andelen syke den fanger, og spesifisitet, andelen friske den frikjenner.
Av hundre tusen testede er tusen syke. Testen finner ni hundre av dem, men slår også alarm for fem prosent av de friske: nesten fem tusen.
Bare femten av hundre positive er faktisk syke.
Senk forekomsten fra én av tjue til én av tusen. Søylen med syke krymper, mens de falske alarmene står nesten stille.
Til slutt er under to av hundre positive syke. Testen ble aldri dårligere; det er de friske som er så mange.
Tilbake til én av hundre. Hva hjelper? Skru først sensitiviteten helt opp, så testen finner alle de syke.
Andelen syke blant de positive går bare fra femten til sytten prosent. De syke var aldri problemet.
Skru heller spesifisiteten fra nittifem til nittini og en halv prosent. De falske alarmene faller til en tidel.
Nå er nesten to av tre positive syke. Når sykdommen er sjelden, er det spesifisiteten som avgjør hva et positivt svar er verdt.
Alle nyfødte i Norge testes for den sjeldne sykdommen PKU, som den norske legen Asbjørn Følling oppdaget i 1934.
Prøv selv: sett forekomsten til én av tusen, og se hvor nær hundre prosent spesifisiteten må før et positivt svar blir til å stole på.

quiz.question: Sykdommen er sjelden. Hva gir færrest falske alarmer?
quiz.right: Høyere spesifisitet: de falske alarmene kommer fra de mange friske, og spesifisiteten bestemmer hvor mange av dem som slår ut.

request: Why does a trial with forty patients so often miss a real effect that a trial with four hundred finds every time?

spec.title: Statistical power, one sample size at a time

elements.code:
n <- Slider(10, 400, default = 40, label = "Patients per arm")
effect <- Slider(0.1, 1.0, step = 0.05, default = 0.4, label = "Effect size")
sizes <- sort(unique(c(seq(10, 400, by = 10), n)))
pw <- 100 * sapply(sizes, function(k) power.t.test(n = k, delta = effect, sd = 1)$power)
here <- 100 * power.t.test(n = n, delta = effect, sd = 1)$power
mark <- ifelse(sizes == n, pw, NA)
label <- sprintf("%d per arm: power %d%%", n, round(here))
goal <- rep(80, length(sizes))

commands.speak: Why does a trial of forty patients so often miss an effect that four hundred find every time? This curve is statistical power: the chance a trial of each size detects a drug that really works.
Trials are usually planned to reach eighty percent.
Two knobs: patients per arm, and the true effect. Here the drug improves the outcome by 0.4 of a standard deviation.
A trial with forty patients per arm sits at forty-two percent.
Let us keep score as we go.
So a small trial of a drug that works comes up empty more often than not. Its 'no significant difference' means 'too small to tell'.
A hundred per arm reaches eighty percent…
…a hundred and sixty, ninety-five…
…and four hundred, nearly certain.

Every patient costs the same, but power flattens out: the step from forty to a hundred buys almost forty points, the step from a hundred and sixty to four hundred barely five. That is why a trial is sized before it starts.
Now halve the effect, to 0.2. The whole curve sinks: even four hundred per arm reaches only eighty-one percent.
Half the effect needs four times the patients: about four hundred per arm instead of a hundred. The size a trial needs grows with one over the effect squared.
In 1962 Jacob Cohen checked a year of psychology studies and found they had, typically, less than an even chance of detecting a medium effect.
Try it: pick a small effect, then find how many patients per arm bring power back up to eighty percent.

quiz.question: 40 per arm, no significant effect. What have we learned?
choices: Little: it would often miss a real effect
quiz.right: Little: with power around forty percent, a trial this size misses a real effect more often than it finds it.

request: How does turning beta and gamma change the epidemic curve?

elements.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
beta = Slider(0.1, 1.0, step=0.01, default=0.3, label="beta")
gamma = Slider(0.05, 0.5, step=0.01, default=0.1, label="gamma")
S, I, R = [0.999], [0.001], [0.0]
for k in range(1500):
    new, rec = beta * S[-1] * I[-1] * 0.1, gamma * I[-1] * 0.1
    S.append(S[-1] - new); I.append(I[-1] + new - rec); R.append(R[-1] + rec)
days = [k * 0.1 for k in range(len(S))]
_ = plt.plot(days, S, label="S")
_ = plt.plot(days, I, label="I")
_ = plt.plot(days, R, label="R")
_ = plt.xlim(0, 150); _ = plt.ylim(0, 1); _ = plt.legend()
print("R0", round(beta / gamma, 1), "| peak", round(100 * max(I)), "% on day", round(days[I.index(max(I))]), "| never infected", round(100 * S[-1]), "%")

commands.speak: An epidemic model has two rates, beta and gamma. What does each one control? Everyone starts here, susceptible.
Contact with an infectious person moves you across, at a rate beta times the share who are infectious.
Recovery moves you on at rate gamma, one over the days you stay infectious: gamma 0.1 means about ten days.
Their ratio, beta over gamma, is R nought: how many people one case infects in a population with no immunity.
Now the same model as a running simulation, with both rates as knobs.
Beta at 0.3, gamma at 0.1: R nought is three.
Infections peak at thirty percent of the population, around day thirty-nine, and six percent are never infected.
Now double both rates together: twice the contacts, but each case infectious for half as long.
The same curve, squeezed into half the time: the peak is still thirty percent, now on day nineteen, and still six percent escape.
Doubling both is just running the clock twice as fast. The rates set the speed; only their ratio sets the size.
Now double only beta, keeping ten infectious days. R nought becomes six.
The peak jumps to over half the population, and almost nobody escapes.
Kermack and McKendrick showed in 1927 that the share ever infected depends on R nought alone: at three, about ninety-four percent.
So shortening how long cases stay infectious, by isolation or treatment, raises gamma, and that shrinks an epidemic rather than merely speeding it up.
Try two different pairs with the same ratio, and watch the curve keep its height while it moves in time.

quiz.question: A new variant passes on twice as easily per contact, but people also recover twice as fast. Compared with the old one, its epidemic is…
quiz.right: Just as large, but quicker: beta over gamma, R nought, is unchanged, and R nought alone sets the peak and the final size.

request: Why is the regression slope the covariance divided by the variance?

spec.title: Where the regression slope comes from

commands.speak: Why is a regression slope the covariance divided by the variance? Take five students: hours studied, against exam score.
Draw a cross through the averages, three hours and fifty-five points. Each student is now a step away from that centre.
This student studied two hours more than average and scored twenty-two more. Multiply the two steps: a rectangle worth plus forty-four.
This one studied an hour less but scored two more: minus one times plus two, a small negative rectangle.
Add up every rectangle: forty, minus two, six and forty-four. Eighty-eight, so hours and scores mostly move together.
That sum is the top of the slope formula.
Below it, how much hours vary on their own: steps of two, one, zero, one and two, squared and summed. Ten.
Eighty-eight over ten: 8.8 points per extra hour.
Hours times points, divided by hours squared, leaves points per hour. The division is what turns moving together into a slope.
The two students farthest from the average hours supply eighty-four of the eighty-eight. Points far out along x steer the slope.
And the student at exactly three hours supplies nothing: a rectangle of zero width. A point at the average x has no say in the slope.
Divide top and bottom by the number of students, and the two sums get their names: covariance over variance.
Adrien-Marie Legendre published the method of least squares in 1805, to fit the orbits of comets.

quiz.question: A sixth student studied exactly 3 hours and scored 95. The slope…
quiz.right: Stays at 8.8: at the average x the rectangle has zero width, so the new point adds nothing to the covariance or the variance.

request: What do μ and σ do in the normal distribution's formula?

spec.title: μ and σ in the normal density

commands.speak: What do mu and sigma do in the normal distribution's formula? Each moves exactly one thing you can see. Take IQ scores.
They are scaled on purpose to follow this bell, with an average of 100 and a sigma of 15.
Here is its formula. It looks fearsome, but only two letters in it ever change.
The exponent only asks how far x is from mu. The bell is highest where that distance is zero.
So mu is where the peak stands: 100.
Set mu to 115, and the whole bell slides right with its shape unchanged.
Back to 100.
Sigma is the width. One sigma out, at 115, the curve has dropped to six tenths of its peak.
Sigma divides the distance: with sigma 15, a score of 130 is just two sigmas out.
And about 95 percent of people lie within two sigmas of the mean: between 70 and 130.
Keep this bell in view.
Now double sigma. The bell spreads twice as wide…
…and sinks to half the height. This front factor forces it: the area under the bell is always one, the whole population.
Gauss used this curve in 1809 for the errors in astronomers' measurements, which is why it is also called the Gaussian.
So mu says where, sigma says how spread, and the rest of the formula keeps the total at one.

quiz.question: Halve σ. What happens to the peak's height?
quiz.right: It doubles: half as wide, and the area must stay one, so the bell stands twice as tall.

request: Why are future QALYs discounted?

commands.speak: Why do health economists count a QALY in the future as worth less than one today? It sounds callous, and the strongest reason is surprising.
A health service has a million dollars. Spent now, on a screening programme, it buys fifty quality-adjusted life years.
Or it could wait. Invested at three and a half percent a year, a million dollars doubles in twenty years.
Spent then, on the same programme at the same price, it buys a hundred QALYs. Twice the health, just for waiting.
Wait twenty more years and it is four million: two hundred QALYs.
If a QALY counts the same whenever it arrives, later always beats now. So the programme is postponed forever, and nobody is ever helped.
Economists call this absurd verdict the paradox of postponement.
The cure is in the QALY sum itself. Undiscounted, it simply adds each year's quality-weighted life.
Discounted, each year's QALYs are divided by one plus r, to the power of how far away that year is.
At the same three and a half percent as money, a hundred QALYs in twenty years count as fifty today.
Two hundred in forty years count as fifty too.
Now waiting gains nothing by itself, and the people falling ill meanwhile tip the choice back to acting now. That is why costs and health share one rate.
Not everyone is at ease.
In 1928 the economist Frank Ramsey called discounting later enjoyments 'ethically indefensible', a weakness of the imagination.

quiz.question: A payer discounts costs at 3.5 % but QALYs at 0 %. When should it fund a programme?
quiz.right: Always next year: invested money keeps growing while the QALYs it buys keep full weight, so waiting always looks better, the paradox of postponement.

request: Hvordan henger gjennomsnitt og standardavvik sammen?

commands.speak: Hvordan henger gjennomsnitt og standardavvik sammen? Standardavviket måles fra gjennomsnittet. Ta fem busser, og hvor mange minutter hver kom for sent.
To, fire, fire, fem og ti minutter.
Gjennomsnittet er summen, 25, delt på fem busser: x-strek er fem minutter.
Det er balansepunktet: legg prikkene som lodd på en planke, og den vipper ikke over fem.
Standardavviket spør hvor langt hver buss ligger fra fem: tre under, én, én, null og fem over.
Hvorfor ikke bare ta snittet av avvikene? De summerer alltid til null: det er nettopp det balansepunktet betyr.
Så vi kvadrerer dem, og alle blir positive: 9, 1, 1, 0 og 25. Summen er 36.
Den ene bussen som kom ti minutter for sent, står alene for 25 av de 36: store avvik teller mye.
Del på n minus én, altså fire, og ta kvadratroten: s er tre minutter, tilbake i minutter igjen.
Innenfor ett standardavvik fra snittet, fra to til åtte minutter, ligger fire av de fem bussene.
Den generelle formelen gjør nøyaktig det samme: avstand fra x-strek, kvadrert, summert, delt på n minus én, og roten til slutt.
Gjennomsnittet står inne i standardavviket. Uten et midtpunkt finnes det ingen avstand å måle.
Navnet standardavvik fikk tallet av den britiske statistikeren Karl Pearson, i 1894.

quiz.question: Buss E kommer 20 minutter for sent. Hva skjer med s?
quiz.right: Mer enn dobbelt, fra 3 til over 7: ett stort avvik teller i andre potens, og drar både snittet og s med seg.

request: Can a three-state Markov model show me where a cohort ends up, and what drives it?

commands.speak: Which number in a Markov model drives its answer? Often not the one that looks biggest. Three states: well, sick and dead.
Each year a tenth of the well fall sick.
Three in ten of the sick recover.
And a few die: five percent of the sick, two percent of the well.
Everyone else stays put for another year.
Where does the cohort end up? All dead, eventually. But among the living the mix settles within a few years: about three well to every one sick.
Followed to the end, a person starting well lives 37.5 years on average. Now halve each probability in turn and see how far that moves.
Halve the biggest arrow, recovery, and life expectancy drops about four years.
Halve falling sick, and it rises about four and a half.
Halve dying when sick, just five percent, and nearly ten years are added.
And halve the smallest arrow of all, two percent, and the cohort gains over fifteen years: the largest swing.
The reason is where people stand. Three quarters of the living are well, so a small risk on that crowded state strikes most people, every year.
An arrow's weight is its probability times the crowd at its tail, summed over the years. Ranking inputs this way is one-way sensitivity analysis.

quiz.question: Which estimate most needs checking before we trust this model?
quiz.right: Dying when well, 0.02: the smallest arrow, but it acts every year on the crowd in the well state, so an error there moves the answer most.

request: Where does the vertex of a parabola come from?

commands.speak: Where is a parabola's lowest point, and why is it there? Take y = x² − 6x + 13: the answer comes from its mirror symmetry.
Draw a level line at height thirteen. It cuts the parabola twice: at x = 0, where the curve starts, and once more further on.
Where exactly? Set the formula equal to thirteen.
The thirteens cancel, and what is left factors: x times x minus six is zero.
So the two crossings are at zero and at six.
A parabola is symmetric, so its lowest point must lie halfway between any two points at the same height: at three.
Lower the line, and the two crossings slide toward each other, but their midpoint never leaves x = 3.
At the bottom they merge into one: the vertex. At x = 3 the formula gives nine minus eighteen plus thirteen: four.
Any parabola ax² + bx + c is back at its starting height c when x is minus b over a, so its vertex lies halfway: minus b over 2a.
Here b is minus six and a is one: six over two, three again.
Galileo showed in 1638 that a thrown stone follows a parabola, so on level ground its flight peaks exactly midway between launch and landing.
Completing the square finds the vertex too, but symmetry says why it sits there: halfway between any two equal heights.

quiz.question: Where is the vertex of y = x² − 10x + 30?
quiz.right: At x = 5: the height 30 comes back at x = 10, and the vertex lies halfway between.

request: Why does the same drug look cost-effective in one country and not in another?

commands.speak: Why can one drug, backed by one trial, be funded in one country and refused in the next? The answer lies on this plane: extra health across, extra cost up.
The trial says the drug adds half a quality-adjusted life year per patient, for forty thousand dollars more than today's treatment.
Forty thousand over a half: eighty thousand dollars per QALY. Both countries read the same trial and agree on this number.
Country A funds anything under a hundred thousand dollars per QALY. That is its line, and the dot lies below it: yes.
Country B's line is at forty thousand. Same dot, same trial, and now it sits above the line: no.
So what is that line? Not the value of a life. Roughly, it is what the budget already pays for a QALY in the treatments this drug would displace.
In B, forty thousand dollars spent elsewhere still buys a whole QALY. The drug buys half, so funding it would cost patients half a QALY, unseen.
B's lever is the price. Knock twenty-five thousand off the extra cost, and the same half QALY costs thirty thousand dollars each.
Now it clears B's line too. Same molecule, same health, different verdict, because the price moved and not the evidence.
Some countries tilt the line itself: Norway lets it rise with the severity of the illness a drug treats.
An old rule of thumb set the line at one to three times a country's income per head. In 2016 authors at the WHO warned against using it that way.
So a verdict has three parts: the dot, which the trial fixes, and the price and the line, which each country sets.

quiz.question: B's budget grows, and its cheap wins get funded. Its line should…
quiz.right: Rise: once the cheap wins are bought, what the budget gives up at the margin buys less health per dollar, so each extra QALY is allowed to cost more.

request: Hvorfor kan arbeidsledigheten falle uten at noen har fått jobb?

commands.speak: Hvordan kan arbeidsledigheten falle uten at en eneste person har fått jobb? Svaret ligger i hvem som telles. Ta hundre i yrkesaktiv alder: sytti er i jobb.
Tre er arbeidsledige: uten jobb, men de har søkt de siste fire ukene og kan begynne innen to uker.
De tjuesju andre står utenfor arbeidsstyrken: studenter, pensjonister, uføre, og de som har gitt opp å søke.
Ledigheten er de ledige delt på arbeidsstyrken, altså de i jobb pluss de som leter: tre av syttitre, fire komma én prosent.
Nevneren er syttitre, ikke hundre. De tjuesju utenfor står ikke i brøken i det hele tatt.
Nå gir én av de tre opp å søke. Hun har ikke fått jobb; hun har bare sluttet å lete.
Dermed forsvinner hun både fra telleren og fra nevneren: to av syttito, to komma åtte prosent.
Ledigheten falt med over ett prosentpoeng, og ingen fikk jobb. De sytti i arbeid er de samme sytti.
Derfor ser økonomer også på sysselsettingsandelen: hvor mange av alle hundre som er i jobb. Den står stille på sytti prosent.
Og det motsatte skjer i en oppgang: når jobbene kommer, begynner folk utenfor å lete igjen, og ledigheten kan stige mens flere får jobb.

quiz.question: Fem studenter begynner å søke, uten å få jobb. Ledigheten?
quiz.right: Den stiger: de fem flytter fra utenfor arbeidsstyrken til ledige, og kommer inn i både teller og nevner.
