request: What does it actually cost a country to build more hospitals?

spec.title: Economics 1 · What a hospital really costs

commands.speak: What does it really cost a country to build more hospitals? The invoice gives one answer, and an economist another. Hospitals along the bottom, schools up the side.
Say that with all its builders, money and staff, a country could build 800 schools in a decade, or 40 hospitals, or any mix on this curve.
Anything under the curve is possible; the curve is the most it can do.
Build ten hospitals and you still get 775 schools. Those ten cost twenty-five schools: two and a half each.
The next ten cost 82 schools: eight each.
The ten after that cost 164: sixteen each.
And the last ten take all 529 schools that were left: fifty-three each.
On average a hospital costs twenty schools. But no hospital costs the average: its price is the slope of the curve where you stand.
The first hospitals take builders and money schools could spare. The last take the very people schools cannot do without.
So the real cost of a hospital is the schools not built, and it depends on how many hospitals you already have.
Milton Friedman put the idea in a book title in 1975: There's No Such Thing as a Free Lunch.

quiz.question: A hospital costs 20 schools on average. The 35th costs…
quiz.right: More than twenty: past thirty hospitals the curve is steep, and each of the last ten costs about fifty-three schools.

request: If nobody sets the price, how does a market end up with one?

commands.speak: If nobody sets the rent, how does a city end up with a going rate? No committee decides it. Flats along the bottom, monthly rent up the side.
Tenants first: the cheaper the flats, the more people want one of their own. Demand slopes down.
Landlords: the higher the rent, the more flats get built, converted and let out. Supply slopes up.
Suppose landlords start out asking too much.
Read across: at that rent, more flats are offered than tenants will take. Some stand empty.
An empty flat earns nothing, so its landlord asks a little less, then a little less again, and the empty flats fill.
Now start too low instead.
Many more tenants now want a flat than landlords offer. That gap is a queue.
People in the queue offer a bit more, landlords notice, and the rent creeps up as the queue shrinks.
Both pressures stop at one rent: the crossing, where every flat offered finds a tenant and nobody queues.
No one had to know where the curves cross. Each landlord saw only an empty flat, each tenant only a queue, and that was enough.
Friedrich Hayek called this a marvel in 1945: prices carry what millions of people know to others who never meet them.

quiz.question: Flats stand empty for months at the going rent. What next?
quiz.right: Rents drift down: every empty month is a reason for a landlord to ask less, until the flats are let.

request: A tax is collected from sellers, so why do buyers end up paying part of it?

spec.title: Economics 3 · Who really pays a tax

commands.speak: A tax on cigarettes is collected from the shop, so why do smokers end up paying part of it? Packs along the bottom, price per pack up the side.
Demand lies flat, because this is a town of casual smokers: if the price moved much, they would quit, or buy in the next town.
Supply rises as always: the better the price, the more shops bother to stock them.
Untaxed, the market settles here.
Now a fixed tax on every pack, paid by the shop. Each pack costs the shop that much more, so the supply curve lifts by exactly the tax.
The new crossing sets the shelf price, and it has not risen by the whole tax: by less than a fifth of it.
Buyers now pay this much, noticeably more than before the tax.
But after paying the tax, the shop keeps only this much.
The band between the two prices, across every pack still sold, is the government's revenue.
The other four fifths come out of the shop's price. With buyers this quick to leave, the seller swallows most of the tax rather than lose them.
And a third thing appears: packs nobody sells any more, though buyers valued them above what sellers would have taken. Nobody collects that. It is simply gone.
England's window tax of 1696 made such a loss visible: people bricked up windows rather than pay, and lived in the dark.
Now the same tax in a town of committed smokers, who buy their packs whatever they cost. Demand steepens.
The shelf price now carries nearly four fifths of the tax. The shop passes on what it can, because these buyers do not leave.
And the lost wedge has shrunk to about a quarter of its size, because few trades were given up. Taxing what people won't give up raises much and wastes little.
What if the shops can walk away too, with shelf space that will happily hold something else?
Then buyers carry about nine tenths of the tax, and the shop barely feels it.
So who pays is not written in the tax law. The tax settles on whichever side finds it harder to walk away.

quiz.question: The same tax is collected from smokers at the till instead of from shops. Who bears more of it?
choices: Smokers now bear all of it
Shops now bear all of it
quiz.right: The split stays the same: buyers and sellers end up facing the same two prices whoever hands over the money, and only how easily each side walks away decides the split.

request: Why does competition leave a firm no profit at all?

commands.speak: Why does competition leave a firm no profit? Take a bakery that opens in a town with none: for a year it prints money, then it stops.
Marginal cost is what one more loaf costs: falling while the ovens fill up, then climbing as the bakers go into overtime.
Average total cost spreads everything over the loaves: flour, wages, rent, the oven. It bottoms out where the bakery is worked just right.
The bakery is too small to move the price of bread, so the market hands it a flat line: 78 cents a loaf.
How much to bake? Keep going while one more loaf sells for more than it costs to make, and stop where marginal cost reaches the price.
There, each loaf costs about 35 cents on average, so about 43 cents of every sale is profit. That rectangle is the total.
Word of a rectangle like that travels.
A second bakery opens, then a third. Together they bake more bread than the town was buying, and the price slides to 40 cents.
Each bakery follows the same rule, bakes a little less, and keeps about 16 cents a loaf.
And newcomers keep arriving while there is anything left to arrive for.
The price comes to rest at the bottom of average cost, and the rectangle is a sliver: under a cent a loaf.
Yet nothing has gone wrong. Average cost already includes a normal return: what the owner's time and money could earn elsewhere.
An accountant would still report a profit. What competition removes is the extra, and it hands that to the customer as cheaper bread.

quiz.question: In the long run, a competitive bakery earns zero economic profit. What does the owner earn?
choices: What her time and money could earn elsewhere
quiz.right: What her time and money could earn elsewhere: that normal return is counted as a cost, so zero economic profit still pays the owner.

request: Where does a recession come from, and what can a government actually do about it?

spec.title: Economics 5 · When the economy falls short

commands.speak: Where does a recession come from? The factories still stand and the workers still know their jobs, yet output falls. Everything produced in a year runs along the bottom.
Aggregate demand is all the spending there is: households, firms, government, foreigners. A lower price level makes money go further and exports cheaper, so more gets bought.
Aggregate supply is what firms produce at each price level. With wages fixed by contract for a while, better prices make them run harder.
Where the two cross is what the economy is doing this year.
This vertical line is what it could produce with everyone who wants a job working: its potential. Just now the two agree.
Lay a second demand curve over the first, and give the economy some bad news.
Firms postpone an investment, households save for a rainy day, an export market closes. Nobody produced less because they could not; nobody ordered it.
That distance is the recession: output below potential, with the factories and workers idle. Economists call it the output gap.
The price level slipped too. A slump of missing spending comes with weak prices, not inflation, and that tells you which medicine it needs.
If what is missing is spending, spending can replace it: a government that cuts taxes or builds something, a central bank that makes borrowing cheap.
Output returns to potential.
That argument is John Maynard Keynes's, published in 1936 in the middle of the slump it describes.
On this picture a recession is not an economy that cannot produce. It is one that is not being asked to, and that is a fixable kind of trouble.

quiz.question: A recession opens a gap below potential output. What is missing?
choices: Spending on what the economy can make
quiz.right: Spending. All the capacity is still there, which is why policy that lifts demand can close the gap.
quiz.wrong: Look at what actually moved in the picture: only the demand curve. The supply side never budged.

request: Hvorfor sprekker en boble, når alle vet at prisen er for høy?

commands.speak: Hvorfor sprekker en boble når alle vet at prisen er for høy, og hvorfor sprekker den ikke med en gang? Ta en aksje som er verdt hundre kroner.
Verdi betyr her det selskapet kommer til å tjene. Likevel stiger prisen, måned etter måned, langt over.
Kjøper én betaler hundre og femti. Hun vet at det er for mye, men hun regner med å selge videre.
Kjøper to betaler to hundre av samme grunn. Hun kjøper ikke selskapet; hun kjøper neste kjøper.
Hele gapet over verdien hviler på én forventning: at noen kommer og betaler enda mer. Økonomer kaller det [english:greater fool]-teorien.
Men hvorfor presser ikke skeptikerne prisen ned? De kan låne aksjer, selge dem nå, og satse på fall.
Problemet er tidspunktet. Den som satser på fall for tidlig, taper for hver måned prisen stiger, og kan gå tom for penger før fallet kommer.
Så betaler kjøper tre to hundre og seksti.
Så kommer det ikke flere nye kjøpere. Da holder ingenting prisen oppe, og alle vil ut først, samtidig.
Den som sitter med aksjen når musikken stopper, taper, som i stolleken.
Å vite at prisen er for høy er altså ikke nok. Du må vite når de andre slutter å kjøpe, og det vet ingen.
Da IT-boblen sprakk i mars 2000, falt Nasdaq-indeksen nesten åtti prosent på to og et halvt år.

quiz.question: Hvorfor selger ikke skeptikerne prisen ned med en gang?
choices: De kan tape før boblen sprekker
Det er forbudt å satse på fall
quiz.right: Den som satser på fall for tidlig, taper for hver måned prisen stiger, og kan gå tom for penger før krakket.

request: Hvordan blir en lov til i Norge?

commands.speak: Hvordan blir et forslag til en norsk lov? Veien er lengre enn én avstemning, og den starter i et departement, lenge før Stortinget ser noe.
Departementet utreder saken og sender et utkast på høring. Fristen er normalt tre måneder, og hvem som helst kan svare.
Så legger regjeringen fram en lovproposisjon for Stortinget. En stortingsrepresentant kan også fremme et eget forslag.
Stortinget sender saken til en fagkomité. Her skjer det meste av arbeidet: høringer, forhandlinger og en innstilling til salen.
Så stemmer salen, med alle 169 representantene. Første gangs behandling ender i et lovvedtak.
Fram til 2009 delte Stortinget seg i to avdelinger for lovsaker: først Odelstinget, så Lagtinget.
I dag sitter hele Stortinget samlet, men den andre sjansen er beholdt: minst tre dager senere behandles vedtaket én gang til.
Da er Stortinget ferdig. Kongen i statsråd sanksjonerer loven: Kongen skriver under, og statsministeren skriver under med.
Til slutt kunngjøres loven i Norsk Lovtidend, og den trer i kraft når vedtaket sier.
Kongen kan nekte, men bare utsette. Adelsloven ble vedtatt av tre storting, sist i 1821, og ble lov uten kongens underskrift.
Så avstemningen i salen er nesten slutten. Den som vil forme en lov, bør svare på høringen eller møte komiteen.

quiz.question: Du vil endre et lovforslag. Når har du best sjanse?
quiz.right: Tidlig: i høringen og i komiteen formes teksten, og når salen stemmer, er innholdet som regel avgjort.

request: Hva skjer med et søk i en søkemotor?

commands.speak: Hva skjer egentlig når du søker? Nesten alt har skjedd før du trykker enter. Her er nettet, krympet til tre sider.
Et program, en robot, følger lenker fra side til side og henter hver side det finner, døgnet rundt.
Så lages indeksen: for hvert ord, en liste over sidene der ordet står. Som registeret bak i en bok.
Fly står på side én og to, Bergen på én og tre. Hos Google gjelder det hundrevis av milliarder sider.
Først nå skriver du: fly bergen.
Søkemotoren leser ikke nettet nå. Det ville tatt uker.
Den har jo allerede gjort jobben.
Den slår opp de to ordene i indeksen og får to korte lister: én og to, én og tre.
Så rangeres treffene. Side én har begge ordene, og havner øverst.
Side to og tre har bare ett ord hver. Hvem av dem som kommer først, må avgjøres på en annen måte.
Én viktig ledetråd er lenkene: en lenke fra en annen side teller som en stemme for siden.
Den ideen var kjernen i PageRank, som Larry Page og Sergey Brin beskrev i 1998, samme år som Google ble grunnlagt.
Så når svaret kommer på under et sekund, er det fordi det tunge arbeidet ble gjort før du spurte.

quiz.question: Du legger ut en ny nettside i dag. Hvorfor dukker den ikke opp i søk med en gang?
choices: Roboten har ikke hentet og indeksert den ennå
Søkemotoren leter bare i gamle sider
Nye sider må betale for å vises
quiz.right: Roboten har ikke vært der ennå: et søk slår bare opp i indeksen, og siden kommer med først når den er hentet og lagt inn.

request: Hvorfor faller ikke en fallskjermhopper fortere og fortere hele veien ned?

commands.speak: Hvorfor faller ikke en fallskjermhopper fortere og fortere hele veien ned? Fordi lufta bremser hardere jo fortere du faller.
Tyngdekraften drar like hardt hele tiden. For en hopper på åtti kilo er det nesten åtte hundre newton.
I det første sekundet er lufta nesten ikke der. Farten øker med nesten ti meter per sekund: trettifem kilometer i timen.
Fortsatte det slik, ville farten vært over tusen seks hundre etter femti sekunder.
Men lufta tar imot. Etter fem sekunder er farten hundre og førti kilometer i timen…
…og luftmotstanden har vokst til halvparten av tyngden. Den vokser med farten i annen: dobbel fart, fire ganger så hard brems.
Jo nærmere luftmotstanden kommer tyngden, jo mindre er det igjen som drar deg fortere, og kurven flater ut.
Etter vel ti sekunder er de to pilene like lange. Summen av kreftene er null, og farten slutter å øke.
Det er sluttfarten: rundt to hundre kilometer i timen, med magen ned.
Sluttfarten er ingen grense noen har satt. Det er farten der lufta bremser akkurat like hardt som tyngden drar.
Når skjermen åpnes, får lufta en mye større flate å bremse, og den nye sluttfarten blir under tjue kilometer i timen.
I tynnere luft er sluttfarten høyere: Felix Baumgartner hoppet fra 39 kilometers høyde i 2012 og nådde over tretten hundre kilometer i timen.

quiz.question: Hvem får høyest sluttfart: en tung eller en lett hopper?
quiz.right: Den tunge: lufta må bremse en større tyngde, og det klarer den først ved høyere fart.

The red zone shows the surplus those ghost trades would have created—but it vanishes.

This vanishing value is deadweight loss: a pure loss to society, gained by no one.
    draw label_DWL

## Non-Linear Growth and a Mathematical Example
Now that we have seen the tax wedge, let's ask: how does the loss grow as the tax gets larger?
    axes axes x_label "Tax rate (t)" y_label "Deadweight loss (DWL)"

The deadweight loss is not proportional to the tax. It is proportional to the tax squared.
    curve dwl_curve #b5482e expr 0.5*x*x/4
    label curve_label "DWL = ½·a·t²" above-right attach_to dwl_curve

    pause 0.4

Suppose demand is Q = 100 − P and supply is Q = P. The equilibrium is Q₀ = 50 at P₀ = 50.

    pause 0.3

A per-unit tax t lowers quantity to Q₁ = 50 − t/2, creating a deadweight loss of exactly DWL = t²/4.

    pause 0.4

When t = 2, the loss is 1. When t = 4, the loss is 4. When t = 6, the loss is 9.
    text row_header "t     DWL" x 650 y 520 font_size 22
    text row_1 "t = 2   DWL = 1" x 650 y 460 font_size 20
    text row_2 "t = 4   DWL = 4" x 650 y 400 font_size 20
    text row_3 "t = 6   DWL = 9" x 650 y 340 font_size 20

Notice: double the tax, quadruple the loss. A small tax of 2 costs society 1 unit of surplus.
    mark highlight_row_1 around row_1 kind box

    pause 0.3

But a tax of 6—only three times larger—costs 9 units, nine times more.
    mark highlight_row_2 around row_2 kind box
    mark highlight_row_3 around row_3 kind box

    pause 0.3

This is why high taxes are so wasteful: each marginal increase in the tax destroys surplus at an accelerating rate.
    highlight dwl_curve effect glow

    pause 0.4

You can now see why governments must balance tax revenue against the waste it creates.

title: A tax's deadweight loss — Sonnet 5
playlist:
# How a Tax Creates a Deadweight Loss

## The Wedge and the Lost Trades
use: supply_demand
with: {"demand":{},"supply":{},"equilibrium":{"show":true,"guides":true,"label":"E0","q_label":"Q0","p_label":"P0"},"tax":{"amount":20,"side":"seller","label":"S + t"},"regions":["government_revenue","deadweight_loss"]}

    arrow gap_arrow price_sellers_point -> price_buyers_point #8f887c hidden true
    label label_t "t" left attach_to gap_arrow hidden true
    label label_Q1 "Q1" below attach_to tax_equilibrium_point hidden true

Every tax on a good does one simple thing: it splits one price into two — what the buyer pays, and what the seller keeps.
    draw axes

Here is a market before any tax: the upward supply curve S, the downward demand curve D, crossing at price P0 and quantity Q0.
    draw demand_curve label_D supply_curve label_S equilibrium_point guide_lines label_E label_Pstar label_Qstar

    pause 0.3

That crossing point is where every trade that helps both sides actually happens — nobody who would gain from trading is left out.
    point at.ref equilibrium_point gesture circle

Now a tax of size t enters: the buyer's price Pb rises above the seller's price Ps by exactly t.
    draw tax_supply_curve label_S_tax price_buyers_point label_Pb price_sellers_point label_Ps gap_arrow label_t

    pause 0.3

Quantity falls from Q0 to Q1, because at the new prices fewer trades clear both sides at once.
    draw tax_equilibrium_point tax_guide_lines label_Q1

The government collects tax revenue equal to t times Q1 — that shaded rectangle.
    draw wedge_region label_wedge

    pause 0.3

But look at the sliver between Q1 and Q0: those are trades where a buyer would have paid more than a seller needed to accept.
    draw dwl_region

Nobody captures that value anymore — not the buyer, not the seller, not the government. That triangle is pure loss.
    draw label_DWL

    pause 0.3

This is the deadweight loss: not money taken from people, but value that simply stops being created.
    highlight dwl_region effect glow

Next, we ask what happens to that triangle as the tax grows.
    point at.ref dwl_region gesture underline

## Loss Grows Faster Than the Tax
use: supply_demand
with: {"demand":{},"supply":{},"equilibrium":{"show":true},"tax":{"amount":12,"label":"S + tax"},"regions":["deadweight_loss"]}

    draw axes demand_curve label_D supply_curve label_S equilibrium_point guide_lines label_E label_Pstar label_Qstar

    pause 0.3

Now that we have seen the triangle appear, watch what happens when the tax itself gets bigger.
    draw tax_supply_curve label_S_tax tax_equilibrium_point tax_guide_lines price_buyers_point label_Pb price_sellers_point label_Ps dwl_region label_DWL

    pause 0.3

With a small tax t1, the wedge between Pb and Ps is short, and quantity barely moves — the triangle is thin.
    highlight dwl_region price_buyers_point price_sellers_point effect glow

Double the tax to t2, and two things happen at once.
    point at.ref tax_equilibrium_point gesture circle

The height of the triangle doubles, because the gap between Pb and Ps is exactly the tax.
    animate {"tax.amount":24} duration 3

But the base also grows, because a bigger price gap pushes quantity down further along both curves.
    highlight equilibrium_point tax_equilibrium_point effect circle

Area is base times height divided by two — so when both dimensions grow with the tax, the area grows with the tax squared.
    math dwl_formula top-right tex "\\text{DWL}=\\tfrac{1}{2}\\,t\\,\\Delta Q\\;\\propto\\;t^2" colors {"t":"#b5482e","\\Delta Q":"#2f6b8f"}

Double the tax, and the lost value roughly quadruples; triple it, and the loss grows ninefold.
    animate {"tax.amount":36} duration 3

This is why economists treat a modest tax as cheap in efficiency terms, and a steep one as expensive out of proportion to its size.
    highlight dwl_region effect glow

The shape of the curves you drew in the first figure already contained this — we just have not yet put numbers on it.
    point at.ref demand_curve gesture underline

## A Formula You Can Compute
domain: {"x":[0,4],"y":[0,4]}

    math eq_demand center tex "P = 10 - Q" in derivation hidden true
    math eq_supply center tex "P = Q" in derivation hidden true
    math eq_eq0 center tex "Q_0 = 5,\\quad P_0 = 5" in derivation hidden true

    math eq_example center tex "t=1:\\ DWL=0.25 \\qquad t=2:\\ DWL=1" colors.DWL #8a5fa8 colors.t #b5482e in derivation hidden true

    axes graph_axes x_label "t (tax)" y_label DWL hidden true
    curve curve_dwl #8a5fa8 expr x*x/4 hidden true

    label label_t1 "$0.25" above attach_to point_t1 hidden true

Now that we know the loss grows with the square of the tax, here is a case where we can compute it exactly.
    card title "A Formula You Can Compute" style center

Take a demand curve P = 10 − Q and a supply curve P = Q — nothing exotic, just two straight lines.
    draw eq_demand eq_supply parallel true

Without any tax they cross at Q0 = 5 and P0 = 5: that is the untaxed equilibrium.
    draw eq_eq0

Put a tax t between buyer and seller: the buyer pays Pb = 10 − Q1, the seller receives Ps = Q1, and Pb − Ps = t.
    draw eq_tax_setup

Solving that gives the new quantity: Q1 = (10 − t) / 2.
    draw eq_q1

The deadweight loss is the triangle's area: one half times its height t times its base, Q0 minus Q1.
    draw eq_dwl_formula

Substitute Q1 in, and the algebra collapses to a strikingly simple result: DWL = t² / 4.
    morph eq_dwl_formula tex "DWL = \\frac{t^2}{4}"

A one-dollar tax costs a quarter of a dollar in lost value; a two-dollar tax costs a full dollar — four times as much for twice the tax.
    draw eq_example

    draw graph_axes

Plot DWL against t and you get a parabola, not a line — the curve itself is the proof of what we saw in the last part.
    draw curve_dwl label_curve point_t1 label_t1 point_t2 label_t2

That is the whole arc: a tax splits one price into two, the gap between them cancels trades that would have paid off, and because both sides of that lost region grow with the tax, the loss itself compounds — visible now as the widening curve on this page.
    highlight curve_dwl eq_dwl_formula effect glow

Check it: 10 gives 25, 20 gives 100, 50 gives 625 — and a tax of 100 gives 2500, which is the entire surplus this market ever had, collected as revenue of zero.
    draw tab

Revenue meanwhile is t times 100 minus t, over two — the hump that tops out at t equals 50.
    draw req

And because loss goes with the square, splitting a tax beats concentrating it: one market taxed at 20 destroys 100 and raises 800, while two similar markets taxed at 10 destroy 25 each and raise 900.
    draw c1 c2 c3 c_lab1 c_lab2

Broad base, low rate is not a slogan — it is t squared divided by four.
    highlight eq8 effect glow

You can now read any tax as three objects at once: a rectangle that changes hands, a triangle that disappears, and a square that decides how fast that triangle grows.
    focus m_rect m_tri eq8 delivery grave

request: Why do bridges come in so many different shapes?

commands.speak: Why do bridges come in so many shapes? Every bridge carries a load across a gap, but materials break in different ways.
Start with a plank on two piers. Load the middle and it sags: the top is squeezed, in blue, and the underside stretched, in red.
Stone takes a squeeze well but cracks when stretched, so a stone beam can only ever be short.
The Romans' answer was to curve the load into an arch.
Now every stone is pushed against its neighbours and none is pulled apart. All blue — exactly what stone is good at.
Iron and steel handle both kinds of force, so engineers could return to a straight beam — built as triangles.
The top chord is squeezed and the bottom one stretched, like the plank, with most of the material taken out. The diagonals alternate.
Go further and hang the road from a cable slung between two towers.
The cable only pulls, which steel wire does better than anything, and the towers only push.
That split is how the Golden Gate's main span reaches almost thirteen hundred metres.
The cable-stayed bridge runs straight cables from a tower down to the deck.
The stays pull and the tower pushes, and because every stay tugs the deck towards the tower, the deck itself is squeezed.
France's Millau Viaduct, the tallest bridge in the world, is built this way.
Now put all five side by side. Every design sends part of the load through something that is squeezed.
And all but one pair it with something stretched. The arch has no red at all.
Those two are mirror images. Robert Hooke put it in 1675: as a hanging chain hangs, so, turned upside down, the rigid arch will stand.

quiz.question: Which of the five uses no tension at all?
quiz.right: The arch — curving the load means every stone is squeezed and none is stretched.
quiz.wrong: That one has red in it — something is stretched. Look for the bridge with only blue.

request: Why are floor tiles squares or hexagons, but never pentagons?

commands.speak: Why do floors use squares and hexagons, but never regular pentagons? Where tiles meet at a corner, their angles must make one full turn: 360 degrees.
A triangle's corner is 60 degrees, and six of them close the turn exactly.
A square's corner is 90: four of them fit.
A pentagon's corner is 108.
Put three pentagon corners together at one point, and they cover 324 degrees.
Thirty-six degrees are left over: too small for a fourth corner, which would overlap. No floor.
A hexagon's corner is 120.
Widen each corner from 108 to 120, and three of them close the turn exactly.
Seven sides give about 128.6 degrees: two corners are too few, three too many.
Eight give 135, the same problem. That is why an octagon floor always needs little squares in the gaps.
Only 60, 90 and 120 go into 360 a whole number of times, so only three regular shapes tile a floor on their own.
Drop 'regular', though, and pentagons can tile. Fifteen lopsided kinds are known; the last was found in 2015, and in 2017 the list was proved complete.

quiz.question: Why can't regular pentagons tile a floor?
choices: They have an odd number of sides
quiz.right: Three corners make 324° and four make 432°: no whole number of them makes a full turn.
quiz.wrong: Triangles have an odd number of sides and tile perfectly; it is the corner angle that decides.

request: Why does gravity rule the universe if it's the weakest force?

elements.text: light, chemistry, the push of a hand
turns protons into neutrons in the Sun
the weakest of all, and it only attracts

commands.speak: Why does the weakest force rule planets and galaxies? Physicists count four forces. Strongest first: the strong force, which holds every atomic nucleus together.
But it reaches barely across one nucleus, about a millionth of a billionth of a metre. Orange marks a short reach.
Electromagnetism is light, every chemical bond, and the reason your hand stops at a table. Purple: it reaches without limit.
The weak force turns one particle into another. The Sun's fusion needs it, and it too stops inside a nucleus.
And gravity, so feeble that a fridge magnet beats the pull of the whole Earth.
Between two protons, their electric push is about ten to the thirty-six times stronger than their gravity.
So why does the weakest win? The two nuclear forces vanish beyond an atom, so across space they drop out.
Of the two with endless reach, electric charge comes as plus and minus, and matter holds almost exactly equal amounts. They cancel.
Mass has no minus. Every kilogram adds to the pull, and a planet's worth adds up.
The cancelling is astonishingly exact. Feynman: two people at arm's length, with one per cent extra electrons each, would repel with enough force to lift the Earth.
So on the scale of planets, gravity is the only force left standing: the weakest, but never cancelled.

quiz.question: The electric force is far stronger. Why doesn't it steer the planets?
quiz.right: Planets hold almost equal plus and minus charge, so the electric pulls cancel, while every kilogram adds to gravity.

request: How long does each kind of note last in music?

commands.speak: How long does each note last? Its shape tells you, before its pitch does. The whole note, an open oval, lasts four beats.
Give it a stem and it lasts half as long: two beats.
Fill the head in, and halve it again: one beat, the one you tap your foot to.
A flag on the stem halves it once more: half a beat.
Two flags, a quarter of a beat. Every new mark says the same thing: halve it.
So one whole note lasts as long as sixteen of these.
The British still call the whole note a semibreve, half a 'short' note. Medieval music had notes so long that the breve counted as short.

quiz.question: How many eighth notes fill one half note?
quiz.right: Four: a half note is two beats, and each eighth lasts half a beat.

request: Why doesn't the Moon fall down onto the Earth?

commands.speak: Why doesn't the Moon fall onto the Earth? It does fall, all the time. Newton showed why it never lands, with a cannon on an impossibly tall mountain.
Fire a ball sideways, gently, and it curves down and lands close by.
Fire harder and it lands farther away, and by now the ground has begun to curve away beneath it.
At about eight kilometres a second, the ground curves away exactly as fast as the ball falls. It falls forever: an orbit.
Faster still, past eleven kilometres a second, and it falls too slowly ever to come back.
Every closed orbit lies between these two. The space station's is close to the first, at almost eight kilometres a second.
The Moon is the same ball, sixty Earth radii out, moving sideways at about one kilometre a second.
In that second it falls just 1.4 millimetres towards us: exactly enough to bend its path round the Earth.
Newton checked that number against an apple, which falls 4.9 metres in its first second.
Sixty times farther from the Earth's centre, gravity is sixty squared, 3,600 times weaker.
And 4.9 metres over 3,600 is 1.4 millimetres. The Moon falls exactly as an apple would, that far away.
So the pull that drops the apple is the one that holds the Moon. It never lands only because it keeps moving sideways.

quiz.question: If the Moon stopped moving sideways, what would happen?
choices: It would fall straight to Earth
It would stay where it is
quiz.right: It would fall straight in: gravity pulls on it all the time, and only its sideways speed makes it keep missing.

request: How do the two hands share a piano score?

params.notes: E4:q E4:q F4:q G4:q G4:q F4:q E4:q D4:q

commands.speak: How do two hands share one page of piano music? It is written on two staves at once. The top one holds the higher notes, mostly the right hand's.
The bottom staff, with the bass clef, holds the low notes: the left hand. The brace says: read these two together.

commands.play: E4:q E4:q F4:q G4:q G4:q F4:q E4:q D4:q
commands.speak: The right hand plays the tune.
The left hand holds long, low notes underneath.
Notes stacked straight above one another are played at the same moment. That is why the two staves line up by beat.

play.notes: E4:q E4:q F4:q G4:q G4:q F4:q E4:q D4:q

commands.speak: Both hands together.
One staff alone could not hold both: the tune and the bass lie more than an octave apart, and would need a ladder of extra lines between them.

quiz.question: When are notes stacked across the staves played?
quiz.right: At the same moment: the two staves line up by beat, so notes stacked in line sound together.

request: Can I write the end of a melody myself?

commands.speak: Can you finish a melody yourself? Every tune is a question and an answer: I'll ask the question, and you write the answer.
Four notes climbing, one white key and one line or space at a time. It sounds unfinished, like a question.
Your turn: click the staff after my notes, or press the keys, and write four notes that sound like an answer. Try ending on C, then press Continue.
Here is the whole line, question and answer.
A tune that comes home to the note it started from sounds finished. That pull back to C is what musicians call the tonic.

quiz.question: Which last note makes this tune sound finished?
quiz.right: C: a tune that comes home to its tonic, the note its scale is built on, sounds finished.

request: How do musicians hear where a note goes on the staff?

commands.speak: How do musicians write down a tune they only hear? It starts with one skill: hearing how high a note is.
Higher notes sit higher on the staff, one line or space per step. This is middle C, on its own little line below.
And this is G, five steps higher, and it sounds it.
Now just listen.

ask.question: Where does that note go? Click it on the staff.
ask.right: E: the bottom line, between the C and the G.

commands.speak: Five more, and you choose. Press the speaker to hear a note again.
You placed {ears} of {ears.total}. Every musician's ear is trained exactly this way, one note at a time.

request: Why do cellos and tubas read a different clef?

params.notes: C2:q E2:q G2:q C3:q E3:q G3:q C4:h

commands.speak: Why do cellos and tubas read a different clef? Their notes lie far below the treble staff, and written there they would hang from a ladder of extra lines.
So low instruments use the bass clef. Its two dots sit either side of the fourth line: that line is F, below middle C.
Up a C major chord, from deep C to middle C: every note sits comfortably on the staff.
And middle C, at the top, is the same note the treble staff writes on a ledger line below it. The two staves meet there.
The clefs are letters in disguise: the treble clef is a curly G, and this one is an old-fashioned F.

quiz.question: Which letter does the bass clef's line mark?
quiz.right: F: the two dots surround the F line, below middle C.

request: What do the two numbers at the start of a piece of music mean?

commands.speak: What do the two stacked numbers at the start of a piece mean? They tell you how to feel the beat. Four over four: four beats in every bar.

commands.play: C3:q E4+G4:q C3:q E4+G4:q C3:q E4+G4:q C3:q E4+G4:q
commands.speak: Each beat is a quarter note. Count it, one, two, three, four: a march, left, right, left, right.
Change the top number to three, and every bar has three beats.

commands.play: C3:q E4+G4:q E4+G4:q C3:q E4+G4:q E4+G4:q
commands.speak: Now it sways: ONE two three, ONE two three. That is a waltz.
Sometimes four-four is written as a C. It looks like C for common time, but it began as a broken circle.
In medieval music a full circle meant counting in threes, the 'perfect' number, and a broken circle meant counting in twos.
The top number counts the beats in a bar; the bottom one says which note gets one beat.

quiz.question: Which time signature makes a waltz?
quiz.right: Three-four: three beats a bar, ONE two three.

request: How do I read the notes on the treble staff?

params.notes: E4:q G4:q B4:q D5:q F5:q F4:q A4:q C5:q E5:q

commands.speak: How do you read the notes on the treble staff? It looks like a secret code, but two short sentences are the whole key.
First the five lines, from the bottom up.
E, G, B, D, F: Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit.
And the four spaces between them.
F, A, C, E: the spaces spell a word, FACE.
Your turn: find five notes on the staff. Say the sentences under your breath.
You found {read} of {read.total}. Two sentences, and every note on the staff has a name.

request: What do the sharp, flat and natural signs do in music?

commands.speak: What do the sharp, flat and natural signs do? A sharp raises the next note by the smallest step on a piano: C to the black key above.
A flat lowers it by the same half step: E down to the black key below.
And a natural cancels either one: the note goes back to its white key.
The shapes are old. Medieval scribes wrote B two ways: a round b for the lower, softer B, and a square b for the higher one.
The round b became the flat; the square one became both the natural and the sharp.

quiz.question: A sharp in front of C sends you to…
choices: the black key just above C
the black key just below C
quiz.right: The black key just above C: a sharp raises by a half step, the smallest step on a piano.

request: Why do network engineers talk about layers?

spec.title: The internet as a stack of layers

card.title: The internet as a stack of layers

commands.speak: At the bottom sits the link layer: the cable or the radio that carries bits to the next machine.
On top of it, the internet layer gives every machine an address and finds a route across many links.
The transport layer turns those loose packets into a reliable conversation between two programs.
And at the top, the application layer: the web, email, a video call.
Each layer only talks to the one below it. A web page never needs to know whether it travelled by fibre or by Wi-Fi.

quiz.question: You swap your Wi-Fi for a network cable. Which layer changed?
quiz.right: The link layer. Everything above it carries on as before, which is the whole point of stacking them.

request: What happens between my browser and a website's database?

commands.speak: Your request first reaches a load balancer, the small box at the front door.
Behind it stand two identical app servers. Either one can answer you.
The balancer hands each request to whichever server is less busy, so no single machine gets swamped.
A server first checks the cache, a fast memory of recent answers.
Only when the cache has nothing does it ask the database, the slow but permanent store.
That is why a popular page loads quickly: most visits never reach the database at all.

request: How much water fits in a glass 6 cm wide and 8 cm tall?

commands.speak: A straight glass is a cylinder: a circle, stacked up to a height.
Six centimetres across means a radius of three.
And it stands eight centimetres tall.
The base circle covers pi times three squared, about twenty-eight square centimetres. Stack that eight high: pi times nine times eight, about two hundred and twenty-six cubic centimetres.

quiz.question: About how much water does the glass hold?
quiz.right: About 226 ml. One cubic centimetre holds one millilitre.

request: What does a tax really cost — beyond the money it raises?

commands.speak: A tax raises money. But what does it cost, beyond the money? Take a six-dollar tax on every concert ticket.
Fans first: the cheaper the ticket, the more tickets they buy.
Organisers: the higher the price, the more shows they put on.
Without the tax, they meet here.
Now the tax. Organisers must hand six dollars to the state for every ticket, so they need six dollars more for each show: supply shifts up.
The market settles again. Fans pay more, organisers keep less: the six dollars is split between them.
In numbers: fans pay about three dollars more, organisers get about three dollars less.
And fewer tickets are sold.
On every ticket still sold, the state collects six dollars: this rectangle.
And this triangle is the rest of the cost: tickets that are no longer sold at all.

Each of those was worth more to a fan than it cost to put on the show. Now the show never happens — and nobody gets that value: not the state, not the fans, not the organisers. Economists call it the deadweight loss.
Now double the tax.
The loss does not double — it roughly quadruples. More tickets vanish, and each one lost was worth more.
Back to six dollars.
How big the triangle is depends on how much people respond. For something they buy anyway — insulin, fuel for the drive to work — demand is steep.
Then few purchases vanish, so the loss is small — but buyers carry most of the tax. A small loss and a fair tax are not the same thing.
Your turn: drag the taxed curve up and down, and watch the rectangle and the triangle.

quiz.question: If a tax is doubled, the deadweight loss…
quiz.right: Roughly quadruples: twice as many tickets vanish, and each one lost was worth about twice as much.

request: What makes a disease severe — and does it matter how we measure it?

details.shortfall_region: Absolute shortfall = QALYs expected without the disease − QALYs expected with it, from the age of diagnosis: $$47.7 - 17.2 = 30.5$$ (30.4 before rounding).
details.shortfall_region_2: Proportional shortfall = the absolute shortfall as a share of what was expected: $$\frac{17.3 - 1.8}{17.3} \approx 90\%$$ Anna’s is $30.4 / 47.7 \approx 64\%$.

commands.speak: Many health services give extra priority to severe diseases. But what makes a disease severe? Two patients show that the answer depends on how you measure it.
This dashed line is a normal life in our sketch: quality of life from one, perfect health, slowly falling, to death at about 82.
Anna falls ill at 25. Without treatment she lives to 55, in much poorer health.
What she could have expected from 25 on, but loses, is this area — quality of life times years, counted in QALYs.
She could have expected about 48 QALYs. She keeps 17 — this area. She loses 30, almost two thirds.
Bjørn falls ill at 60 and dies at 66, in very poor health.
He could have expected about 17 QALYs. He keeps under two: he loses 15.5 — nine tenths of what he had left.
So whose disease is the more severe?
Take Anna’s loss out of the figure…
…and Bjørn’s, and set them side by side.
Count the QALYs lost — the absolute shortfall — and Anna’s is about twice the size: 30 against 15. Norway measures severity this way.
Now measure each loss against what was expected. Bjørn could expect this whole area; his loss fills nine tenths of it.
Anna’s loss fills about two thirds of hers. Count the share lost — the proportional shortfall — and Bjørn’s is the more severe: 90 percent against 64. The Netherlands measures it this way.

The absolute measure counts the health actually lost, and a young patient has the most to lose. Its weakness: an old person facing a terrible prognosis can never count as very severe — too few years are left to lose.
The proportional measure calls a disease severe when it takes almost everything you had left, at any age. Its weakness: it ranks losing thirty QALYs below losing fifteen.
A third view looks back instead of forward: fair innings — the health a person gets over a whole life. Anna, all of hers: about 40 QALYs.
Bjørn, all of his: about 55. He has had most of his innings; she has not — so this view favours Anna even more, and it is openly about age.
None of these is neutral; each is a value judgement. England’s NICE uses both measures: a disease counts as severe if either loss is large.

quiz.question: Which measure ranks Bjørn’s disease as the more severe?
quiz.right: The proportional shortfall: he loses 90 percent of the health he had left, Anna 64.

request: What are the different ways a drawcast can use a piece of code?
playlist:
playlist:
  title: One script, five ways
  advance: auto
  gap: 1
---
title: 1 · Code you never see
template: bar_chart
params:
  labels: ["10", "100", "1,000", "10,000"]
  values: "{coin.share}"
  ylim: [0, 100]
  y_label: "Heads (%)"
  x_label: "Flips"
  box: { x: 60, y: 95, w: 620, h: 520 }
elements:
  - id: coin
    type: code
    language: r
    show: none
    code: |-
      set.seed(42)
      flips <- rbinom(10000, 1, 0.5)
      n <- c(10, 100, 1000, 10000)
      share <- sapply(n, function(k) round(100 * mean(flips[1:k]), 1))
      first <- share[1]
      last <- share[4]
  - { id: note_first, type: text, text: "10 flips: {coin.first}% heads", x: 840, y: 480, font_size: 26 }
  - { id: note_last, type: text, text: "10,000 flips: {coin.last}%", x: 840, y: 430, font_size: 26 }
commands:
  - card: { title: "One script, five ways" }
  - draw: [axes, bar_1, bar_2, bar_3, bar_4]
    parallel: true
    speak: "The same small idea, how often a fair coin lands heads, used five ways. First, code you never see: R flips a coin ten thousand times and hands the numbers to an ordinary drawcast chart."
  - draw: [note_first, note_last]
    speak: "Even the notes on the side are the script's numbers, written into the author's own text: ten flips gave eighty percent heads — a loaded coin, you might think — while ten thousand gave fifty."
---
title: 2 · A picture drawn by code
elements:
  - id: walk
    type: code
    language: r
    show: output
    width: 820
    code: |-
      library(ggplot2)
      set.seed(3)
      flips <- rbinom(2000, 1, 0.5)
      df <- data.frame(n = seq_along(flips), share = cumsum(flips) / seq_along(flips))
      ggplot(df, aes(n, share)) + geom_line() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") + labs(x = "Flips", y = "Share of heads")
commands:
  - card: { title: "A picture drawn by code" }
  - draw: [walk, walk_out]
    speak: "Second, a picture that is easier to make in code: the share of heads after every single flip. The code stays hidden, and the chart is drawn in drawcast's own ink and paper."
  - highlight: { target: [walk_out] }
    speak: "Wild at first, then settling on one half. Anyone curious can still open the script from the tray."
---
title: 3 · Knobs to turn
elements:
  - id: knob
    type: code
    language: r
    pane: controls
    width: 820
    controls: [p, n]
    code: |-
      library(ggplot2)
      p <- Slider(0.1, 0.9, step = 0.05, default = 0.5, label = "Chance of heads")
      n <- Slider(50, 2000, default = 500, label = "Flips")
      set.seed(3)
      flips <- rbinom(n, 1, p)
      df <- data.frame(n = seq_along(flips), share = cumsum(flips) / seq_along(flips))
      ggplot(df, aes(n, share)) + geom_line() + geom_hline(yintercept = p, linetype = "dashed") + ylim(0, 1) + labs(x = "Flips", y = "Share of heads")
commands:
  - card: { title: "Knobs to turn" }
  - draw: [knob, knob_out, knob_ctl_p, knob_ctl_n]
    speak: "Third, the same chart with knobs: the chance of heads, and the number of flips."
  - run: { code: knob, values: { p: [0.5, 0.7] } }
    speak: "Bend the coin to seventy percent heads, and the share settles on seventy instead."
  - explore: { code: knob }
    speak: "Your turn: try a very short run, and see how far from the truth it can land."
---
title: 4 · Reading the code
elements:
  - id: lesson
    type: code
    language: r
    show: left
    width: 900
    marks: ["cumsum(flips) / seq_along(flips)"]
    code: |-
      library(ggplot2)
      set.seed(3)
      flips <- rbinom(200, 1, 0.5)
      share <- cumsum(flips) / seq_along(flips)
      df <- data.frame(n = seq_along(flips), share = share)
      ggplot(df, aes(n, share)) + geom_line()
commands:
  - card: { title: "Reading the code" }
  - draw: [lesson, lesson_line_1, lesson_line_2]
    parallel: true
    speak: "Fourth, a lesson about the code itself, so it keeps R's own look. Load the plotting package, and fix the random seed so the run can be repeated."
  - draw: [lesson_line_3]
    speak: "rbinom flips two hundred coins: each a one for heads or a zero for tails."
  - draw: [lesson_line_4]
    speak: "The running share: add up the heads so far, and divide by the number of flips so far."
  - draw: [lesson_mark_1]
    speak: "cumsum is the running total; seq_along counts one, two, three, and so on."
  - draw: [lesson_line_5, lesson_line_6]
    speak: "Put both in a table, and draw the line."
  - draw: [lesson_out]
    speak: "And here it is, exactly as R draws it."
  - explore: { code: lesson }
    speak: "Change two hundred to twenty, run it, and watch how rough a short run is."
---

elements:
  - id: c64
    type: code
    language: basic
    frame: c64
    width: 620
    code: |-
      10 H=0
      20 FOR I=1 TO 100
      30 IF RND(1)<0.5 THEN H=H+1
      40 NEXT I
      50 PRINT "HEADS IN 100:";H
commands:
  - card: { title: "The same idea in 1982" }
  - draw: [c64, c64_line_1, c64_line_2, c64_line_3, c64_line_4, c64_line_5]
    speak: "Fifth, the same idea on a Commodore 64: flip a hundred coins in BASIC and count the heads."
  - draw: [c64_out]
    speak: "The machine agrees: about half. Five uses, one idea — the code hidden, drawn, turned, read, or run on the machine itself."

request: What does a treatment gain, measured in QALYs?

details.gain_regions: A QALY is one year in full health. Each year counts by its quality: $$\text{QALYs} = \sum_{\text{years}} \text{quality} \times \text{time}$$ so the area between the two paths is the QALYs the treatment adds.
details.net_note: Net gain = QALYs gained − QALYs lost to side effects. Cost per QALY = extra cost ÷ net gain: $$\frac{£200{,}000}{10.7} \approx £19{,}000$$

commands.speak: How do you measure what a treatment gives a patient? Health economists answer with an area. Take Kari, just diagnosed with cancer.
Without treatment, her quality of life falls from 0.65, and she dies within ten years.
With treatment she feels worse at first — the side effects — then better than before, and she lives twenty-four years.
This red sliver is what the treatment costs her early on.
And the green area is what it gives: every extra year counted by how good it is. That is what a quality-adjusted life year, a QALY, measures.
About two of them come from better years, while she would have been alive anyway…
…and about nine from years she would not have had at all.
Gained minus lost: close to eleven QALYs.

Is that worth paying for? Say the treatment costs two hundred thousand pounds. That is about nineteen thousand pounds per QALY — inside the twenty to thirty thousand that England's NICE has long used as its yardstick.
But suppose it only kept her alive for fourteen years.
The gain falls to about four and a half QALYs, and the same price becomes about forty-three thousand pounds per QALY. Same drug, same price: whether it is worth it depends on the area.

quiz.question: Which adds more QALYs?
choices: One extra year in full health
quiz.right: One year in full health is one QALY; two years at 0.4 are only 0.8.
